A help-desk ticket shows a PC with 169.254.33.7, so the analyst checks the cable and the DHCP server first. Broadcast addressesIETF RFC 919 / RFC 922 · Concept · Layer 3 · Current 255.255.255.255 is the limited broadcast; the all-ones host address of a subnet (e.g. 192.168.1.255) is its directed broadcast. A DHCP Discover is sent to 255.255.255.255 because the new PC does not yet know any addresses. Network and host portionsIETF RFC 950 · Concept · Layer 3 The mask marks which bits name the network and which name the host; the all-zeros host is the network address. In 172.16.5.40/16, the network is 172.16.0.0 and the host portion is 5.40. Default gatewayIETF RFC 1122 · Concept · Layer 3 The router a host sends packets to when the destination is outside its own subnet. A printer with a wrong gateway can print locally but cannot send scan-to-email messages to the cloud mail server. Unspecified / 'this network' 0.0.0.0IETF RFC 6890 · Concept · Layer 3 Means 'no address yet' as a source, 'all interfaces' to a server, and 'any destination' as the default route 0.0.0.0/0. A server listening on 0.0.0.0:443 accepts HTTPS connections on every one of its IP addresses. Documentation rangesIETF RFC 5737 · RFC · Layer 3 · Current 192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24 and 203.0.113.0/24 are reserved for examples in books and manuals. A training guide shows a firewall rule for 203.0.113.10 so nobody accidentally copies a real company's address. Special-purpose address registryIETF RFC 6890 / IANA · RFC · Layer 3 · Current The official list of reserved IPv4 and IPv6 blocks and what each may be used for. Engineers check the IANA registry when building 'bogon' filters that block reserved addresses at the Internet edge. IPv4 exhaustionIANA / Regional Internet Registries · Concept · Layer 3 IANA handed out its last free /8 blocks in February 2011; regional registries ran dry afterwards (RIPE NCC in November 2019). A start-up buying IPv4 space today pays on the transfer market or leases addresses instead of getting them free. Shared Address Space (CGNAT) 100.64.0.0/10IETF RFC 6598 · RFC · Layer 3 · Current A block reserved for ISPs between their carrier-grade NAT and customers' routers, so it never clashes with RFC 1918 ranges. A mobile phone shows 100.72.14.9 as its address because the carrier shares public IPv4 addresses using CGNAT. Regional Internet Registries (RIRs)ARIN, RIPE NCC, APNIC, LACNIC, AFRINIC under IANA · Organisation Five organisations that allocate IP addresses and AS numbers to ISPs and companies in their region. A European hosting company becomes a RIPE NCC member to receive IPv6 space and an AS number.

docs.title: 3.2 Subnetting & CIDR
docs.text:
Subnetting means cutting one big network into smaller ones by borrowing bits from the host part of the address. CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) writes the size of a network as a slash number, such as /24, which says how many bits belong to the network. Smaller subnets mean less broadcast noise, better security boundaries and less wasted address space.

Usable hosts per prefix. Every bit you move from host to network halves the subnet: each step left of /30 doubles the hosts.

Think of it like…

Subnetting is like dividing a large office floor into separate rooms with walls: same building (the original network), but each team gets its own room (subnet) with its own door (gateway).

Real-world example

Riverbend Dental has 192.168.10.0/24 and needs 4 equal subnets. Borrowing 2 bits gives /26 (mask 255.255.255.192), block size 64, 62 usable hosts each. Subnet 1: network 192.168.10.0, hosts .1–.62, broadcast .63. Subnet 2: network .64, hosts .65–.126, broadcast .127. Subnet 3: network .128, hosts .129–.190, broadcast .191. Subnet 4: network .192, hosts .193–.254, broadcast .255.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Work out how many subnets (or hosts per subnet) you need.
  2. Borrow enough host bits: 2^n subnets for n borrowed bits; usable hosts = 2^h − 2 for h host bits.
  3. Find the block size: 256 minus the interesting mask octet (e.g. 256 − 192 = 64).
  4. List networks in steps of the block size; first address = network, last = broadcast, everything between = hosts.
  5. With VLSM, allocate the largest subnets first, then fit smaller ones into the remaining space.
  6. Summarise contiguous subnets into one shorter prefix to keep routing tables small.

Who uses it

Network engineers, cloud architects designing VPCs, and anyone sitting CompTIA Network+ or Cisco CCNA must subnet quickly and accurately.

Key takeaway

Learn the cheat sheet by heart: /24 = 254 hosts, /25 = 126, /26 = 62, /27 = 30, /28 = 14, /29 = 6, /30 = 2.

Going deeper

  • The 'magic number' (256 minus the last non-255 mask octet) works in any octet: a /20 has mask 255.255.240.0, so subnets step 0, 16, 32, 48 in the third octet.
  • To summarise, write the networks in binary and keep the common leading bits: 172.16.8.0/24 to 172.16.15.0/24 share 21 bits, so they become 172.16.8.0/21.
  • Cloud subnets lose extra addresses: AWS and Azure reserve five per subnet (network, three provider addresses and the last), so a /28 gives 11 usable hosts, not 14.
  • IPv6 subnetting is easier: LANs are always /64, and splitting on 4-bit nibble boundaries (/48 → /52 → /56 → /60 → /64) keeps addresses readable.
  • The old rule of 2^n − 2 subnets (avoiding 'subnet zero' and the all-ones subnet) is obsolete; modern equipment uses all 2^n subnets.
  • Good VLSM designs sort requirements largest first, leave 20-30% growth room, and keep each site inside one summarisable block so the routing table stays small.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Forgetting to subtract 2 for network and broadcast addresses: a /26 has 64 addresses but only 62 usable hosts (the /31 and /32 exceptions aside).
  • Using a host address as the subnet ID, e.g. 192.168.1.20/27; the correct network is 192.168.1.0/27 because blocks start on multiples of 32.
  • Overlapping subnets when allocating VLSM or cloud VPCs; overlapping CIDRs later block VPC peering, VPN routing and mergers.
  • Typing a subnet mask where Cisco ACLs or OSPF network statements expect a wildcard mask (0.0.0.255, not 255.255.255.0).

docs.title: Try it: Calculate subnet details with a subnet calculator (Linux)
docs.text:
ipcalc 192.168.10.64/26
# or in Python:
python -c "import ipaddress;n=ipaddress.ip_network('192.168.10.0/24');print([str(s) for s in n.subnets(new_prefix=26)])"

docs.title: 3.3 IPv6
docs.text:
IPv6 is the newer version of the Internet Protocol, using 128-bit addresses written in hexadecimal, like 2001:db8::1. It provides so many addresses that every device can have a globally unique one without NAT. Devices can configure themselves automatically, and most modern networks run IPv4 and IPv6 side by side.

IPv4 vs IPv6 at a glance

IPv4 IPv6 Address size 32 bits (~4.3 billion) 128 bits (~3.4 × 10^38) Written as 192.168.1.20 2001:db8:4a:10::42 Header 20-60 bytes, checksum 40 bytes fixed, no checksum Address resolution ARP (broadcast) NDP (ICMPv6 multicast) Auto-configuration DHCP or APIPA SLAAC and/or DHCPv6 Fragmentation Sender or routers Sender only (min MTU 1280) Private space RFC 1918 + NAT ULA fd00::/8; NAT rarely needed Loopback 127.0.0.1 ::1

IPv6 is not just longer addresses: broadcast, ARP, header checksum and router fragmentation are all gone.

Think of it like…

If IPv4 is a city phone book that has run out of numbers, IPv6 is a new numbering plan with enough numbers for every grain of sand to have its own phone line.

Real-world example

Ahmed's phone joins his home Wi-Fi and immediately gets fe80::1c2a:4bff:fe11:9a3d (link-local). The router sends a Router Advertisement with prefix 2001:db8:4a:10::/64, so the phone builds its own global address with SLAAC. The full address 2001:0db8:004a:0010:0000:0000:0000:0042 shortens to 2001:db8:4a:10::42 by dropping leading zeros and replacing one run of all-zero groups with '::'. YouTube now reaches him over IPv6 with no NAT in the way.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. An address is 128 bits written as eight groups of four hex digits separated by colons.
  2. Shorten it: drop leading zeros in each group, and replace one longest run of all-zero groups with '::' (only once).
  3. Every interface automatically has a link-local fe80:: address for talking on the local link.
  4. Routers advertise the network prefix (normally a /64); hosts use SLAAC, DHCPv6, or both, to build global addresses.
  5. Packets use a simpler fixed 40-byte header; there is no broadcast, multicast is used instead.
  6. Dual stack runs IPv4 and IPv6 together while the world migrates.

Who uses it

Mobile carriers, cloud providers, ISPs and large enterprises run IPv6 at scale; around half of Google's users reached it over IPv6 by 2026.

Key takeaway

You may use '::' only once in an address, and a standard LAN subnet is always a /64.

Going deeper

  • The 128-bit space holds about 3.4 × 10^38 addresses; one /64 alone has 18.4 quintillion interface IDs, which is why scanning IPv6 subnets address-by-address is impractical.
  • Extension headers are chained by the Next Header field: Hop-by-Hop (0), Routing (43), Fragment (44), ESP (50), AH (51), Destination Options (60), then TCP (6) or UDP (17).
  • An interface normally holds several addresses at once: link-local, one or more global addresses, temporary privacy addresses and possibly a ULA; RFC 6724 rules choose the source address.
  • Router Advertisement flags decide configuration: A (autonomous) allows SLAAC, M asks hosts to use stateful DHCPv6 and O offers extra options; the default gateway always comes from RAs.
  • Transition tools: dual stack is the default, NAT64/DNS64 and 464XLAT serve IPv6-only mobile networks, and old tunnels such as 6to4 and Teredo are deprecated.
  • Reverse DNS for IPv6 uses ip6.arpa with every hex nibble reversed, so automated tooling, not hand-written zone files, is normal in practice.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Writing '::' twice in one address (2001::db8::1); it becomes ambiguous, so only one run of zero groups may be compressed.
  • Using a LAN prefix longer than /64; SLAAC and many features assume 64-bit interface IDs, so keep /64 on every LAN segment.
  • Believing IPv6 is insecure 'because there is no NAT'; a stateful firewall gives the same inbound protection without address translation.
  • Blocking all ICMPv6 like old IPv4 habits; Neighbour Discovery, router discovery and Path MTU Discovery all stop working.

docs.title: Try it: Check your IPv6 addresses and test IPv6 connectivity
docs.text:
ipconfig                 # Windows: look for 'IPv6 Address' and 'Link-local'
ip -6 addr show          # Linux
ping -6 google.com

It explains why ff02::1 reaches all nodes on a link and ::1 is loopback. docs.title: 3.4 NAT & Address Translation
docs.text:
Network Address Translation (NAT) is a router feature that rewrites IP addresses (and often port numbers) as packets pass through. It lets many devices with private addresses share one or a few public addresses. It was created to save IPv4 addresses, and it also hides internal addresses from the outside world.

PAT rewriting a web request. The router changes the source on the way out and the destination on the way back, using its translation table.

Think of it like…

NAT is like a company receptionist: outsiders only know the main phone number, and the receptionist keeps a list of which extension asked for which call so replies get to the right desk.

Real-world example

The Okafor family has 12 devices on 192.168.0.0/24 but only one public address, 198.51.100.23. When a laptop at 192.168.0.15:51544 opens a website, the router rewrites the source to 198.51.100.23:40001 and records this mapping. The reply arrives on port 40001, the router looks up its table and forwards it to 192.168.0.15:51544. For their game server, they add a port-forwarding rule so incoming traffic on UDP 27015 goes to 192.168.0.40.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. An inside host sends a packet with its private source address.
  2. The NAT router replaces the source address (and port, for PAT) with a public one.
  3. It stores the mapping in a translation table.
  4. Replies to the public address and port are matched against the table and rewritten back.
  5. Unsolicited inbound traffic is dropped unless a static NAT or port-forwarding rule exists.

Who uses it

Every home router, office firewall and mobile carrier uses NAT; VoIP and video-call apps rely on STUN, TURN and ICE to work through it.

Key takeaway

PAT (NAT overload) is what home routers do: many inside hosts share one public IP, distinguished by port numbers.

Going deeper

  • One public address offers about 64,000 usable source ports per protocol, so CGNAT gear hands each subscriber a block (often 512 to a few thousand ports) and logs it for legal traceability.
  • Mappings expire: RFC 4787 asks UDP mappings to last at least two minutes and RFC 5382 asks established TCP mappings to survive at least 2 hours 4 minutes of idleness.
  • Application Level Gateways rewrite addresses embedded in payloads (FTP, SIP); the SIP ALG on cheap routers is notorious for breaking VoIP and is usually disabled.
  • Hairpinning (NAT loopback) lets an inside host reach another inside host via the public address; without it, internal users cannot open their own port-forwarded service by its public name.
  • On Linux, nftables or iptables implement NAT with SNAT/MASQUERADE (source) and DNAT (destination) rules on top of the conntrack connection table.
  • IPv6 normally avoids NAT; NPTv6 (RFC 6296) exists for stateless prefix translation, but a stateful firewall is the standard edge design.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating NAT as a firewall; it hides addresses, but security comes from stateful filtering rules, which IPv6 networks need too.
  • Setting up port forwarding behind CGNAT; if the router's WAN address is in 100.64.0.0/10, the ISP's NAT must forward instead, or use IPv6 or a tunnel.
  • Forgetting that a static NAT or port forward still needs a matching firewall or ACL permit before inbound traffic will pass.

docs.title: Try it: Compare your private address with the public address the Internet sees
docs.text:
ipconfig | findstr IPv4          # Windows: your private address
curl https://api.ipify.org       # public address after NAT

A small office firewall translates its 10.0.0.0/24 LAN to one public address. 'show ip nat translations' lists inside local 192.168.0.15:51544 mapped to inside global 198.51.100.23:40001. Mail server 10.0.0.25 is always reachable from outside as 203.0.113.25. Dynamic NATIETF RFC 3022 · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Inside hosts borrow a public address from a pool while they need it, one-to-one, then release it. A branch has a pool of 8 public addresses shared by staff PCs as they go online. Twenty phones in a café all appear online as 198.51.100.7, each with a different port. NAT mapping behaviour (cone vs symmetric)IETF RFC 4787 (UDP), RFC 5382 (TCP) · RFC · Layer 4 · Current Endpoint-independent ('cone') NATs reuse one public port for all destinations; symmetric NATs pick a new port per destination, defeating STUN. Two gamers behind cone NATs connect peer-to-peer, but a symmetric corporate NAT forces their console onto a relay server. Port forwardingRouter feature (destination NAT) · Concept · Layer 4 · Current A rule that sends inbound traffic on a public port to a chosen inside host and port. TCP 8443 on the public IP is forwarded to a home NAS at 192.168.1.50:443. A gamer cannot host a server because the ISP's CGNAT, not their home router, holds the public address. STUNIETF RFC 8489 (replaced RFC 5389) · Protocol · Layer 7 · Current Lets a device ask a server 'what public address and port do you see me as?'; usually UDP 3478. A video-call app learns its public mapping via STUN before sharing it with the other caller. TURNIETF RFC 8656 (replaced RFC 5766) · Protocol · Layer 7 · Current A relay server that forwards media when two peers cannot connect directly through their NATs. Behind strict corporate firewalls, a WebRTC meeting falls back to relaying through a TURN server. ICEIETF RFC 8445 (replaced RFC 5245) · Protocol · Layer 7 · Current Interactive Connectivity Establishment: gathers local, STUN and TURN candidates and tests them to find the best working path. WebRTC in every browser uses ICE to connect two users' cameras peer-to-peer. UPnP IGD and PCPOpen Connectivity Foundation (UPnP); IETF RFC 6887 (PCP) · Protocol · Layer 7 · Current Protocols that let applications ask the router to open port mappings automatically. A game console opens its own ports via UPnP; security teams often disable UPnP on business routers. NAT Traversal for IPsec (NAT-T)IETF RFC 3947 / RFC 3948 · RFC · Layer 4 · Current Wraps IPsec ESP packets in UDP port 4500 so VPNs work through NAT devices. A remote worker's IPsec VPN switches to UDP 4500 when it detects a home NAT router.

docs.title: 3.5 IPv6 Transition: Dual Stack, Tunnels & Translation
docs.text:
The Internet cannot switch from IPv4 to IPv6 overnight, so transition mechanisms let both work side by side. There are three families: dual stack (run both), tunnelling (carry one inside the other) and translation (convert between them). Most networks use dual stack today, while mobile networks increasingly run IPv6-only and translate for the IPv4 sites that remain.

NAT64 + DNS64 in action. The phone only ever speaks IPv6; DNS64 invents the address and NAT64 does the translation.

Think of it like…

It is like a country changing which side of the road it drives on in stages: some roads get lanes for both (dual stack), some vehicles ride a train through the other system (tunnels), and at borders cars swap number plates (translation).

Real-world example

Northgate Mobile runs its phone network IPv6-only to save scarce IPv4 addresses. A phone visiting an IPv6-ready site connects natively. For an IPv4-only site, the DNS64 resolver invents an address inside 64:ff9b::/96 and the carrier's NAT64 gateway translates the traffic. An old game app with a hard-coded IPv4 address still works because the phone's own translator (CLAT) converts it to IPv6 first: that combination is 464XLAT.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Start with dual stack in the core, data centre and Internet edge, then enable IPv6 on hosts.
  2. Where an access network cannot carry IPv6, tunnel it (6in4, 6rd) as a temporary bridge.
  3. Where IPv4 addresses run out, go IPv6-only and translate (NAT64/DNS64, 464XLAT).
  4. ISPs may carry customers' IPv4 inside IPv6 (DS-Lite, MAP-E/MAP-T) to share public IPv4 addresses.
  5. Clients choose the best path with Happy Eyeballs; IPv4 is retired wherever possible.

Who uses it

ISP and mobile network engineers, enterprise and cloud architects planning IPv6, and government networks with IPv6-only mandates; CCNA expects IPv6 basics and Network+ lists transition methods.

Key takeaway

Group mechanisms into three families: dual stack (both protocols), tunnelling (6in4, 6to4, Teredo, 6rd, DS-Lite) and translation (NAT64/DNS64, 464XLAT, SIIT); 6to4 and Teredo are obsolete.

Going deeper

  • Order of preference: dual stack where IPv4 is still plentiful, IPv6-only plus translation where it is not, and tunnels only as a temporary bridge across IPv4-only segments.
  • The NAT64 well-known prefix 64:ff9b::/96 (RFC 6052) embeds the IPv4 address in the last 32 bits; 64:ff9b:1::/48 (RFC 8215) is reserved for local translation deployments.
  • DNS64 cannot help apps that use literal IPv4 addresses and complicates DNSSEC validation of synthesised answers; 464XLAT's on-device CLAT solves the literal-address problem.
  • Apple has required iOS apps to work on IPv6-only NAT64 networks since 2016, and Android has included a 464XLAT CLAT since version 4.3, which is why mobile carriers moved first.
  • US OMB memo M-21-07 (2020) set federal targets of 20% of IP-enabled assets IPv6-only by the end of FY2023, 50% by FY2024 and 80% by FY2025.
  • Tunnels shrink the usable MTU (6in4 costs 20 bytes, DS-Lite 40 bytes), so path MTU discovery and ICMPv6 'Packet Too Big' messages must never be blocked.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Enabling IPv6 on hosts but forgetting IPv6 firewall rules, so devices become reachable over IPv6 paths that IPv4 rules never covered.
  • Assuming IPv6 can wait because NAT works; mobile, cloud and government networks already prefer or require IPv6.
  • Blocking all ICMPv6, which breaks neighbour discovery and path MTU discovery, especially across tunnels.
  • Treating 6to4 or Teredo as valid choices today; both are obsolete and should be disabled.

docs.title: Try it: Is your connection IPv6, IPv4 or translated? (your own machine)
docs.text:
curl -6 https://ifconfig.co          # your IPv6 address, if you have one
curl -4 https://ifconfig.co          # your IPv4 address
nslookup -type=AAAA ipv4only.arpa    # on a NAT64/DNS64 network: 64:ff9b::c000:aa
ping -6 example.com

docs.title: Key protocols, devices, standards & tools

A browser uses Happy Eyeballs (RFC 8305) to try IPv6 and IPv4 and pick whichever connects first. 6in4 manual tunnelIETF RFC 4213 (IP protocol 41) · Protocol · Layer 3 · Current Wraps IPv6 packets directly inside IPv4 (protocol 41) between two configured endpoints; simple and stateless, with no encryption. A home lab gets IPv6 from a tunnel broker such as Hurricane Electric's tunnelbroker.net over a 6in4 tunnel. 6to4IETF RFC 3056; anycast relays deprecated by RFC 7526 (2015) · Protocol · Layer 3 · Obsolete Automatic tunnelling using 2002::/16 prefixes built from a public IPv4 address; unreliable public relays led to its deprecation. An old router config with addresses starting 2002:c000:221:: reveals forgotten 6to4 tunnelling that should be removed. TeredoIETF RFC 4380 (designed by Microsoft); UDP 3544 · Protocol · Layer 3 · Obsolete Tunnels IPv6 inside UDP so it can cross IPv4 NAT routers; once enabled by default in Windows, now deprecated and rarely used. Security teams block UDP 3544 outbound because Teredo tunnels could bypass IPv4-only firewall rules. 6rd (IPv6 Rapid Deployment)IETF RFC 5969 · Protocol · Layer 3 · Legacy An ISP-controlled variant of 6to4 using the ISP's own prefix, letting IPv4-only access networks deliver IPv6 to homes quickly. French ISP Free used 6rd in 2007 to give its subscribers IPv6 within weeks, long before its access network was upgraded. DS-LiteIETF RFC 6333 (B4 and AFTR elements) · Technology · Layer 3 · Current Dual-Stack Lite: the home router tunnels IPv4 inside IPv6 to the ISP, where a carrier-grade NAT called the AFTR translates it. A cable customer has native IPv6 but shares a public IPv4 address through the ISP's AFTR, so IPv4 port forwarding is impossible. MAP-E / MAP-TIETF RFC 7597 (MAP-E), RFC 7599 (MAP-T) · Technology · Layer 3 · Current Stateless ISP methods that share one public IPv4 address among customers by giving each a fixed port range, carried over IPv6. Many Japanese ISPs use MAP-E: a subscriber's router may only use ports inside its assigned block for IPv4. NAT64IETF RFC 6146 · Protocol · Layer 3 · Current Translates between IPv6-only clients and IPv4-only servers using the well-known prefix 64:ff9b::/96. An IPv6-only phone reaches an IPv4-only website through the carrier's NAT64 gateway. DNS64IETF RFC 6147 · Protocol · Layer 7 · Current A DNS server that invents IPv6 (AAAA) answers for IPv4-only names so clients use NAT64. The resolver returns 64:ff9b::c000:221 for a site that only has the IPv4 address 192.0.2.33. 464XLATIETF RFC 6877 · Technology · Layer 3 · Current Double translation (IPv4 to IPv6 on the device, back to IPv4 at the carrier) so IPv4-only apps work on IPv6-only networks. Android phones on IPv6-only mobile networks use 464XLAT for old apps with hard-coded IPv4 addresses. SIIT (stateless IP/ICMP translation)IETF RFC 7915 (replaced RFC 6145) · RFC · Layer 3 · Current The algorithm that converts IPv4 headers to IPv6 and back, field by field; the engine inside NAT64 and 464XLAT. A data centre uses stateless translation so IPv6-only web servers can still be reached by IPv4 visitors through mapped addresses. IPv6-only preferred (DHCP option 108)IETF RFC 8925 (2020) · RFC · Layer 7 · Current DHCPv4 option letting capable clients give up their IPv4 address and run IPv6-only, while older devices still receive IPv4. On an IPv6-mostly conference Wi-Fi, phones and laptops that support it drop IPv4, so the IPv4 pool serves only a few old devices. PREF64 (NAT64 prefix discovery)IETF RFC 8781 (Router Advertisement option); RFC 7050 (ipv4only.arpa method) · RFC · Layer 3 · Current Ways for hosts to learn which NAT64 prefix the network uses, so their built-in translator (CLAT) can work correctly. A router advertises PREF64 64:ff9b::/96 in its Router Advertisements, and a laptop's CLAT starts translating immediately. IPv6-mostly networksOperational practice (RFC 8925 plus CLAT on hosts); IETF v6ops guidance · Concept · Layer 3 · Emerging One network serving both kinds of client: IPv6-only for devices that support it, dual stack for those that do not. A university's Wi-Fi goes IPv6-mostly; most clients stop using IPv4, while legacy printers carry on as before. IPv6 adoption & mandatesGoogle IPv6 statistics; US OMB memo M-21-07 · Concept · Current Google measured IPv6 above 50% of its traffic for the first time in March 2026; US federal agencies are being pushed to IPv6-only. France and India both exceed 70% IPv6 use, while some countries remain far lower, so dual stack will be needed for years.

docs.title: 3.6 IP Address Planning: A Design Case Study
docs.text:
An IP address plan decides which address ranges go to which sites, buildings and VLANs before anything is configured. A good plan leaves room to grow, keeps related networks in neat blocks that routers can summarise, and makes addresses easy to read. Fixing a bad plan later means renumbering, which is slow and risky.

A hierarchical address plan. Each level sits inside its parent's block, so one summary route covers everything below it.

Think of it like…

Planning addresses is like planning street numbers for a new town: you reserve a block of numbers for each district and leave gaps for future houses, so the post office can sort by district and nobody has to change address later.

Real-world example

Rowan Logistics has a head office and 20 depots. The engineer keeps 10.0.0.0/16 for head office and gives each depot a /20 from 10.16.0.0/12 (depot 1 = 10.16.0.0/20, depot 2 = 10.16.16.0/20), so all depots summarise as one route. Inside each depot, staff VLAN 10 and voice VLAN 20 get a /24 each, cameras a /25, and router links come from /31s. For IPv6, the company's /48 gives each depot a /56 and every VLAN a /64, with the VLAN number visible in the address.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Gather requirements: sites, VLANs per site, and hosts per VLAN today and in five years.
  2. Choose private space (usually 10.0.0.0/8) that avoids ranges used by partners, VPN users and cloud.
  3. Allocate hierarchically (region, site, VLAN) on bit boundaries so each level summarises.
  4. Fix conventions inside every subnet: gateway at .1, static infrastructure low, DHCP pool high.
  5. Design IPv6 in parallel: a /48 per organisation or site, a /64 per VLAN, aligned to nibbles.
  6. Record everything in IPAM before configuring, and review usage regularly.

Who uses it

Network designers and architects, cloud engineers choosing VPC ranges and anyone setting up a new office; interviews often ask candidates to sketch a simple address plan.

Key takeaway

Allocate on bit boundaries and size for growth: a /20 must start where the third octet is a multiple of 16, and a well-aligned block can be advertised as a single summary route.

Going deeper

  • Summarisation shrinks routing tables and hides instability: a flapping VLAN inside 10.16.0.0/20 stays behind one stable summary instead of disturbing every router in the network.
  • Cloud providers impose limits: an AWS VPC block must be between /16 and /28, and AWS reserves five addresses in every subnet, so plan cloud blocks generously.
  • Leave room to grow in place: if site 1 (10.16.0.0/20) might double, start site 2 at 10.16.32.0 so site 1 can later expand into the contiguous 10.16.0.0/19.
  • RFC 6177 recommends giving end sites enough IPv6 space for many subnets, commonly a /48 for businesses and a /56 for homes; RIPE-690 documents current ISP practice.
  • Mergers often collide on 10.0.0.0/8 or 192.168.1.0/24; NAT between overlapping networks works, but complicates every application, firewall rule and troubleshooting session.
  • Helpful tools: IPAM systems such as NetBox or Infoblox, command-line subnet calculators like ipcalc, and Python's ipaddress module for scripting allocations.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Sizing subnets exactly for today's host count, so one new floor of devices forces a disruptive renumbering.
  • Scattering a site's subnets across unrelated blocks, so the site cannot be summarised and every router learns dozens of extra routes.
  • Using 192.168.0.0/24 or 192.168.1.0/24 for office networks, which collide with remote workers' home routers over VPN.
  • Making IPv6 client subnets smaller than /64, which breaks SLAAC and many devices.

docs.title: Try it: Plan subnets with Python's built-in ipaddress module (runs locally)
docs.text:
python3
>>> import ipaddress as ip
>>> site = ip.ip_network('10.16.0.0/20')
>>> list(site.subnets(new_prefix=24))[:3]
[IPv4Network('10.16.0.0/24'), IPv4Network('10.16.1.0/24'), IPv4Network('10.16.2.0/24')]
>>> list(ip.ip_network('2001:db8:acad::/48').subnets(new_prefix=56))[1]
IPv6Network('2001:db8:acad:100::/56')

All switch management addresses live in 10.254.0.0/16, and only the admin jump-host subnet may open SSH sessions to it. A firm that used 1.1.1.0/24 internally found Cloudflare's public DNS resolver unreachable from every office.

docs.title: 3.7 ARP & IPv6 Neighbour Discovery
docs.text:
To send a frame on a local network, a device needs the neighbour's MAC (hardware) address, not just its IP address. ARP (for IPv4) and Neighbour Discovery (for IPv6) ask 'who has this IP address?' and remember the answer. Neighbour Discovery also helps IPv6 hosts find routers and check that their address is not already in use.

ARP resolving a printer's MAC. The request is broadcast to everyone, but the reply is unicast back to the asker only.

Think of it like…

ARP is like shouting in an office 'Who is Sam Lee?' and Sam replying 'Me, I'm at desk 14', so you can walk straight to the right desk next time.

Real-world example

Maria's PC (192.168.1.10) wants to print to 192.168.1.30. It checks its ARP cache, finds nothing, and broadcasts an ARP Request to ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff. The printer replies with its MAC 3c:52:82:aa:10:07, which Maria's PC caches for a few minutes. Later, an attacker on the same Wi-Fi sends fake ARP replies claiming to be the gateway, which is why the switch has Dynamic ARP Inspection turned on.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The host checks whether the destination IP is on its own subnet (if not, it resolves the gateway's MAC instead).
  2. It looks in its ARP or neighbour cache for a matching MAC address.
  3. If missing, IPv4 broadcasts an ARP Request; IPv6 sends a Neighbour Solicitation to a solicited-node multicast address.
  4. The owner replies with its MAC address (ARP Reply or Neighbour Advertisement).
  5. The answer is cached for a short time and the frame is sent.

Who uses it

Network and security engineers troubleshoot ARP and NDP when devices 'can't see' each other, and attackers abuse them for man-in-the-middle attacks on LANs.

Key takeaway

ARP never crosses a router: for remote destinations, the host ARPs for its default gateway's MAC address.

Going deeper

  • Cache lifetimes differ widely: Windows and Linux keep entries reachable for roughly 15-45 seconds before re-checking, while Cisco IOS routers keep ARP entries for 4 hours by default.
  • A 4-hour router ARP timeout versus a 5-minute switch MAC-aging timer causes unicast flooding when hosts go quiet; designers often align the two timers.
  • NDP messages must arrive with Hop Limit 255, so a packet that crossed a router (which lowers it) is rejected, blocking off-link spoofing.
  • Gratuitous ARP and unsolicited Neighbour Advertisements announce moves instantly: FHRP failovers, VM live migration and firewall cluster failovers all depend on them.
  • Attack tools such as arpspoof, Ettercap and Bettercap automate ARP poisoning; defences are DAI with DHCP snooping, RA Guard, 802.1X and encrypting traffic end to end.
  • IPv6 uses multicast instead of broadcast: an NS goes to the solicited-node group, so only hosts whose address ends in the same 24 bits process it.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Expecting a host to ARP for a remote server's IP; it ARPs only for its default gateway and sends the frame there.
  • Clearing the ARP cache to 'fix' an IP address conflict; two devices still claim the address, so find and correct the duplicate.
  • Thinking IPv6 neighbour discovery broadcasts like ARP; IPv6 has no broadcast and uses solicited-node multicast instead.

docs.title: Try it: View your ARP and IPv6 neighbour caches
docs.text:
arp -a                       # Windows / macOS / Linux
ip neigh show                # Linux (IPv4 and IPv6)
netsh interface ipv6 show neighbors   # Windows IPv6

Wireshark shows opcode 1 with target MAC 00:00:00:00:00:00 asking for 192.168.1.30, then opcode 2 carrying the printer's MAC. ARP cacheHost operating system · Concept · Layer 2 · Current A short-lived table of recently learned IP-to-MAC mappings, so the host does not ARP for every packet. 'arp -a' shows 192.168.1.1 mapped to the router's MAC as a dynamic entry. Gratuitous ARPIETF RFC 5227 (ARP announcements) · Concept · Layer 2 · Current An unrequested ARP announcing a device's own IP and MAC, to update neighbours or detect conflicts. After a firewall failover, the new active unit sends gratuitous ARPs so switches and hosts update instantly. IPv4 Address Conflict DetectionIETF RFC 5227 · RFC · Layer 2 · Current Uses ARP probes before using an address to make sure no other device already has it. Windows shows 'IP address conflict' when its ARP probe gets a reply from another machine. Proxy ARPIETF RFC 1027 · RFC · Layer 2 · Legacy A router answers ARP requests on behalf of hosts on another network, hiding the router from the sender. Old hosts with a wrong subnet mask still reach remote servers because the router answers their ARPs. ARP spoofing / poisoningAttack technique · Concept · Layer 2 Sending forged ARP replies so victims send traffic to the attacker's MAC instead of the real gateway. In a lab, students see how a spoofed gateway lets an attacker intercept unencrypted traffic, then enable defences. A university switch blocks a student's laptop from claiming to be the gateway 10.20.0.1. Neighbour Discovery Protocol (NDP)IETF RFC 4861 · Protocol · Layer 3 · Current IPv6's replacement for ARP, plus router discovery and redirects, using ICMPv6 messages types 133–137. An IPv6 PC uses NDP to find both its neighbours' MACs and its default router. Router Solicitation / Router AdvertisementIETF RFC 4861 (ICMPv6 types 133/134) · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Hosts ask for routers (RS); routers announce prefixes, default gateway and flags (RA) to ff02::1. A new laptop sends an RS and gets an RA with prefix 2001:db8:5:1::/64 within milliseconds. Neighbour Solicitation / Neighbour AdvertisementIETF RFC 4861 (ICMPv6 types 135/136) · Concept · Layer 3 · Current The IPv6 question-and-answer pair for resolving an address to a MAC and checking reachability. Wireshark shows an NS for 2001:db8::30 followed by an NA carrying the printer's MAC. Solicited-node multicast addressIETF RFC 4291 · Concept · Layer 3 · Current ff02::1:ffXX:XXXX built from the last 24 bits of an address, so NS messages reach only likely owners. To find 2001:db8::1:abcd, a host sends the NS to ff02::1:ff01:abcd instead of everyone. Duplicate Address Detection (DAD)IETF RFC 4862 · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Before using a new IPv6 address, a host sends an NS for it; any reply means the address is taken. A server marks its address 'duplicate' and refuses to use it after a colleague manually configured the same one. Neighbour Unreachability Detection (NUD)IETF RFC 4861 · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Tracks each IPv6 neighbour cache entry through INCOMPLETE, REACHABLE, STALE, DELAY and PROBE states to spot dead neighbours. 'ip -6 neigh' shows the gateway as STALE; the next packet triggers DELAY then PROBE, and an NA puts it back to REACHABLE. ICMPv6 RedirectIETF RFC 4861 (ICMPv6 type 137) · Concept · Layer 3 · Current A router tells a host that a better first-hop router exists for a particular destination. Router A redirects a host to Router B on the same link for traffic to the lab network. RA GuardIETF RFC 6105 · RFC · Layer 2 · Current A switch feature that blocks Router Advertisements from ports where no legitimate router should be. A rogue RA from a misconfigured hobby router is dropped before it can hijack users' default gateway. Exam questions mention SEND as the theoretical fix for NDP spoofing; real networks usually use RA Guard instead.

docs.title: 3.8 ICMP & Path Diagnostics
docs.text:
ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) is how routers and hosts report problems and test connectivity, such as 'destination unreachable' or 'time exceeded'. Tools like ping and traceroute use ICMP to check whether a host is reachable and which routers a packet passes through. It also helps devices discover the largest packet size a path can carry.

How traceroute reveals each hop. Each probe dies one hop further away, and the router that discards it identifies itself.

Think of it like…

ICMP is like the postal service returning a letter stamped 'address unknown' or 'too heavy for this route', telling the sender what went wrong.

Real-world example

Leo cannot reach a supplier's portal. He runs 'ping portal.example.com' and gets 'Request timed out', so he runs 'tracert'. Hops 1–6 answer, but from hop 7 onwards he sees asterisks, showing traffic dies inside the supplier's ISP. Separately, a VPN user's large file uploads hang because a firewall drops ICMP 'Fragmentation Needed' messages, breaking Path MTU Discovery; allowing that ICMP type fixes it.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. ping sends ICMP Echo Requests (type 8, or ICMPv6 128) and waits for Echo Replies (type 0, or ICMPv6 129).
  2. Every router decreases a packet's TTL (Hop Limit in IPv6) by 1; at zero it drops it and returns Time Exceeded.
  3. traceroute sends probes with TTL 1, 2, 3... so each router along the path reveals itself.
  4. If a router cannot deliver a packet, it returns Destination Unreachable with a code explaining why.
  5. If a packet is too big for the next link and cannot be fragmented, the router returns Fragmentation Needed or Packet Too Big, and the sender lowers its packet size (PMTUD).

Who uses it

Help-desk staff, network engineers and NOC operators use ping and traceroute as their first troubleshooting tools every day.

Key takeaway

Do not block all ICMP at firewalls: ICMPv6 is essential for IPv6 to work, and dropping 'Packet Too Big' breaks Path MTU Discovery.

Going deeper

  • An ICMP error carries the type, code and checksum plus the offending packet's IP header and first 8 bytes, which lets the sender match the error to the right socket.
  • Types to memorise: 0 Echo Reply, 3 Destination Unreachable (code 0 net, 1 host, 3 port, 4 fragmentation needed, 13 administratively prohibited), 5 Redirect, 8 Echo Request, 11 Time Exceeded.
  • Unix traceroute sends UDP probes to ports starting at 33434, ending when the target returns Port Unreachable; Windows tracert sends ICMP Echo Requests instead.
  • Default ping sizes differ: Windows sends 32 data bytes, Linux 56 (64 with the ICMP header); 1472 bytes of data plus 28 bytes of headers tests a 1500-byte MTU.
  • RFC 4890 lists which ICMPv6 messages firewalls must allow: Packet Too Big, Time Exceeded, Parameter Problem, Destination Unreachable and the Neighbour Discovery types.
  • Latency that jumps at one hop and stays high for all later hops is real; latency that spikes at one hop only is usually that router slowly answering ICMP.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Concluding a host is down because ping fails; Windows Firewall and many servers block Echo Requests while services still work.
  • Blaming a middle hop for loss shown only at that hop; real loss continues to the destination and all later hops.
  • Blocking all ICMP 'for security', which breaks Path MTU Discovery and causes mysterious hangs on large transfers and VPNs.

docs.title: Try it: Basic path diagnostics against a public host
docs.text:
ping -c 4 example.com          # Linux/macOS (Windows: ping -n 4)
tracert example.com            # Windows (ICMP probes)
traceroute example.com         # Linux/macOS (UDP probes by default)
ping -f -l 1472 example.com    # Windows: test 1500-byte MTU with Don't Fragment

A router sends an ICMP message back when it has no route to a destination. Blocking all ICMPv6 on a firewall stops hosts from finding routers and neighbours. Sending to a closed UDP port returns type 3 code 3 'port unreachable'. A routing loop shows up as repeated Time Exceeded messages from the same two routers. Fragmentation Needed / Packet Too BigIETF RFC 792 (type 3 code 4); RFC 4443 (type 2) · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Tells the sender a packet exceeds the next link's MTU and gives the allowed size. A tunnel router replies 'MTU 1400' so the sender shrinks its packets. ICMP RedirectIETF RFC 792 (type 5) · Concept · Layer 3 · Legacy A router tells a host to use a better gateway on the same subnet; often disabled for security. Security baselines disable accepting ICMP redirects on servers to prevent traffic hijacking. A host starts at 1500 bytes, learns a VPN hop allows 1420, and adjusts automatically. Packetization Layer PMTUDIETF RFC 4821 (TCP), RFC 8899 (datagrams) · RFC · Layer 4 · Current Discovers path MTU by probing with real data, without relying on ICMP messages that firewalls may drop. QUIC uses datagram PLPMTUD to find a safe packet size even when ICMP is filtered. ICMP rate limitingIETF RFC 1812 / RFC 4443; vendor control-plane policing · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Routers cap how many ICMP errors they generate to protect their CPU, so some traceroute hops show '*' or odd latency. Hop 5 of an mtr report shows 40% loss while later hops show 0%, meaning hop 5 is rate-limiting replies, not dropping traffic. IP fragmentationIETF RFC 791 / RFC 8200 · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Splitting a packet into smaller pieces; IPv4 routers may fragment, IPv6 only the sender may (minimum IPv6 MTU 1280). A 4000-byte UDP packet over 1500-byte Ethernet arrives as three IPv4 fragments reassembled by the receiver. pingMike Muuss, 1983; built into all OSes · Command · Layer 3 · Current Sends ICMP echo requests and reports replies, round-trip time and packet loss. 'ping 8.8.8.8' working but 'ping google.com' failing points to a DNS problem. traceroute / tracertVan Jacobson, 1987; Windows tracert · Command · Layer 3 · Current Lists each router hop by sending probes with increasing TTL; Unix uses UDP by default, Windows uses ICMP. tracert shows latency jumping from 10 ms to 180 ms at the hop where traffic crosses an ocean. TCP and Paris traceroutetcptraceroute / traceroute -T; Paris traceroute (2006 research) · Tool · Layer 4 · Current Traceroute variants that probe with TCP SYNs to an open port, or keep flow fields constant so load balancers don't scramble paths. An ISP support engineer asks a customer for an mtr report to prove packet loss at a specific hop.

docs.title: 3.9 Routing Fundamentals
docs.text:
A router connects different networks and decides where to send each packet next by looking at its routing table. Routes can be learned automatically from directly connected networks, typed in by hand (static) or learned from other routers through routing protocols (dynamic). When several routes match, the router picks the most specific one.

A router's forwarding decision. Longest prefix match picks the route; the IP addresses stay the same while the Layer 2 header is rebuilt at every hop.

Think of it like…

A router is like a motorway junction with signposts: it does not know the whole journey, only which exit gets each car one step closer to its destination.

Real-world example

Router R1 at Harbour Logistics has these routes: 10.1.0.0/16 via R2, 10.1.5.0/24 via R3, and a default route 0.0.0.0/0 via the ISP. A packet for 10.1.5.9 matches all three, but /24 is the longest match, so it goes to R3. A packet for 10.1.9.9 matches /16, so it goes to R2. A packet for 8.8.8.8 only matches the default route, so it goes to the ISP.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A packet arrives and the router reads its destination IP address.
  2. It searches the routing table for every route that contains that address.
  3. It picks the longest prefix match (most specific route); ties between sources are broken by administrative distance, then metric.
  4. It decreases the TTL, rewrites the Layer 2 header for the next hop, and forwards the packet out of the chosen interface.
  5. If nothing matches and there is no default route, it drops the packet and returns ICMP Destination Unreachable.

Who uses it

Network engineers, ISPs, cloud providers (VPC route tables) and even your home router all rely on these rules.

Key takeaway

Longest prefix match always wins first; administrative distance only decides between different sources offering the same prefix.

Going deeper

  • Routers split work into a control plane (routing protocols building the RIB), a data plane (the FIB, often in TCAM or ASICs) and a management plane (SSH, SNMP, APIs).
  • At every hop the source and destination IP stay the same (unless NAT is used) but the Ethernet source and destination MACs change; TTL drops and the IPv4 checksum is recalculated.
  • A static route to a next-hop IP needs a second, recursive lookup to find the exit interface; pointing a route at an Ethernet interface alone relies on proxy ARP.
  • The global IPv4 BGP table passed about one million routes in the mid-2020s; on 12 August 2014 older routers whose FIBs held only 512,000 routes overflowed and caused outages.
  • If several routes tie on prefix, AD and metric, routers load-share with ECMP; Cisco IGPs default to four equal paths (maximum-paths), configurable higher.
  • Linux can hold many routing tables and choose between them with 'ip rule', which is how VPN clients, containers and policy routing are built.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Applying administrative distance before longest prefix match; a /24 from RIP beats a /16 from OSPF because specificity is checked first.
  • Adding a route to a remote network but no return route, so pings leave successfully and the replies are dropped on the way back.
  • Adding default routes to two ISPs without tracking; if one ISP fails upstream but its link stays up, half the traffic is black-holed.

route print          # Windows
ip route show        # Linux
netstat -rn          # macOS/Linux

show ip route

docs.title: Key protocols, devices, standards & tools
docs.text: Name What it does Example RouterCisco, Juniper, Nokia, Arista, MikroTik and others · Device · Layer 3 · Current A device that forwards packets between networks using a routing table and builds that table with routing protocols. A branch router links the office LAN to the head office over an SD-WAN tunnel. Routing table (RIB) and forwarding table (FIB)General routing concept · Concept · Layer 3 · Current The RIB holds all learned routes; the best ones are copied into the FIB used for fast forwarding in hardware. 'show ip route' displays the RIB; the switch ASIC uses the FIB to forward millions of packets a second. Longest prefix matchIETF RFC 1812 / RFC 4632 · Concept · Layer 3 · Current When several routes match, the one with the longest (most specific) prefix is used. Routes 10.0.0.0/8 and 10.20.30.0/24 both match 10.20.30.5; the /24 wins. Connected routeGeneral routing concept · Concept · Layer 3 · Current A route added automatically for a subnet configured on an active router interface; administrative distance 0. Configuring 192.168.5.1/24 on an interface adds 'C 192.168.5.0/24' to the table. Route codes and local host routesCisco IOS 'show ip route' legend · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Letters show each route's source: C connected, L local /32 of the router's own address, S static, O OSPF, D EIGRP, B BGP, R RIP. 'O IA 10.3.0.0/20 [110/30] via 10.0.0.2' means an inter-area OSPF route with AD 110 and metric 30. Static routeGeneral routing concept · Concept · Layer 3 · Current A route typed in manually by an administrator; simple and predictable but does not adapt to failures by itself. 'ip route 172.16.0.0 255.255.0.0 10.0.0.2' sends the lab network to a neighbour router. Floating static routeCisco and others · Concept · Layer 3 · Current A backup static route with a higher administrative distance, used only when the main route disappears. A 4G backup route with distance 250 takes over when the fibre link's OSPF route vanishes. Dynamic routingRouting protocols (OSPF, IS-IS, EIGRP, BGP, RIP) · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Routers exchange information automatically, learning new networks and routing around failures. When a link fails, OSPF recalculates and traffic shifts to the remaining path within seconds. Default route0.0.0.0/0 (IPv4), ::/0 (IPv6) · Concept · Layer 3 · Current The route of last resort, used when no more specific route matches. A home router's only real route is a default pointing at the ISP. Administrative distanceCisco (Juniper calls it route preference) · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Trustworthiness of a route source; lower wins. Connected 0, static 1, eBGP 20, EIGRP 90, OSPF 110, IS-IS 115, RIP 120, iBGP 200. If OSPF and RIP both offer 10.5.0.0/16, the OSPF route (110) is installed. MetricProtocol-specific · Concept · Layer 3 · Current A protocol's cost for a path, used to choose between routes from the same protocol: hops, cost, delay or bandwidth. OSPF prefers a path with total cost 20 over one with cost 65. ConvergenceGeneral routing concept · Concept · Layer 3 · Current The time until all routers agree on the new topology after a change; faster means less disruption. Old RIP networks could take minutes to converge; tuned OSPF with BFD converges in under a second. Distance-vector routingBellman-Ford algorithm (RIP) · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Routers share their whole table with neighbours and trust their view: 'routing by rumour'. RIP routers advertise 'network X is 3 hops away from me' every 30 seconds. Link-state routingDijkstra SPF algorithm (OSPF, IS-IS) · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Every router learns the full map of links and calculates its own shortest paths. Each OSPF router in an area holds an identical link-state database and runs SPF on it. Path-vector routingBGP · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Routes carry the full list of networks (AS path) they passed through, allowing policy and loop detection. A BGP router rejects a route whose AS_PATH already contains its own AS number. Routing loops and split horizonDistance-vector loop prevention · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Loops send packets in circles; split horizon (never advertise a route back where it came from), poison reverse and hold-down timers prevent them. With split horizon off, two RIP routers keep 'counting to infinity' (16 hops) after a network fails.

docs.title: 3.10 Interior Gateway Protocols
docs.text:
Interior Gateway Protocols (IGPs) are routing protocols used inside one organisation's network to share routes automatically. The main ones are RIP (simple, old), OSPF (the most common open standard), EIGRP (originally Cisco) and IS-IS (popular with large ISPs). They find the best paths and react quickly when links fail.

OSPF multi-area design. Every area attaches to backbone Area 0 through an ABR, which can summarise its routes.

Think of it like…

An IGP is like a company's internal traffic-update radio: every depot shares road closures with the others so delivery vans always take the best route inside the company's own region.

Real-world example

Northwind College runs OSPF across 20 routers. The core routers are in Area 0 and each campus is its own area, so a flapping link in Campus 3 does not force every router to recalculate. On the main hall's Ethernet segment, Router A becomes the DR (highest priority) and Router B the BDR, so the other routers only exchange updates with them. Campus 3 summarises its 16 subnets as one 10.3.0.0/20 route into Area 0.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Routers discover neighbours by sending Hello packets on their interfaces.
  2. Neighbours exchange routing information: whole tables (distance-vector) or link-state advertisements (link-state).
  3. Each router calculates best paths using its metric (hops, cost, or bandwidth and delay).
  4. Best routes are installed in the routing table.
  5. When a link changes, updates flood or propagate and routers reconverge.

Who uses it

Enterprise and campus network engineers (OSPF, EIGRP), service providers (IS-IS, OSPF), and CCNA/CCNP and JNCIA candidates.

Key takeaway

Comparison to memorise: RIP = hop count, max 15, AD 120; OSPF = cost, AD 110, areas; EIGRP = bandwidth + delay, AD 90 internal; IS-IS = metric, AD 115, levels.

Going deeper

  • OSPF uses five packet types: Hello, Database Description (DBD), Link-State Request, Link-State Update and Link-State Acknowledgement; LSAs are refreshed every 30 minutes and age out at 60.
  • OSPF router ID is chosen in order: manually configured, else highest loopback IP, else highest active interface IP; duplicate router IDs cause strange flapping.
  • Classic EIGRP metric with default K-values is 256 × (10^7 / slowest bandwidth in kbps + total delay in tens of microseconds); successors and feasible successors are pre-computed by DUAL.
  • IS-IS carries everything in TLVs, so IPv6 and Segment Routing were added without a new protocol version; routers are identified by NET addresses such as 49.0001.0000.0000.0001.00.
  • Sub-second convergence combines BFD for detection, SPF and LSA throttling, and precomputed Loop-Free Alternates or TI-LFA backup paths that switch in about 50 ms.
  • Redistributed routes appear as OSPF E2 (fixed external cost, the default) or E1 (external plus internal cost); E1 is preferred over E2 for the same prefix.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Leaving OSPF's reference bandwidth at 100 Mbps, so 1, 10 and 100 Gbps links all get cost 1 and paths are chosen badly; set it identically on every router.
  • Building a non-backbone area that does not touch Area 0; its routes never reach other areas unless a virtual link is configured as a stopgap.
  • Panicking over DROTHER neighbours stuck in 2-WAY; on Ethernet segments that is normal, as full adjacency forms only with the DR and BDR.

docs.title: Try it: Basic single-area OSPF on a lab router (Cisco IOS)
docs.text:
router ospf 1
 router-id 1.1.1.1
 network 10.0.0.0 0.0.255.255 area 0
!
show ip ospf neighbor
show ip route ospf

docs.title: Key protocols, devices, standards & tools
docs.text: Name What it does Example RIPv2IETF RFC 2453 · Protocol · Layer 3 · Legacy Distance-vector protocol using hop count (max 15); updates every 30 seconds to 224.0.0.9 on UDP 520; supports CIDR. A tiny lab or old branch network uses RIPv2 because it needs almost no configuration. RIPngIETF RFC 2080 · Protocol · Layer 3 · Legacy RIP for IPv6, using UDP port 521 and multicast group ff02::9. Students configure RIPng to practise IPv6 routing before moving on to OSPFv3. OSPFv2IETF RFC 2328 · Protocol · Layer 3 · Current Link-state IGP for IPv4 using Dijkstra's SPF; runs directly on IP (protocol 89) using multicast 224.0.0.5 and 224.0.0.6. A hospital network runs OSPF so traffic reroutes within seconds if a fibre between buildings is cut. OSPFv3IETF RFC 5340 · Protocol · Layer 3 · Current OSPF for IPv6 (and IPv4 via address families), forming adjacencies over link-local addresses. A dual-stack campus runs OSPFv3 to carry its 2001:db8:100::/48 subnets. OSPF neighbour statesIETF RFC 2328 · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Down → Init → 2-Way → ExStart → Exchange → Loading → Full; Full means link-state databases are synchronised. 'show ip ospf neighbor' stuck in EXSTART between two routers usually reveals mismatched interface MTUs. OSPF Hello and Dead timersIETF RFC 2328 · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Hellos every 10 s and Dead 40 s on Ethernet and point-to-point (30/120 on NBMA); neighbours must agree on timers, area, subnet and authentication. A router with Hello 5 never becomes neighbours with one using the default 10 until the timers match. OSPF areasIETF RFC 2328 · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Groups of routers sharing one link-state database; all areas connect to backbone Area 0 through Area Border Routers. Each regional office is its own area, limiting how far link-state changes spread. DR / BDRIETF RFC 2328 · Concept · Layer 3 · Current On multi-access segments like Ethernet, a Designated Router and Backup reduce updates; elected by priority, then highest router ID. Five routers on one VLAN form full adjacencies only with the DR and BDR, not each other. OSPF LSAsIETF RFC 2328 / RFC 5340 · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Link-State Advertisements describe the network: Type 1 router, 2 network, 3 summary, 4 ASBR summary, 5 external, 7 NSSA external. Routes redistributed from a static route appear in other areas as Type 5 external LSAs. Stub, totally stubby and NSSA areasIETF RFC 2328; NSSA RFC 3101 · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Special areas that block external (Type 5) LSAs, and optionally inter-area routes, replacing them with a default route to shrink databases. A small branch area is made totally stubby, so its routers hold only local routes plus one default to the ABR. OSPF costIETF RFC 2328 · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Per-interface metric; on Cisco, cost = reference bandwidth (default 100 Mbps) divided by interface bandwidth. Engineers raise the reference bandwidth to 100 Gbps so 10G and 1G links get different costs. EIGRPCisco; IETF RFC 7868 (Informational, 2016) · Protocol · Layer 3 · Current Advanced distance-vector protocol using bandwidth and delay as its metric; IP protocol 88, multicast 224.0.0.10. A retail chain built entirely on Cisco routers uses EIGRP for fast, simple branch routing. DUAL (Diffusing Update Algorithm)J.J. Garcia-Luna-Aceves; used in EIGRP · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Keeps a loop-free backup path (feasible successor) ready, so EIGRP can switch instantly when the main path fails. When the primary WAN fails, EIGRP promotes the feasible successor without recalculating. IS-ISISO/IEC 10589; IETF RFC 1195 (for IP) · Protocol · Layer 3 · Current Link-state IGP that runs directly over Layer 2 (not IP), easily carries IPv4 and IPv6, and scales well. Many tier-1 ISPs and large data centres run IS-IS as the IGP underneath BGP and MPLS. IS-IS levelsISO/IEC 10589 · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Level 1 routes within an area, Level 2 routes between areas (the backbone); routers can be L1, L2 or L1/L2. An ISP runs its whole core as a single Level 2 domain for simplicity. IGP comparison tableStudy summary · Concept · Layer 3 RIP: hops, slow, small networks. OSPF: cost, open, areas. EIGRP: bandwidth/delay, fast, Cisco-centric. IS-IS: scalable, ISP favourite. A multi-vendor enterprise picks OSPF because both its Juniper and Aruba routers support it fully.

docs.title: 3.11 BGP & How the Internet Routes
docs.text:
The Internet is made of tens of thousands of independent networks called autonomous systems (ISPs, cloud providers, universities, big companies). BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is the protocol they use to tell each other which IP addresses they can reach. It chooses paths based on business policy, not just speed, and mistakes in BGP can knock large services offline.

Transit and peering between ASes. Customers pay providers for transit; peers swap only their own customers' routes, often at an IXP.

Think of it like…

BGP is like airlines agreeing which routes they will sell to each other: each one announces 'I can get you to these cities', and each picks partners based on contracts and price, not just the shortest flight.

Real-world example

On 4 October 2021, a maintenance command at Facebook (now Meta) accidentally cut all connections between its data centres. Its DNS servers, seeing the backbone was gone, automatically withdrew their BGP announcements. The rest of the Internet suddenly had no route to Facebook's DNS servers, so facebook.com, Instagram and WhatsApp stopped resolving for about six hours. Even staff badge systems and internal tools were affected, slowing the recovery.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Each organisation gets an AS number and IP prefixes from its Regional Internet Registry.
  2. BGP routers form TCP sessions on port 179 with neighbours (peers).
  3. They announce prefixes they own or can reach, with attributes such as AS_PATH and NEXT_HOP.
  4. Each router applies import and export policies, then selects one best path per prefix.
  5. Best paths are passed on to other peers, adding the router's own AS number to the AS_PATH.
  6. Withdrawals tell everyone a prefix is no longer reachable through that path.

Who uses it

ISP, cloud and data-centre network engineers, Internet exchange operators and large enterprises with multiple Internet providers.

Key takeaway

BGP uses TCP port 179; eBGP runs between different ASes (AD 20) and iBGP inside one AS (AD 200).

Going deeper

  • Cisco's best-path order: highest Weight, highest LOCAL_PREF, locally originated, shortest AS_PATH, lowest ORIGIN, lowest MED, eBGP over iBGP, lowest IGP cost to next hop, oldest route, lowest router ID.
  • In the mid-2020s the Internet routing table held roughly one million IPv4 and over 200,000 IPv6 prefixes from more than 75,000 autonomous systems.
  • Outbound traffic is steered with LOCAL_PREF; inbound traffic with AS-path prepending, MED, communities or announcing more-specific prefixes (up to /24 IPv4 and /48 IPv6 are widely accepted).
  • Multiprotocol BGP (RFC 4760) uses address families (AFI/SAFI) so one protocol carries IPv4, IPv6, L3VPN, EVPN and FlowSpec routes.
  • iBGP never re-advertises routes learned from one iBGP peer to another, so n routers need n(n−1)/2 sessions; route reflectors or confederations remove the full mesh.
  • Cisco defaults to 60-second keepalives and a 180-second hold time; pairing BGP with BFD cuts failure detection to under a second.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming BGP picks the fastest path; it follows policy and AS-path length and knows nothing about latency or bandwidth.
  • Peering with two ISPs without outbound filters, accidentally re-advertising one provider's routes to the other and becoming a route leak.
  • Forgetting 'next-hop-self' on iBGP edge routers, so internal routers learn external routes whose next hop they cannot reach.
  • Expecting eBGP between loopbacks to work by default; it needs ebgp-multihop (or TTL security) and update-source settings.

docs.title: Try it: Explore real BGP data for a public prefix
docs.text:
whois -h whois.radb.net 1.1.1.0/24     # routing registry entry
# Browse https://bgp.he.net/AS13335 for Cloudflare's peers and prefixes
# Lab router (Cisco IOS): show ip bgp summary

docs.title: Key protocols, devices, standards & tools
docs.text: Name What it does Example BGP-4IETF RFC 4271 · Protocol · Layer 7 · Current Border Gateway Protocol version 4: path-vector protocol that exchanges reachability between autonomous systems over TCP port 179. Every ISP in the world uses BGP to announce its customers' prefixes to other networks. BGP messages and session statesIETF RFC 4271; ROUTE-REFRESH RFC 2918 · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Messages OPEN, UPDATE, KEEPALIVE, NOTIFICATION, ROUTE-REFRESH; the session moves Idle → Connect → Active → OpenSent → OpenConfirm → Established. A neighbour flapping between Active and Idle usually means TCP 179 is blocked or the peer IP/AS is misconfigured. Autonomous System (AS)IETF RFC 1930 / RFC 4271 · Concept · Layer 3 · Current A network or group of networks under one administration with a single, clearly defined routing policy. Cloudflare is AS13335 and Google is AS15169. AS Number (ASN)IETF RFC 6793 (32-bit ASNs); RFC 6996 (private ASNs) · RFC · Layer 3 · Current Unique AS identifier, originally 16-bit, now 32-bit; 64512–65534 and 4200000000–4294967294 are private. A company uses private AS 65001 to run BGP with its MPLS provider. eBGPIETF RFC 4271 · Concept · Layer 3 · Current BGP between routers in different ASes, normally directly connected; administrative distance 20. A bank's edge router runs eBGP with two ISPs so it stays online if one fails. iBGP and route reflectorsIETF RFC 4271; RFC 4456 (route reflection) · Concept · Layer 3 · Current BGP inside one AS to share external routes; needs a full mesh, or route reflectors to avoid it. An ISP's 200 edge routers each peer with two route reflectors instead of 199 other routers. Path attributes and best-path selectionIETF RFC 4271 · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Attributes such as LOCAL_PREF, AS_PATH, ORIGIN, MED and NEXT_HOP decide the best route, compared in a fixed order. Setting higher LOCAL_PREF on routes from the fibre ISP makes it the preferred exit over the backup. TransitInternet business model · Concept A paid service where a provider carries your traffic to and from the entire Internet. A regional ISP buys transit from a tier-1 carrier to reach every network worldwide. PeeringInternet business model · Concept Two networks exchange traffic directly between their own customers, usually without payment. A streaming service peers with a national ISP so video skips the paid transit path. Internet Exchange Point (IXP)e.g. DE-CIX, AMS-IX, LINX, Equinix IX · Service · Layer 2 · Current A shared switching fabric where many networks meet to peer, often through route servers. Hundreds of networks connect at DE-CIX Frankfurt to exchange traffic locally. BGP communitiesIETF RFC 1997; RFC 8092 (large communities) · RFC · Layer 3 · Current Tags attached to routes that signal policy, such as 'do not export' or 'prepend to this peer'. A customer tags a route with its provider's community to blackhole traffic during a DDoS attack. BGP hijackSecurity incident type · Concept · Layer 3 A network announces IP prefixes it does not own, attracting traffic meant for someone else. In February 2008, Pakistan Telecom's announcement of a YouTube /24 accidentally took YouTube offline globally for hours. Route leakIETF RFC 7908 (definition) · RFC · Layer 3 Routes passed on beyond their intended scope, e.g. a customer re-announcing one provider's routes to another. In June 2019 a leak via a small ISP and Verizon misrouted traffic for Cloudflare and others. RPKI and Route Origin ValidationIETF RFC 6480 (RPKI), RFC 6811 (ROV) · Standard · Layer 3 · Current Signed records (ROAs) state which AS may originate a prefix; routers drop 'invalid' announcements. An ISP rejects a hijacked route because the ROA says only AS64500 may announce that prefix. ASPAIETF SIDROPS working group (draft) · Standard · Layer 3 · Emerging Autonomous System Provider Authorization: signed lists of a network's upstream providers, helping detect route leaks and path forgery. Early adopters publish ASPA objects in RPKI so others can spot impossible AS paths. MANRSGlobal Cyber Alliance (initiative launched with Internet Society) · Organisation Mutually Agreed Norms for Routing Security: an initiative promoting filtering, anti-spoofing, coordination and validation. A hosting provider joins MANRS and commits to filtering its customers' BGP announcements.

docs.title: 3.12 Gateway Redundancy & High Availability
docs.text:
Most devices have only one default gateway configured, so if that router fails, they lose all off-network access. First Hop Redundancy Protocols (FHRPs) like HSRP and VRRP let two or more routers share one virtual gateway address, so a backup takes over automatically. Other tools such as ECMP and BFD spread traffic over several paths and detect failures in milliseconds.

VRRP failover. Hosts never change their gateway setting; the virtual IP and MAC simply move to the backup.

Think of it like…

An FHRP is like a shop with one front-door phone number answered by whichever manager is on duty: customers dial the same number even when the manager changes.

Real-world example

Sunrise Clinic's PCs use gateway 10.10.10.1, which is a VRRP virtual address shared by routers R1 (priority 120) and R2 (priority 100). R1 is master and answers for the virtual IP and virtual MAC 00:00:5e:00:01:0a. When R1's power supply fails, R2 stops hearing R1's advertisements, becomes master in about three seconds and sends gratuitous ARPs. Staff only notice a brief pause in a video call.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Two or more routers are configured with the same virtual IP address and group number.
  2. They exchange hello or advertisement messages and elect an active (master) router by priority.
  3. Hosts use the virtual IP as their default gateway; the active router answers ARP with a virtual MAC.
  4. If the active router or a tracked uplink fails, the standby takes over the virtual IP and MAC.
  5. With preemption enabled, the higher-priority router reclaims the role when it recovers.

Who uses it

Enterprise, data-centre and hospital network engineers designing networks that must stay up 24/7.

Key takeaway

HSRP and GLBP are Cisco proprietary; VRRP is the open standard (now RFC 9568, replacing RFC 5798) and works across vendors.

Going deeper

  • Default timers: HSRP hellos every 3 s with a 10 s hold; VRRP advertises every 1 s and declares the master dead after about 3.6 s; both can be tuned to sub-second values.
  • HSRPv1 uses groups 0-255 and multicast 224.0.0.2; HSRPv2 supports groups 0-4095, multicast 224.0.0.102, IPv6 and virtual MACs 0000.0c9f.fxxx.
  • In VRRP, a router whose real interface address equals the virtual IP is the 'address owner' with priority 255 and always becomes master.
  • Good campus design makes the FHRP active router for each VLAN also the spanning-tree root for that VLAN, so traffic does not take a detour across the inter-switch link.
  • Firewall and load-balancer HA pairs use the same idea plus state synchronisation, so established sessions survive a failover without users reconnecting.
  • Sub-second failover typically combines BFD on routed links, tuned FHRP timers, graceful restart and redundant supervisors running stateful switchover (SSO).

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming preemption is automatic: it is disabled by default in HSRP (enabled in VRRP), so a repaired primary does not take back the active role.
  • Running an FHRP without uplink tracking; the active router keeps the gateway role even after its WAN link dies, black-holing traffic.
  • Mismatched group numbers, versions or authentication between peers, so both routers become active and hosts see duplicate-address warnings.

docs.title: Try it: VRRP on a lab router (Cisco IOS-XE syntax)
docs.text:
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 10.10.10.2 255.255.255.0
 vrrp 10 address-family ipv4
  address 10.10.10.1 primary
  priority 120
!
show vrrp brief

docs.title: Key protocols, devices, standards & tools
docs.text: Name What it does Example First Hop Redundancy Protocol (FHRP)Umbrella term (HSRP, VRRP, GLBP) · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Any protocol that provides a fault-tolerant default gateway shared by several routers. Every access VLAN in a campus core is protected by an FHRP on two distribution switches. HSRPCisco (proprietary); v1 described in IETF RFC 2281 · Protocol · Layer 3 · Current Hot Standby Router Protocol: one active and one standby router share a virtual IP; uses UDP 1985. Two Cisco core switches run HSRP version 2 for each user VLAN's gateway. VRRP (version 3)IETF RFC 9568 (2024, replaced RFC 5798) · Protocol · Layer 3 · Current Open-standard FHRP for IPv4 and IPv6; master and backups, IP protocol 112, multicast 224.0.0.18 / ff02::12. A Juniper and an Aruba router share gateway 10.0.0.1 using VRRP because both support the standard. GLBPCisco (proprietary) · Protocol · Layer 3 · Legacy Gateway Load Balancing Protocol: one virtual IP but up to four virtual MACs, so several routers forward traffic at once. Half the PCs get router A's virtual MAC in ARP replies, half get router B's, sharing the load. Virtual IP and virtual MACFHRP mechanism · Concept · Layer 2 · Current The shared gateway address and its MAC; VRRP uses 00:00:5e:00:01:XX, HSRPv1 uses 00:00:0c:07:ac:XX (XX = group). After a failover, hosts keep the same ARP entry because the virtual MAC moves with the role. Priority and preemptionFHRP mechanism · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Higher priority wins the active role (default 100); preemption lets it take back control after recovering. With preemption on, R1 (priority 120) becomes active again once it reboots. Interface / object trackingVendor feature · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Lowers a router's FHRP priority when an uplink or route fails, so a better-connected router takes over. If R1's ISP link goes down, its priority drops by 30 and R2 becomes the gateway. IP SLA / reachability probesCisco IP SLA; Juniper RPM; similar on other vendors · Technology · Layer 3 · Current Routers send regular test packets (ping, HTTP, jitter) to a target and remove a route or lower FHRP priority if probes fail. IP SLA pings 8.8.8.8 via ISP A every 5 seconds; after three failures the tracked default route is withdrawn and ISP B takes over. Multihoming (dual ISPs)Network design practice · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Connecting to two or more providers, using static routes with tracking or BGP, so the site survives a provider outage. A hospital runs eBGP with a fibre ISP and a cable ISP, announcing its /24 to both for automatic failover. Anycast gateway (distributed)EVPN-VXLAN fabrics (IETF RFC 9135) · Technology · Layer 3 · Current Every leaf switch hosts the same gateway IP and MAC, so hosts always use their local switch as gateway. A virtual machine moves between racks and keeps the same gateway without any failover delay. ECMPSupported by OSPF, IS-IS, BGP (RFC 2992 analysis) · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Equal-Cost Multi-Path: traffic is spread across several best paths of equal cost, usually by hashing flows. A data-centre leaf uses four equal uplinks to the spines, using all of them at once. BFDIETF RFC 5880; RFC 5881 (single-hop, UDP 3784) · Protocol · Layer 3 · Current Bidirectional Forwarding Detection: lightweight hellos that detect link failures in milliseconds and alert routing protocols. BFD at 300 ms × 3 lets OSPF react in under a second instead of waiting 40 seconds. Graceful restart / Non-Stop ForwardingIETF RFC 3623 (OSPF), RFC 4724 (BGP) · RFC · Layer 3 · Current Lets a router keep forwarding while its control plane restarts, with neighbours keeping its routes. A software upgrade on a dual-supervisor chassis causes no packet loss thanks to NSF.

docs.title: 3.13 MPLS, Segment Routing & VRFs
docs.text:
MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) forwards packets using short labels instead of looking up full IP addresses at every hop, which makes private VPNs and traffic engineering possible. VRFs (Virtual Routing and Forwarding) give one router several completely separate routing tables, like having many virtual routers in one box. Segment Routing is a newer, simpler way to steer traffic by listing the path in the packet itself.

An L3VPN packet crossing an MPLS core. Core routers only ever look at the top label; customer routes live only on the PEs.

Think of it like…

MPLS is like a parcel depot that sticks a coloured routing label on each box at the entrance; every sorting centre just reads the label, not the full address, until the last depot peels it off.

Real-world example

Carrier NetLink sells an MPLS L3VPN to Bluebird Bakeries (20 shops) and Greenleaf Pharmacy (15 shops). Both customers use 10.0.0.0/8 internally, but each sits in its own VRF on NetLink's PE routers, so their routes never mix. A packet from a Bluebird shop gets a VPN label and a transport label at the ingress PE, P routers swap the transport label hop by hop, and the egress PE uses the VPN label to place it in Bluebird's VRF.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The ingress Label Edge Router (PE) classifies the packet and pushes one or more labels.
  2. Label Switch Routers (P) in the core swap the top label and forward based on a label table.
  3. With penultimate hop popping, the second-to-last router removes the transport label.
  4. The egress PE reads the remaining VPN label to choose the right VRF and forwards the IP packet.
  5. With Segment Routing, the ingress router lists the path as a stack of segment IDs (labels or IPv6 addresses) instead of using LDP or RSVP signalling.

Who uses it

Service-provider and large-enterprise WAN engineers, data-centre architects and candidates for CCNP/CCIE Service Provider or JNCIP-SP.

Key takeaway

An MPLS label header is 32 bits: 20-bit label, 3-bit Traffic Class, 1-bit Bottom-of-Stack, 8-bit TTL; MPLS sits between Layer 2 and Layer 3 ('Layer 2.5').

Going deeper

  • Labels 0-15 are reserved: 0 IPv4 explicit null, 1 router alert, 2 IPv6 explicit null, 3 implicit null (asks the upstream router to pop); ordinary labels go up to 1,048,575.
  • Each label adds 4 bytes, so an L3VPN packet with two labels needs a core MTU of at least 1508 bytes to carry full 1500-byte customer packets.
  • Routers keep a Label Information Base (all bindings learned) and a Label Forwarding Information Base (the labels actually used to forward), mirroring the RIB/FIB split.
  • Layer 2 services over MPLS include point-to-point pseudowires (VPWS), multipoint VPLS and the modern BGP-based EVPN, which now replaces VPLS in most new designs.
  • Segment Routing nodes share a global label block (SRGB, often 16000-23999); a node SID is an index into it, and TI-LFA gives about 50 ms protection for any topology.
  • Enterprises increasingly replace MPLS VPN circuits with SD-WAN over Internet links, but carriers still run MPLS or SR cores underneath many of those services.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Believing an MPLS VPN is encrypted; it separates traffic by labels and VRFs but provides no confidentiality, so sensitive data still needs IPsec or TLS.
  • Mixing up Route Distinguisher and Route Target: RD only makes routes unique, RT decides which VRFs import them.
  • Forgetting the extra label bytes in MTU planning, which causes silent drops of large packets only on VPN traffic.

docs.title: Try it: Create a VRF on a Linux lab machine
docs.text:
sudo ip link add blue type vrf table 10
sudo ip link set blue up
sudo ip link set eth1 master blue
ip route show vrf blue

An L3VPN packet carries two labels: a transport label on top and a VPN label beneath. A Provider Edge router connects a customer's CE router and holds that customer's VRF. An operator removes LDP and RSVP from its network, simplifying operations with Segment Routing.
