AF41 (DSCP 34) for video calls; AF21 (DSCP 18) for business apps; AF23 dropped before AF21. FIFOQueuing method · Concept First In, First Out: one queue, no priorities; the default on many fast interfaces. On FIFO, a voice packet waits behind 200 queued download packets, adding noticeable delay. WFQ / CBWFQQueuing methods (Weighted Fair Queuing; Class-Based WFQ) · Concept WFQ shares bandwidth fairly between flows; CBWFQ guarantees a minimum bandwidth to each defined class. CBWFQ guarantees the ERP class 30% of a WAN link even when backups try to take everything. LLQLow Latency Queuing (CBWFQ + strict priority queue) · Concept Adds a strict-priority queue to CBWFQ for voice/video, policed so it cannot starve other classes. priority percent 20 sends voice first but caps it at 20% of the link. Policing vs shapingTraffic conditioning · Concept Policing drops or re-marks traffic above a rate immediately; shaping buffers excess and sends it later, smoothing bursts. An ISP polices a customer to 100 Mbps; the customer shapes outbound traffic to 95 Mbps to avoid those drops. WREDWeighted Random Early Detection · Concept Drops a few low-priority packets early as a queue fills, making TCP senders slow down before the queue overflows. WRED drops AF13 packets before AF11, protecting more important traffic in the same class. QoS for voice and videoGuidelines: IETF RFC 4594; ITU-T G.114 · Concept Voice needs low delay, jitter under about 30 ms and loss under 1%; video needs more bandwidth with similar limits. A design reserves EF for voice, AF41 for video and makes sure total priority traffic stays under a third of the link. Trust boundaryQoS design practice · Concept · Multi-layer · Current The point where the network starts believing packet markings; traffic from untrusted devices is re-marked to safe values. Access switches trust DSCP only from IP phones detected via CDP or LLDP-MED; a PC marking its downloads EF is reset to 0. WMM (Wi-Fi Multimedia)Wi-Fi Alliance certification based on IEEE 802.11e · Standard · Layer 2 · Current Wi-Fi QoS with four access categories (voice, video, best effort, background) giving time-sensitive traffic a better chance at airtime. A Wi-Fi phone's voice frames use the voice category, so they wait less for the air than a laptop's background file sync.

docs.title: 7.10 Troubleshooting Methodology
docs.text:
Troubleshooting is finding and fixing the cause of a network problem in an organised way rather than guessing. A methodology is a repeatable checklist so you don't skip steps, fix the wrong thing, or forget to write down what you did. Most problems are simple ones (a cable, a setting, DNS) once you look methodically.

CompTIA's 7-step troubleshooting method. Steps 2 and 3 loop until a theory is confirmed or the problem is escalated.

Think of it like…

A good troubleshooter works like a doctor: ask about symptoms, form a likely diagnosis, run tests to confirm, treat, check the patient recovered, and write it in the notes.

Real-world example

Sales staff on the third floor cannot reach the CRM, while other floors can. Using divide and conquer, the technician pings the floor's gateway: no reply. The switch shows the uplink port in VLAN 1 instead of trunking VLAN 30 after a switch replacement last night. Correcting the trunk restores access; she verifies with users, documents the cause and adds the trunk config to the replacement checklist.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Identify the problem: gather information, question users, find symptoms, check recent changes, duplicate it.
  2. 2-3. Establish a theory of probable cause, then test it (question the obvious; if wrong, form a new theory or escalate).
    1. Establish a plan of action and identify potential effects.
    1. Implement the solution or escalate as necessary.
    1. Verify full system functionality and implement preventive measures.
    1. Document findings, actions, outcomes and lessons learned.

Who uses it

Help-desk staff, field technicians, network and systems engineers, and anyone sitting CompTIA Network+ or A+.

Key takeaway

CompTIA asks the 7 steps in order; remember 'Identify, Theory, Test, Plan, Implement, Verify, Document', and always check 'what changed recently?' first.

Going deeper

  • Ask scoping questions first: who is affected, since when, what changed, is it constant or intermittent, and can you reproduce it? One user versus a whole floor points to very different layers.
  • Change correlation solves many incidents: check change tickets, config diffs from Oxidized or Git, and device logs from the hour before symptoms began before exploring exotic theories.
  • Interface counters tell a story: rising CRC or FCS errors suggest cabling or interference, output drops suggest congestion, and late collisions on a full-duplex link indicate a duplex mismatch.
  • Half-split testing finds faults fastest on long paths: test the middle point, then the half that fails, so a path of ten devices needs only about four tests.
  • Escalate with evidence: a good ticket lists symptoms, timestamps, affected users, tests run with their output and what you have already ruled out, saving the next engineer hours.
  • Intermittent problems need data over time: continuous ping or mtr, Smokeping graphs, logging and ring-buffer packet captures running until the fault reappears.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Changing several things at once; if the problem disappears you will not know which change fixed it or which one broke something else.
  • Skipping verification with the user; the link may be up while the original application still fails for another reason.
  • Assuming the latest change is innocent because 'it was tiny'; small ACL, VLAN or DNS edits cause a large share of outages.
  • Not documenting the fix, so the same fault costs another engineer the same hours next month.

docs.title: Try it: Bottom-up checks from a Windows PC in four commands
docs.text:
ipconfig /all              # L1-L3: link up? valid IP? gateway? DNS?
ping 192.168.1.1          # can I reach my gateway?
ping 1.1.1.1              # can I reach the internet by IP?
nslookup example.com      # does name resolution work?

docs.title: Key protocols, devices, standards & tools
docs.text: Name What it does Example CompTIA 7-step troubleshooting methodCompTIA (Network+ N10-009 objectives) · Standard Identify, theorise, test, plan, implement or escalate, verify and prevent, then document lessons learned. A Network+ question asks what to do after implementing a fix: answer 'verify full system functionality'. Bottom-up approachOSI-based troubleshooting · Concept Start at Layer 1 (cables, lights) and work up through addressing, routing and applications. No link light on the PC's port means stop there: test the cable before blaming DNS. Top-down approachOSI-based troubleshooting · Concept Start at the application (Layer 7) and work down; good when lower layers obviously work. Other websites load fine, so begin with the failing web app's settings and certificate. Divide and conquerOSI-based troubleshooting · Concept Start in the middle (often Layer 3 with ping) and move up or down depending on the result. Ping to the server works, so Layers 1-3 are fine; next check the service port and application. Follow the pathTroubleshooting technique · Concept Trace the traffic's route device by device from source to destination, checking each hop. tracert stops after the branch firewall, so its rules and routes are examined next. Duplex mismatchCommon Layer 1/2 fault · Concept · Layer 2 One side runs full duplex and the other half; the link works but is slow with late collisions and CRC errors. A server hard-set to 100/full facing an auto-negotiating switch port falls back to half duplex; set both to auto. IP address conflictCommon Layer 3 fault · Concept · Layer 3 Two devices share one IP address, causing intermittent connectivity and OS warnings. A static printer at 10.0.0.50 sits inside the DHCP pool; exclude it from the scope or use a reservation. DNS failureCommon Layer 7 fault · Concept · Layer 7 Pings by IP work but names fail; caused by wrong DNS server settings, a down server or bad records. ping 1.1.1.1 works but ping example.com fails, so nslookup reveals the DNS server is unreachable. Wrong default gatewayCommon Layer 3 fault · Concept · Layer 3 The device reaches its own subnet but nothing beyond, because the gateway address is wrong or missing. A PC set to gateway 192.168.1.254 when the router is .1 can print locally but cannot browse. VLAN mismatchCommon Layer 2 fault · Concept · Layer 2 A port is in the wrong VLAN, a VLAN is missing from a trunk, or native VLANs differ between switches. show interfaces trunk shows VLAN 30 not allowed on the uplink, so the third floor is cut off. MTU issuesCommon Layer 3 fault · Concept · Layer 3 Packets larger than a link's MTU are dropped when fragmentation is blocked; small pages load, big transfers hang. ping -f -l 1472 example.com fails over a VPN but -l 1400 works, revealing a reduced tunnel MTU. Switching loopsCommon Layer 2 fault (prevented by STP, IEEE 802.1D/802.1w) · Concept · Layer 2 A redundant cable without Spanning Tree causes broadcast storms that freeze the whole network within seconds. A user plugs both ends of a patch cable into a desk switch; BPDU Guard shuts the port and saves the network. Cable faultsCommon Layer 1 fault · Concept · Layer 1 Broken, crushed, badly terminated or too-long cables cause no link, slow speeds or rising error counters. A cable tester shows pair 3-6 open on a crushed cable behind a filing cabinet. Troubleshooting toolsField and software tools · Tool Cable tester, tone generator and probe, OTDR, Wi-Fi analyzer, protocol analyzer and command-line tools. Use a toner to find the cable, a tester to check it, then ipconfig and ping to confirm the PC works. Interface error countersshow interfaces (Cisco), ip -s link (Linux), Get-NetAdapterStatistics (Windows) · Concept · Layer 2 Counters for CRC errors, input errors, drops, collisions and resets reveal physical faults, duplex problems and congestion on a port. show interfaces Gi1/0/12 shows 48,000 CRC errors and rising, so the patch lead is replaced and the counter stops climbing. Common wireless issuesCommon Layer 1/2 wireless faults · Concept · Layer 1 Weak signal, co-channel interference, wrong channel width, roaming problems and too many clients per AP cause slow or dropping Wi-Fi. Meeting-room laptops show -78 dBm; adding an AP and narrowing channels from 80 to 40 MHz restores stable video calls.

docs.title: 7.11 Network Cabling & Field Tools
docs.text:
Field tools are the hand tools and test devices technicians carry to build and repair the physical network: cutting and fitting cables, finding cables in walls, and proving that copper, fibre and Wi-Fi meet the required standard. Many network problems turn out to be physical, so these tools solve a lot of tickets.

Which field tool for which job

Copper Fibre Find the cable Tone generator & probe VFL red light Check wiring Wiremap verifier Polarity check with VFL Prove performance Certifier (NEXT, loss) Light source + power meter Locate a fault TDR distance-to-fault OTDR trace Prevent faults Keep twists to the contact Inspect and clean end-faces Check a live port Link tester (PoE, VLAN) SFP optical power (DOM)

Copper and fibre need different tools for the same questions.

Think of it like…

They are the electrician's toolbox for data: crimpers instead of pliers, testers instead of a voltmeter, and a toner instead of a stud finder.

Real-world example

Jordan is installing an office: he terminates Cat6 cables onto a patch panel with a punch-down tool and fits RJ45 plugs with a crimper. A basic tester shows one cable has pairs crossed. After fixing it, a Fluke certifier proves every run passes Cat6 limits, and the report goes to the client. In a corner office, a Wi-Fi analyzer shows a neighbour's network on the same channel, so he moves the access point to a clear one.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Plan and pull cable, keeping under 100 m for copper Ethernet channels.
  2. Terminate: punch down at the patch panel/jack, crimp RJ45 plugs following T568A or T568B.
  3. Test continuity and wiring with a cable tester, or certify against the standard with a certifier.
  4. For fibre: inspect and clean connectors, use a VFL for breaks and an OTDR for long runs.
  5. Survey Wi-Fi with an analyzer to choose channels and AP locations.

Who uses it

Cabling installers, field technicians, data-centre staff, Wi-Fi engineers and help-desk staff who visit desks.

Key takeaway

'Inspect before you connect': a dirty fibre connector is the most common cause of fibre problems, so always inspect and clean first.

Going deeper

  • Copper testers come in three tiers: verifiers check wiremap and continuity, qualifiers prove a link can carry a speed such as 1 or 10 Gb/s, and certifiers prove compliance with a TIA or ISO category.
  • TIA fibre testing has two tiers: Tier 1 measures end-to-end loss with a light source and power meter, while Tier 2 adds an OTDR trace showing every connector and splice.
  • OTDRs need a launch fibre, and ideally a receive fibre, of a few hundred metres so the first and last connectors fall outside the instrument's dead zone and can be measured.
  • Common wiremap faults are opens, shorts, reversed pairs, crossed pairs and split pairs; split pairs pass simple continuity tests but fail certification because of crosstalk.
  • Most SFP transceivers report digital optical monitoring (DOM): transmit and receive power in dBm, temperature and voltage, viewable with show interfaces transceiver, often saving a site visit.
  • Wi-Fi tools differ: analyzers list visible networks, survey tools map coverage on floor plans, and spectrum analyzers reveal non-Wi-Fi interference such as microwave ovens, wireless cameras or Bluetooth.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Looking into a fibre end to check for light; invisible infrared lasers can damage eyes, so use a power meter or VFL instead.
  • Assuming a continuity pass means the cable supports gigabit; split pairs and poor terminations need a qualifier or certifier to detect.
  • Connecting fibre without inspecting both end-faces, transferring dirt to the mating connector and damaging expensive optics.
  • Untwisting too much wire when terminating Cat6; keep pairs twisted to within about 13 mm (0.5 in) of the contacts to avoid crosstalk failures.

docs.title: Try it: Check what the physical link negotiated and look at Wi-Fi channels
docs.text:
# Linux: link speed, duplex and error counters
ethtool eth0
ip -s link show eth0
# Windows: nearby Wi-Fi networks, signal and channel
netsh wlan show networks mode=bssid

docs.title: Key protocols, devices, standards & tools
docs.text: Name What it does Example Crimping toolVarious manufacturers · Tool · Layer 1 Presses an RJ45 (8P8C) plug onto twisted-pair cable, pushing the contacts into each wire. Jordan untwists minimal wire, follows T568B (orange-white first) and crimps a new patch cable. Punch-down toolVarious manufacturers (110 and Krone blades) · Tool · Layer 1 Pushes wires into insulation-displacement contacts on patch panels and keystone jacks and trims the excess. Each Cat6 run is punched into the back of the patch panel using a 110 blade. Copper tester tiers (verifier, qualifier, certifier)e.g. Fluke Networks (MicroScanner verifier, DSX certifier), Klein, NetAlly · Device · Layer 1 Verifiers check wiremap and length, qualifiers prove a link supports a given Ethernet speed, and certifiers prove compliance with a cable category. A MicroScanner finds swapped pairs at one desk, while a DSX certification report proves 400 new runs meet Cat6A for the warranty. Tone generator and probe (toner)Various (often called 'fox and hound') · Device · Layer 1 The generator puts a tone on a cable; the probe beeps when held near that cable, so you can find it in a bundle. The technician clips the toner to a wall jack and finds the matching unlabelled cable at the patch panel. Loopback plugVarious · Device · Layer 1 Plug that sends a port's transmit signal back to its receive pins, testing the port without another device. An RJ45 loopback plug makes a switch port light up, proving the port works and the fault is the cable. Fibre test kit (scope, VFL, power meter, OTDR)Tier 1 and Tier 2 testing per ANSI/TIA-568; vendors such as EXFO, VIAVI, Fluke Networks · Device · Layer 1 Inspect and clean end-faces, find breaks with a red VFL, measure total loss with a power meter, and locate faults by distance with an OTDR. Loss reads 6 dB against a 3 dB budget, so the technician shoots an OTDR trace and finds a bad splice 1.37 km away. MultimeterVarious · Device · Layer 1 Measures voltage, resistance and continuity; useful for PoE checks and power issues in racks. The technician confirms a UPS outlet supplies 230 V before plugging in a new switch. Wi-Fi analyzer appse.g. WiFi Analyzer apps (Android, Windows), NetSpot · Software · Layer 1 Show nearby networks, signal strength (dBm), channels and overlap, helping pick the clearest channel. The analyzer shows five networks on channel 6, so the AP is moved to channel 11 on 2.4 GHz. NetSpotEtwok · Software · Layer 1 Wi-Fi survey and analysis tool for Windows and macOS that draws heatmaps of signal across a floor plan. A walk-through survey heatmap reveals a dead zone in the meeting room, so another AP is added. EkahauEkahau (part of Ookla) · Software · Layer 1 Professional Wi-Fi design and survey suite with a dedicated measurement device; an industry standard for enterprise Wi-Fi. A hospital Wi-Fi engineer predicts coverage in Ekahau before installing, then validates it with an on-site survey. inSSIDerMetaGeek · Software · Layer 1 Wi-Fi scanner showing networks, channel use and signal strength, popular with beginners and small businesses. inSSIDer shows the office SSID using an 80 MHz channel overlapping a neighbour, so it is narrowed to 40 MHz. Console cableRJ45-to-DB9 rollover, USB-to-serial and USB console cables · Cable · Layer 1 Connects a laptop to a device's console port for direct CLI access even with no IP configured; usually 9600 baud, 8N1. A new switch has no IP address yet, so the technician uses a USB-to-RJ45 console cable and PuTTY at 9600 baud to configure it. Spectrum analyzere.g. Ekahau Sidekick 2; spectrum features in many enterprise APs · Device · Layer 1 Shows raw radio energy across a band, revealing non-Wi-Fi interference that ordinary Wi-Fi scanners cannot see. The spectrum view shows a wide 2.4 GHz spike every lunchtime: the staff-room microwave oven next to the access point. Network link testere.g. NetAlly LinkRunner · Device · Multi-layer Handheld tester for live ports showing link speed, PoE power, the nearest switch and port via LLDP/CDP, VLAN and DHCP results. At a dead desk socket, the tester shows switch port Gi1/0/22 in VLAN 99, so the port is moved to the staff VLAN.

docs.title: 7.12 Network Change, Backup & High Availability Practices
docs.text:
This topic is about running a network safely: planning changes so they don't cause outages, keeping backups of every device's settings, and designing with spare parts and paths so one failure doesn't stop the business. It also covers how you get back in when the network itself is broken, and how you recover from a disaster.

Allowed downtime per year. Each extra nine of availability cuts permitted downtime by a factor of ten.

Think of it like…

It is like planning a house renovation: get the plan approved, do the noisy work when nobody's home, keep the old keys, have a spare generator, and know where the family meets if there's a fire.

Real-world example

A logistics company needs to upgrade its core switch firmware. The change is approved by the change board with a rollback plan and scheduled for Sunday 02:00-04:00. Configs are backed up first, and the redundant core pair is upgraded one switch at a time so traffic keeps flowing. When one switch fails to boot, the engineer reaches it through the console server and restores the previous image. Nobody in the warehouse notices.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Raise a change request: what, why, risk, impact, test, implementation and rollback plan.
  2. Get approval (e.g. from a Change Advisory Board) and schedule a maintenance window.
  3. Back up configs and verify the backup before starting.
  4. Implement, verify, and roll back if checks fail.
  5. Design for failure: redundant devices, links and power, plus out-of-band access.
  6. Document the result and test disaster recovery plans regularly.

Who uses it

Network engineers, IT managers, change managers, data-centre and NOC teams, and auditors checking compliance.

Key takeaway

Always have a tested rollback plan, and remember the 3-2-1 backup rule: 3 copies, on 2 types of media, with 1 off-site.

Going deeper

  • Availability can be estimated as MTBF ÷ (MTBF + MTTR): raise it with more reliable equipment (higher MTBF) or by recovering faster with spares, backups and runbooks (lower MTTR).
  • ITIL change types: standard changes are pre-approved and low risk, normal changes go through assessment and approval, and emergency changes are fast-tracked but reviewed afterwards.
  • Platforms offer safety nets: Junos and IOS XR commit confirmed, Arista EOS configuration sessions with commit timers, and Cisco IOS configure terminal revert timer all undo changes automatically unless confirmed.
  • Disaster recovery sites trade cost for speed: a hot site mirrors production and takes over in minutes, a warm site needs data and configs restored, and a cold site is only space and power.
  • Out-of-band networks usually combine a separate ISP or 4G/5G link, a management VRF and console servers, so engineers can reach devices even when routing or the firewall is broken.
  • Test backups and failover regularly: a backup that has never been restored, or a redundant link never failed over, is an assumption rather than real protection.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Redundant devices sharing one hidden single point of failure, such as both core switches on one UPS or both ISP circuits in the same trench.
  • Making 'quick' changes outside the change process during business hours; many outages trace back to unreviewed manual edits.
  • Keeping config backups only on the device or in the same rack, so fire, theft or ransomware destroys every copy at once.
  • Upgrading both members of a redundant pair at the same time, removing the very redundancy meant to keep traffic flowing.

docs.title: Try it: Save and back up a lab Cisco config, with an automatic rollback safety net
docs.text:
copy running-config startup-config
copy running-config tftp://192.168.56.5/core1-before-change.cfg
show archive
! IOS safety net: auto-rollback in 10 minutes unless confirmed
configure terminal revert timer 10
! ... make change, test ...
configure confirm

docs.title: Key protocols, devices, standards & tools
docs.text: Name What it does Example Change managementITIL 4 'change enablement' practice · Concept A formal process to request, assess, approve, schedule and review changes so risks are understood beforehand. A firewall rule change goes through a ticket with risk rating, peer review and a planned rollback. Change Advisory Board (CAB)ITIL · Concept A group of stakeholders that reviews and approves significant changes and spots clashes between them. The CAB delays a WAN change because the finance team is running month-end payroll that night. Maintenance windowOperations practice · Concept A pre-agreed, low-impact time slot when disruptive changes are allowed and users are warned. Retail stores allow network changes only Sunday to Monday 01:00-05:00 when tills are closed. Config backupOperations practice (tools: Oxidized, RANCID, vendor managers) · Concept Regular, automatic copies of every device's configuration, stored securely with version history. A failed switch is replaced and its config restored from last night's backup within 20 minutes. Golden configNetDevOps practice · Concept An approved standard configuration template; devices are checked against it to catch drift and errors. A compliance report shows 12 switches missing the standard NTP and logging lines from the golden config. Rollback planChange management · Concept Exact, pre-written steps to undo a change if it fails, with a clear decision time to trigger it. If users cannot log in by 03:00, restore the saved config and reload the previous firmware. Redundancy designHigh-availability design · Concept Removing single points of failure with paired devices, first-hop redundancy (VRRP/HSRP), multiple links, diverse paths and dual ISPs. Two core switches, dual uplinks from every access switch, and two ISPs on different cable routes. UPSVarious (e.g. APC by Schneider Electric, Eaton) · Device · Layer 1 Uninterruptible Power Supply: battery that keeps equipment running through power cuts and cleans up power spikes. A rack UPS keeps the core and firewall running for 25 minutes until the building generator starts. Out-of-band managementOperations practice · Concept A separate path to manage devices (console, dedicated management network or cellular link) that works when production fails. When a bad ACL locks everyone out, the engineer logs in through the out-of-band network and fixes it. Console servere.g. Opengear, Lantronix, Cisco · Device · Layer 1 Device with many serial console ports, reachable remotely (often with 4G/5G backup), giving console access to every device. From home, the engineer opens a console session to a router stuck in ROMMON through the console server. Disaster recovery (RTO / RPO)Business continuity practice (e.g. NIST SP 800-34, ISO 22301) · Concept Plans to restore service after major failure. RTO is how fast you must recover; RPO is how much data you can lose. RTO 4 hours, RPO 15 minutes: the DR site must be running within 4 hours with data no older than 15 minutes. 3-2-1 backup ruleBackup best practice · Concept Keep 3 copies of data, on 2 different media types, with 1 copy off-site (ideally one offline or immutable). Configs live in Git on-site, are copied to a NAS, and synced to cloud storage in another region. Post-implementation reviewITIL / operations practice · Concept Checks after a change or incident whether it met its goals and what to improve next time. A blameless review after a failed change adds a pre-check script to the standard procedure. Single point of failure (SPOF)High-availability design · Concept Any one component whose failure stops the whole service: a lone firewall, one ISP circuit, a single power feed or one shared trench. A design review finds both 'diverse' ISP circuits enter the building through one duct, so a second entry point is ordered. MTBF / MTTRReliability engineering · Concept Mean Time Between Failures measures how long equipment usually runs; Mean Time To Repair measures how quickly service is restored. Keeping a spare, pre-configured switch on site cuts MTTR from a four-hour vendor dispatch to twenty minutes. Hot, warm and cold sitesBusiness continuity practice · Concept Disaster recovery locations ranked by readiness: hot sites run ready to take over, warm sites need restoring, cold sites offer only space and power. A bank uses a hot site for card payments with an RTO of minutes, but a cold site for its archive systems.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Network Security Basics, Standards, RFCs & Your Learning Path
docs.text: This chapter ties everything together: the defences that keep networks safe (firewalls, ACLs, zero trust and network access control), the official documents (RFCs and IEEE standards) that define how networks work, and a practical road map for learning. You will meet free labs, respected certifications, classic books and the interview questions employers really ask. Think of it as your toolkit and travel guide for the journey from beginner to job-ready.

docs.title: 8.1 Network Security Essentials for Students
docs.text:
Network security means stopping the wrong people or traffic from reaching things they should not, while letting the right traffic through. No single tool does it all, so networks stack several layers of protection, from switch port settings up to firewalls and monitoring systems. This is called 'defence in depth'.

Defence in depth, outside in. An attacker must defeat every layer; each one buys time and creates evidence.

Think of it like…

A well-run office building has a fence, a reception desk that checks badges, locked doors on each floor, cameras in the corridors and a guard who calls the police; network security layers its protections in exactly the same way.

Real-world example

Brightwater College puts student Wi-Fi, staff PCs and servers in separate VLANs. Students must log in with 802.1X before getting network access, switch ports use DHCP snooping and Dynamic ARP Inspection to stop fake routers, and a stateful firewall only lets the public web server in the DMZ accept HTTPS. An IPS watches for attack patterns, and teachers working from home connect through a WireGuard VPN.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Know what you protect: list devices, data and who needs access to what.
  2. Control who connects: 802.1X/NAC, port security and strong Wi-Fi (WPA3).
  3. Protect the local network: DHCP snooping, Dynamic ARP Inspection, separate VLANs.
  4. Control traffic between zones: ACLs and firewalls, with a DMZ for public servers.
  5. Protect remote and site-to-site links with VPNs (IPsec, TLS VPN, WireGuard).
  6. Watch and respond: IDS/IPS, logs and DDoS protection; assume breach (zero trust).

Who uses it

Network and security engineers, SOC analysts and anyone running a home, school or company network.

Key takeaway

Know the CCNA vocabulary: a threat is a potential danger, a vulnerability is a weakness, an exploit abuses it, and mitigation reduces the risk; layered defences beat any single control.

Going deeper

  • The CIA triad frames every control: encryption protects confidentiality, hashes and signatures protect integrity, and redundancy plus DDoS defences protect availability.
  • Vulnerabilities are catalogued as CVE IDs and scored from 0 to 10 with CVSS; Internet-facing VPN gateways and firewalls are favourite targets, so patch them first and follow vendor advisories.
  • Layer 2 attacks such as MAC flooding, ARP poisoning, rogue DHCP and VLAN hopping are stopped at the access port with port security, DAI, DHCP snooping and disabled DTP.
  • Social engineering bypasses technology entirely, which is why CCNA lists user awareness, training and physical access control as security program elements alongside technical controls.
  • Zero trust replaces 'trusted inside, untrusted outside' with per-request decisions using identity, device posture and context; ZTNA products apply it to remote access instead of full-tunnel VPNs.
  • An IDS watches a copy of traffic from SPAN or a TAP and cannot block; an IPS sits inline, so a false positive blocks real users and a failure cuts traffic unless it fails open.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Believing NAT is a firewall; it hides addresses as a side effect, but only explicit stateful rules decide what may enter or leave.
  • Adding a temporary 'permit any any' rule during troubleshooting and forgetting it, leaving a hole that auditors or attackers find months later.
  • Relying on one perimeter firewall while every internal VLAN can reach every other, so malware spreads freely once inside.
  • Leaving SSH, HTTPS and SNMP management reachable from user or guest networks instead of a dedicated management network.

docs.title: Key protocols, devices, standards & tools
docs.text: Name What it does Example CIA triadInformation security fundamentals · Concept Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability: the three goals every security control protects, used to classify threats and defences. A VPN protects confidentiality, a file hash protects integrity, and dual ISP links with DDoS protection protect availability. Common network attacksThreat landscape (catalogued in e.g. MITRE ATT&CK) · Concept · Multi-layer Spoofing, man-in-the-middle, DoS/DDoS, rogue DHCP servers or access points, VLAN hopping, password attacks and phishing are the classics to recognise. An evil-twin access point named 'Cafe_Free_WiFi' tricks users into connecting so the attacker can watch their unencrypted traffic. Access-port hardening checklistSwitch security best practice (Cisco, Juniper, HPE Aruba and others) · Concept · Layer 2 · Current Combine port security, DHCP snooping, Dynamic ARP Inspection, BPDU Guard and shutting unused ports on every user-facing switch port. A school template applies all five to 800 classroom ports, so a student's rogue router or ARP-spoofing tool gets nowhere. Network segmentationDesign practice using VLANs, subnets, VRFs, microsegmentation · Concept · Multi-layer · Current Splitting a network into separate zones so a problem in one area cannot spread freely. Limits damage from malware and intruders. A factory keeps machine controllers, office PCs and guest Wi-Fi in different VLANs, with firewall rules between them. IDS / IPSOpen source Snort, Suricata, Zeek; built into many firewalls · Tool · Multi-layer · Current An intrusion detection system alerts on suspicious traffic; an intrusion prevention system sits inline and blocks it automatically. Suricata spots a known exploit pattern aimed at a web server and the IPS drops the packets before they reach it. DDoS protectionProviders such as Cloudflare, Akamai, AWS Shield; ISP scrubbing · Service · Multi-layer · Current Absorbs or filters floods of junk traffic from many machines so a website or network stays online during an attack. An online game's servers face a huge UDP flood; the DDoS provider's global network soaks it up and forwards only real players. Device hardeninge.g. CIS Benchmarks, vendor hardening guides · Concept · Multi-layer · Current Securing network devices themselves: change defaults, disable Telnet and unused services, use SSH and AAA, log centrally and patch firmware. A hardening script replaces Telnet with SSHv2, disables HTTP management, adds login banners and points AAA at a TACACS+ server. Threats, vulnerabilities & exploitsCCNA security vocabulary; CVE list (MITRE), CVSS scores (FIRST) · Concept · Multi-layer · Current A threat is a potential danger, a vulnerability is a weakness, an exploit is the method that abuses it; risk combines likelihood and impact. An unpatched VPN appliance (vulnerability) with a public exploit and active ransomware gangs (threat) is a critical risk: patch tonight. MalwareViruses, worms, trojans, ransomware, botnets · Concept · Multi-layer · Current Malicious software: worms spread across networks by themselves, ransomware encrypts data for payment, and botnets turn devices into remote-controlled attackers. The Mirai botnet hijacked IoT cameras that still had default passwords and used them for record-breaking DDoS attacks in 2016. Social engineeringCommon attack techniques (phishing, vishing, pretexting, tailgating) · Concept · Current Tricking people rather than machines into giving away passwords, money or physical access. A caller pretending to be the ISP asks the receptionist for the router password; her training tells her to hang up and call back. Physical securitySecurity practice (CCNA and Network+ objectives) · Concept · Layer 1 · Current Locks, badge readers, cameras and locked racks stop people touching network equipment, because physical access defeats most software controls. Comms cupboards use logged badge access, so the audit shows exactly who opened the core switch cabinet on Saturday. Passwords, MFA & password alternativesNIST SP 800-63B guidance; CCNA objective · Concept · Current Long, unique passphrases plus multi-factor authentication; alternatives include certificates, biometrics and passkeys (FIDO2). Network admins log in to the firewall with a hardware security key and PIN, so a phished password alone is useless. Security awareness & trainingSecurity program element (CCNA) · Concept · Current Teaching users and staff to spot phishing, report incidents and follow policy; people are often the first line of defence. After a year of monthly phishing simulations, staff at the fictional Ridgeway Bank report suspicious emails within minutes. Honeypots & deceptione.g. open-source OpenCanary and T-Pot; commercial deception platforms · Technology · Multi-layer · Current Decoy systems, files or credentials with no real purpose, so any interaction with them strongly signals an intruder. A fake 'HR-backup' file server alerts the SOC when an infected PC tries to log in to it.

docs.title: 8.2 Firewalls & Security Zones
docs.text:
A firewall is a checkpoint that decides which network traffic may pass between two places, using rules written by an administrator. Firewalls range from simple filters that only look at addresses and ports to 'next-generation' firewalls that also recognise applications and users. They sit at the edge of a network, between internal zones, on each computer and inside cloud networks.

Three generations of firewall

Packet filter Stateful NGFW Looks at L3-L4 headers Headers + connection state + apps, users, content Return traffic Needs its own rule Allowed automatically Allowed automatically Blocks an app on any port No No Yes Typical example Router ACL, cloud NACL Security group, home router FortiGate, Palo Alto Performance cost Lowest Low Higher with IPS/TLS inspection

Each generation keeps the abilities of the one before and adds more context.

Think of it like…

A firewall is like border control: officers check each traveller's passport (addresses), destination (port) and reason for travel (application) against a list of rules, and turn away anyone the rules do not allow.

Real-world example

Fernhill Clinic's FortiGate firewall has four zones: Inside (staff), Guest, DMZ and Outside. Rules let Inside reach the Internet on HTTPS, let Outside reach only the booking web server in the DMZ on TCP 443, and block Guest from every internal network. Because the firewall is stateful, replies to staff web requests come back automatically, while unsolicited inbound connections are dropped and logged.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Group interfaces or VLANs into zones by trust level, e.g. Inside, DMZ, Guest, Outside.
  2. Write rules: source, destination, service or application, action (allow/deny) and logging.
  3. Each new connection is checked against the rules top-down; the first match wins, then an implicit deny.
  4. Allowed connections enter the state table, so their return traffic passes without extra rules.
  5. NAT, VPN, IPS and TLS inspection are applied to matching traffic as configured.
  6. Logs go to a SIEM, and rules are reviewed regularly so unused ones can be removed.

Who uses it

Network and security engineers, firewall administrators, SOC analysts and cloud engineers build and audit firewall rules every day; firewall skills appear in almost every network job advert.

Key takeaway

Know the generations: packet filter (stateless, looks at Layer 3-4 headers), stateful inspection (tracks connections) and NGFW (adds application awareness, user identity and IPS); a WAF protects web applications specifically.

Going deeper

  • Stateful firewalls follow TCP states (SYN, established, FIN) and use idle timeouts for UDP and ICMP 'sessions'; long idle connections such as database links can silently time out and break.
  • NGFWs identify applications by signatures and behaviour (Palo Alto App-ID, Fortinet application control), so 'allow web-browsing' is far narrower than 'allow TCP 443', which any tunnel can use.
  • Datasheet throughput varies hugely: plain firewall throughput can be several times higher than 'threat protection' throughput with IPS, anti-malware and TLS inspection enabled, so size for the realistic figure.
  • Cloud security groups are stateful and allow-only, while cloud network ACLs are stateless with numbered allow and deny rules; many cloud designs layer both, plus a managed firewall for inspection.
  • Rule hygiene: name every rule, record an owner and change ticket, log denies, use address and service objects instead of raw IPs, and review regularly to remove shadowed or unused rules.
  • Linux netfilter processes packets at hooks (prerouting, input, forward, output, postrouting); conntrack supplies the state, which is why 'ct state established,related accept' appears near the top of most rule sets.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Allowing 'any' service between zones to save time; open only the ports and applications that are needed, and record why each rule exists.
  • Putting a broad allow rule above a specific deny; the deny never matches, so order rules from most specific to most general.
  • Enabling TLS inspection before deploying the company root certificate to devices, causing certificate warnings and broken apps everywhere.
  • Disabling host firewalls on servers because 'the perimeter firewall protects us', so one compromised machine can reach all the others.

A router ACL must explicitly permit replies from web servers, because it cannot tell a reply from a brand-new inbound connection. Stateful inspectionPopularised by Check Point FireWall-1 (1994); now standard in all firewalls · Concept · Layer 4 · Current Tracks every connection in a state table, so replies to allowed sessions return automatically while unsolicited inbound packets are dropped. A laptop opens HTTPS to a bank; the firewall records the connection and lets the bank's replies in, but drops a stranger's probe to port 445. Next-generation firewall (NGFW)e.g. Palo Alto Networks, Fortinet FortiGate, Cisco Secure Firewall, Check Point; open source OPNsense · Device · Multi-layer · Current Stateful firewall that also identifies applications and users, inspects TLS and blocks threats, enforcing rules between security zones. A ticketing website's WAF blocks a login request containing ' OR 1=1-- before it ever reaches the database. On hotel Wi-Fi a laptop switches to the Windows 'Public' profile, blocking inbound file sharing so other guests cannot browse its folders. nftables / iptablesLinux kernel netfilter project (nftables merged in Linux 3.13, 2014) · Software · Multi-layer · Current Linux's built-in packet filtering and NAT framework; nftables replaces iptables with one syntax for IPv4, IPv6 and bridging. 'nft list ruleset' shows a server's tables, chains and rules; firewalld and ufw are friendlier tools that write these rules for you. Cloud firewall servicesAWS Network Firewall, Azure Firewall, Google Cloud NGFW · Service · Multi-layer · Current Managed, automatically scaling firewalls inside cloud networks that inspect traffic between virtual networks, the Internet and on-premises links. A retailer sends all traffic leaving its Azure virtual networks through Azure Firewall, which allows only approved software-update domains. Rule base order (first match wins)Universal firewall behaviour · Concept · Multi-layer · Current Rules are evaluated from the top; the first rule that matches decides, so specific rules must sit above broad ones. A broad 'allow Staff to Any' rule above 'deny Staff to Payroll' makes the deny useless, because traffic never reaches it. Only the mail relay may send SMTP on TCP 25 to the Internet, so a compromised PC cannot spew spam directly. TLS inspection (decryption)NGFW and secure web gateway feature · Technology · Layer 7 · Current The firewall decrypts HTTPS with a company-trusted certificate, inspects the content and re-encrypts it; powerful but privacy-sensitive and CPU-heavy. Firewall high availabilityVendor features (FortiGate clustering, Palo Alto HA, Cisco Secure Firewall failover) · Concept · Multi-layer · Current Two firewalls run as an active/passive or active/active pair and synchronise session state, so a failure does not drop existing connections. During a firmware upgrade the passive unit takes over in under a second, and staff video calls continue without reconnecting.

docs.title: 8.3 Access Control Lists (ACLs)
docs.text:
An access control list (ACL) is an ordered list of permit and deny statements that a router, switch or firewall checks to decide whether a packet may pass. Each line matches things such as source address, destination address, protocol and port. ACLs are also used simply to select traffic for other features, such as NAT or QoS.

How a router processes an ACL. Processing stops at the first match; a packet that matches nothing meets the implicit deny.

Think of it like…

An ACL is like a bouncer reading a guest list from top to bottom: he stops at the first line that matches you and does exactly what it says, and if you are not on the list at all you are turned away.

Real-world example

At Kestrel Engineering only the IT subnet 10.10.99.0/24 should manage routers, so an engineer creates standard ACL MGMT-ONLY permitting 10.10.99.0 0.0.0.255 and applies it to the VTY lines. Separately, extended ACL BLOCK-GUEST, applied inbound on the guest VLAN interface, denies guest traffic to 10.0.0.0/8 and then permits web and DNS traffic, so guests reach only the Internet. 'show access-lists' hit counters prove both are working.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Decide what to match: source only (standard) or source, destination, protocol and ports (extended).
  2. Write entries in order, most specific first; each entry has a sequence number.
  3. Remember the invisible 'deny any' at the end; add an explicit permit if other traffic should pass.
  4. Apply the ACL to an interface in one direction (in or out), or to VTY lines for management access.
  5. Verify with 'show access-lists' hit counts and test from both an allowed and a blocked host.

Who uses it

CCNA candidates, network engineers and firewall administrators write ACLs; the same top-down logic appears in cloud network ACLs, Linux firewalls and switch security features.

Key takeaway

Exam rules: one ACL per interface, per direction, per protocol; standard ACLs go close to the destination and extended ACLs close to the source; every ACL ends with an implicit deny.

Going deeper

  • Cisco numbered ranges: standard 1-99 and 1300-1999, extended 100-199 and 2000-2699; named ACLs avoid the ranges and let you edit single lines by sequence number (default steps of 10).
  • Wildcard masks are inverted subnet masks: a 0 bit must match and a 1 bit is ignored. Subtract the mask from 255.255.255.255, so /26 (255.255.255.192) becomes 0.0.0.63.
  • Router ACLs are stateless: return traffic must be permitted explicitly or matched with 'established'; reflexive ACLs, zone-based firewalls and dedicated firewalls add proper connection state.
  • Hardware switches store ACL entries in TCAM, so very long ACLs can exhaust it; summarise address ranges and use object groups to keep the entry count low.
  • Outbound ACLs on Cisco routers do not filter packets the router creates itself, such as its own pings or routing updates; protect the device with VTY access-class and control-plane policing.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Writing only deny lines and forgetting a final permit, so the implicit deny blocks all other traffic and users lose access.
  • Typing a subnet mask where a wildcard mask belongs, e.g. 255.255.255.0 instead of 0.0.0.255, which matches completely different addresses.
  • Applying an ACL in the wrong direction or on the wrong interface; trace where the packet enters and leaves before choosing.
  • On classic IOS, typing 'no access-list 10 deny ...' to remove one line deletes the entire ACL; edit by sequence number in ACL configuration mode instead.

docs.title: Try it: Lab-only Cisco IOS: a named extended ACL that keeps guests off internal networks
docs.text:
ip access-list extended BLOCK-GUEST
 10 deny   ip 192.168.50.0 0.0.0.255 10.0.0.0 0.255.255.255
 20 permit udp 192.168.50.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 53
 30 permit tcp 192.168.50.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 443
 40 deny   ip any any log
!
interface Vlan50
 ip access-group BLOCK-GUEST in
!
show access-lists BLOCK-GUEST

docs.text: Name What it does Example Standard ACLCisco IOS (numbers 1-99, 1300-1999) and similar on other vendors · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Access control list that permits or denies packets using only the source IP address. Simple but blunt, so place it near the destination. access-list 10 permit 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255 applied to a router's management lines lets only the IT subnet reach SSH. Extended ACLCisco IOS (numbers 100-199, 2000-2699) and similar on other vendors · Concept · Multi-layer · Current ACL that matches source and destination IP, protocol and port numbers. Precise, so place it near the source to drop bad traffic early. access-list 110 permit tcp 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.2.2.10 eq 443 lets one office reach only the HTTPS service on a server. Named ACLCisco IOS 'ip access-list standard | extended NAME' · Concept · Multi-layer · Current An ACL identified by a descriptive name instead of a number, whose sequence-numbered lines can be inserted or deleted individually. Inside 'ip access-list extended WEB-IN', typing '15 permit tcp any host 10.1.1.20 eq 443' slots a new line between entries 10 and 20. Implicit denyCisco IOS and most ACL and firewall implementations · Concept · Multi-layer · Current The unseen final entry 'deny any' that drops every packet not matched by an earlier line. An ACL containing only 'deny host 10.1.1.9' blocks everyone, because all other traffic falls through to the implicit deny. ACL keywords: host and anyCisco IOS ACL syntax · Concept · Layer 3 · Current 'host 10.1.1.5' is shorthand for wildcard 0.0.0.0 (exactly one address); 'any' means 0.0.0.0 255.255.255.255 (every address). 'permit tcp any host 203.0.113.10 eq 443' lets anyone reach only the public web server's HTTPS port. ACL placementCisco design guidance (CCNA) · Concept · Multi-layer · Current Put extended ACLs close to the source to drop unwanted traffic early, and standard ACLs close to the destination so they block nothing extra. A standard ACL denying 10.2.0.0/16 at the branch would cut that branch off from everything, so it goes on the server-room router instead. Inbound vs outbound ACLsCisco IOS 'ip access-group NAME in | out' · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Inbound ACLs filter packets as they enter an interface, before routing; outbound ACLs filter packets after routing, as they leave. Applying the guest ACL 'in' on Vlan50 drops forbidden packets before the router spends effort routing them. VTY access-classCisco IOS 'access-class' under 'line vty' · Command · Layer 7 · Current Applies an ACL to the remote management lines, so only listed addresses can open SSH sessions to the device itself. 'line vty 0 15' then 'access-class MGMT-ONLY in' blocks SSH attempts from everywhere except the IT subnet. ACL hit counters & loggingCisco IOS 'show access-lists' and the 'log' keyword; similar counters on other vendors · Command · Multi-layer · Current Every entry counts its matches, and the log keyword sends matches to syslog, proving which line a flow actually hits. 'show access-lists' shows 1,240 matches on the deny-internal line, proving guests really tried to reach internal servers. IPv6 ACLsCisco IOS 'ipv6 access-list' and 'ipv6 traffic-filter' · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Always named; their implicit end rules permit neighbour discovery messages before the final deny, so ND keeps working. Adding an explicit 'deny ipv6 any any log' at the end also blocks neighbour discovery unless ND permits are written above it. TCP 'established' keywordCisco IOS extended ACL option · Concept · Layer 4 · Legacy Matches TCP segments with the ACK or RST flag set, crudely allowing replies to inside-initiated sessions without real state tracking. 'permit tcp any 10.1.0.0 0.0.255.255 established' lets web replies in, but cannot handle UDP replies such as DNS. Object groupsCisco IOS object-group; address and service groups on firewalls · Concept · Multi-layer · Current Named groups of addresses or services reused across many ACL entries, keeping lists short and readable. Group WEB-SERVERS holds six hosts, so one line permits HTTPS to all of them; adding a seventh server needs no new ACL line. ACLs as traffic selectorsCisco IOS (NAT, QoS class maps, route maps, crypto maps) · Concept · Multi-layer · Current ACLs also classify traffic for other features: which hosts get NAT, which traffic gets QoS, policy routing or VPN encryption. 'ip nat inside source list 1 interface g0/0 overload' uses ACL 1 to choose which inside hosts are translated. Port ACLs & VLAN ACLs (PACL / VACL)Cisco Catalyst switch features; similar filters on other vendors · Technology · Layer 2 · Current Switch ACLs applied to a Layer 2 port (PACL) or to all traffic inside a VLAN (VACL), filtering even between hosts in one subnet. A VACL stops cameras in VLAN 40 from talking to each other while still letting them reach the video recorder.

docs.title: 8.4 Zero Trust & Network Access Control (NAC)
docs.text:
Zero trust is a security approach that never trusts a user or device just because it is connected to the 'inside' network; every access request is checked using identity, device health and context. Network access control (NAC) is one building block: it checks who and what a device is before a switch port or Wi-Fi network lets it on, and then places it in the right segment.

Wired 802.1X with EAP-TLS. The switch only relays; the RADIUS server decides, and the port opens after Access-Accept.

Think of it like…

Old-style security is a castle: once over the drawbridge you can wander anywhere. Zero trust is a modern office where your badge is checked at every door you open, and the system also checks the badge really belongs to you.

Real-world example

Orchard Valley Council runs Cisco ISE. When a staff laptop is plugged into a meeting-room socket, the switch asks for 802.1X credentials; the laptop presents its certificate, and ISE checks the user's group and that disk encryption and antivirus are on before telling the switch to use the Staff VLAN. A printer without 802.1X software is identified by MAC Authentication Bypass and profiling and lands in the Printers VLAN. Remote staff use ZTNA instead of a full VPN, reaching only the apps they are approved for.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A device connects; the switch port or access point allows only authentication traffic.
  2. 802.1X (or MAB for devices without 802.1X software) sends the identity to a RADIUS/NAC server.
  3. The policy server checks identity, group, device posture and context such as time and location.
  4. It returns an authorisation result: a VLAN, a downloadable ACL or a security group tag.
  5. Checks continue; a Change of Authorization (CoA) can quarantine the device later.
  6. For applications, ZTNA grants per-app access instead of whole-network VPN access.

Who uses it

Security architects, network engineers deploying NAC (Cisco ISE, HPE Aruba ClearPass), identity teams and cloud teams applying zero trust; Network+ covers zero trust architecture and CCNA covers 802.1X and AAA.

Key takeaway

Memorise the three 802.1X roles: supplicant (the client), authenticator (the switch or access point) and authentication server (RADIUS); EAPOL runs between the first two and RADIUS between the last two.

Going deeper

  • NIST SP 800-207 tenets include: every data source and service is a resource, all communication is secured regardless of location, access is granted per session, and policy is dynamic.
  • 802.1X rollouts usually start in monitor (open) mode, logging failures without blocking, then move to low-impact mode and finally closed mode once every device type authenticates.
  • EAP-TLS with certificates issued by an internal PKI or device management is the strongest common method; PEAP-MSCHAPv2 is weaker and relies on clients validating the server certificate.
  • MAB alone is weak because MAC addresses are easy to spoof; combine it with profiling, restricted VLANs or ACLs, and alerts when a 'printer' suddenly behaves like a laptop.
  • Zero trust is a strategy, not a product: single sign-on with MFA, device management, segmentation, ZTNA and central logging must work together, and migration usually takes years.
  • Wired NAC can be paired with MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE) to encrypt the link between the authenticated device and the switch, defeating taps on the cable.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Jumping straight to closed mode on day one; unknown printers, phones and cameras fail authentication and whole departments go offline.
  • Believing zero trust is a single product to buy; it is an architecture combining identity, device health, segmentation and monitoring.
  • Having no plan for RADIUS outages; without a critical VLAN or local fallback, a dead policy server locks every user out.
  • Rolling out ZTNA but leaving the old full-access VPN running for everyone, so the wide-open path still exists.

A school district rates itself 'Initial' for devices and 'Advanced' for identity, then plans device posture checks for next year. An architect copies an SP 1800-35 example to design how laptops, identity provider and ZTNA gateway should work together. Web servers may reach the application tier only on TCP 8443, so ransomware on one web server cannot scan the others. The backup service account can read file shares but cannot log in interactively or change firewall rules.
