docs.title: Key protocols, devices, standards & tools
docs.text: Name What it does Example NodeGeneral networking concept · Concept Any device that connects to a network and can send, receive or forward data, such as a PC, phone, printer, switch or router. In a home network the laptop, smart TV, phone and the Wi-Fi router are all nodes. Link (transmission medium)General networking concept · Concept · Layer 1 The physical or wireless path that carries signals between two nodes: copper cable, fibre-optic glass or radio waves. A Cat 6 patch cable joining a desktop PC to a switch is a wired link; the Wi-Fi signal to a phone is a wireless link. PAN (Personal Area Network)IEEE 802.15 / Bluetooth SIG · Concept · Current A very small network around one person, usually within a few metres, linking personal gadgets. A smartwatch, wireless earbuds and a phone talking over Bluetooth form a PAN. LAN (Local Area Network)IEEE 802.3 (Ethernet) · Concept · Current A network covering one home, office or building, owned and run by one person or organisation, usually fast and low-cost. Twenty office PCs plugged into Ethernet switches on one floor make up a LAN. WLAN (Wireless LAN)IEEE 802.11 (Wi-Fi) · Concept · Current A LAN where devices connect by radio (Wi-Fi) instead of cables, through wireless access points. A café's Wi-Fi network that customers join with a password is a WLAN. CAN (Campus Area Network)General networking concept · Concept · Current Several LANs in nearby buildings joined together, typically over fibre, on a university, hospital or business campus. A university links its library, labs and dormitories with fibre so students roam on one network. MAN (Metropolitan Area Network)IEEE 802 LAN/MAN Standards Committee; Metro Ethernet · Concept · Current A network spanning a city or large town, often built by a city council or telecom provider. A city connects all its schools, libraries and traffic cameras over its own fibre ring. WAN (Wide Area Network)Carriers and ISPs (MPLS, SD-WAN, leased lines) · Concept · Current A network covering large distances, such as countries or continents, usually using links rented from telecom providers. A retail chain links its London head office to 300 shops across Europe over an SD-WAN. SAN (Storage Area Network)INCITS T11 (Fibre Channel); IETF RFC 7143 (iSCSI) · Concept · Current A dedicated high-speed network that connects servers to shared disk storage, so storage appears like a local drive. A hospital's database servers store patient records on a disk array reached over a Fibre Channel SAN. VPN (Virtual Private Network)IETF RFC 4301 (IPsec); WireGuard; TLS-based VPNs · Technology · Current An encrypted tunnel across a public network that makes a remote device or site behave as if it were on the private network. Sam works from home and connects through a VPN to reach his company's internal file server securely. InternetInterconnected networks using IP (IETF RFC 791, RFC 8200) · Concept · Current The global public 'network of networks': tens of thousands of independently run networks interconnected using the Internet Protocol. Streaming a film from a server in another country crosses your ISP, transit providers and the streaming company's network. IntranetGeneral networking concept · Concept · Current A private network using Internet technologies (web, email) that only an organisation's own staff can access. Employees at Northwind Logistics open an internal web portal for HR forms that is unreachable from outside. ExtranetGeneral networking concept · Concept · Current Part of an intranet opened up, with logins and controls, to trusted outsiders such as suppliers, partners or customers. Suppliers log into a carmaker's extranet portal to check parts orders and delivery schedules. Network protocolIETF, IEEE and other standards bodies · Concept An agreed set of rules for message format, order and meaning, so devices from different makers can understand each other. HTTP defines how a browser asks for a page; Ethernet defines how bits are framed on the cable. End devices vs intermediary devicesGeneral networking concept (Cisco CCNA terminology) · Concept · Multi-layer End devices (hosts) create or consume data; intermediary devices such as switches, routers and access points move it between them. In Maya's bakery the laptops and card terminal are end devices; the Wi-Fi router is the intermediary device.

docs.title: 1.2 Network Topologies
docs.text:
A topology is the shape or layout of a network: how the devices are connected to each other. The physical topology is how the cables actually run; the logical topology is how data really flows. Choosing a topology is a trade-off between cost, reliability and how easy it is to grow.

Star vs full mesh vs ring

Star Full mesh Ring Links for n devices n (one per device) n(n-1)/2 n 10 devices 10 links 45 links 10 links One cable fails Only that device drops Traffic reroutes Reroutes if dual ring Weak spot Central switch Cost and complexity Two breaks split it Typical use Office and home LANs Small WAN or core Metro fibre, SONET

Star is cheap and easy to fault-find; mesh buys resilience with many more links.

Think of it like…

Topologies are like ways of seating people at a party: everyone on one long bench (bus), everyone around a host (star), holding hands in a circle (ring), or everyone able to talk to everyone else (mesh).

Real-world example

Greenfield Secondary School uses a star in each classroom: every PC cables back to one switch. Those classroom switches connect up to building switches, which connect to a core switch in the server room, forming a tree. The two core switches and the two internet routers are cross-linked in a partial mesh, so one failed link does not take the school offline. Overall the school runs a hybrid topology.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Decide what matters most: lowest cost, highest reliability, easy expansion or predictable speed.
  2. Star is the default for modern wired LANs: every device has its own cable to a central switch.
  3. Add redundant links (partial mesh) between important devices so a single failure does not stop traffic.
  4. Combine shapes (tree, hybrid) as the network grows across floors, buildings and sites.
  5. In data centres, use spine-leaf so every server is the same small number of hops from every other server.

Who uses it

Network designers, installers and data-centre architects choose topologies; exam questions on CompTIA Network+ and Cisco CCNA often ask you to identify them.

Key takeaway

Full mesh needs n(n-1)/2 links: 5 devices need 10 links, 10 devices need 45, which is why full mesh is rare except in small cores or WAN designs.

Going deeper

  • Link counts drive cost: a full mesh of 20 sites needs 20 x 19 / 2 = 190 links, whereas hub-and-spoke needs only 19, which is why large WANs are rarely fully meshed.
  • Spine-leaf gives every leaf one uplink to each spine, so with 4 spines every rack has 4 equal-cost paths (ECMP); adding spines adds bandwidth without redesign.
  • Oversubscription measures how much a tier is overbooked: 48 x 25G server ports (1,200G) on 4 x 100G uplinks (400G) gives 3:1, a common data-centre target.
  • Small campuses often merge the core and distribution layers into a 'collapsed core' two-tier design, saving cost while keeping the hierarchical model's structure.
  • Wireless has its own topologies: infrastructure mode (clients via an access point), ad hoc (device to device) and mesh, where access points relay traffic to each other over radio.
  • Logical and physical can differ: Ethernet hubs were wired as a physical star but behaved as a logical bus, because every device heard every frame.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming a star is fully resilient: the central switch is a single point of failure, so critical sites use redundant switches and dual uplinks.
  • Thinking more mesh is always better: every extra link adds cost, configuration and failure modes, and in Layer 2 networks spanning tree may simply block it.
  • Mixing up physical and logical topology on exams: ask how the cables run versus how the data flows.

docs.title: Key protocols, devices, standards & tools
docs.text: Name What it does Example Physical vs logical topologyGeneral networking concept · Concept Physical topology is the real cable or radio layout; logical topology is the path data actually takes between devices. Token Ring was wired as a physical star to a hub, but data travelled around a logical ring. Bus topologyIEEE 802.3 10BASE5 / 10BASE2 (legacy Ethernet) · Concept · Layer 1 · Legacy All devices tap into one shared backbone cable with terminators at each end; one cable break stops everyone. 1980s offices ran thin coaxial cable (10BASE2) from PC to PC with T-connectors. Star topologyIEEE 802.3 switched Ethernet · Concept · Layer 1 · Current Every device has its own link to a central switch or access point; one broken cable affects only one device. Each desk in an office has a cable running back to a switch in the communications cupboard. Ring topologyIEEE 802.5 Token Ring, FDDI (legacy); SONET/SDH rings · Concept · Legacy Each device connects to two neighbours forming a circle; data travels around the ring, often in both directions for resilience. Telecom providers still build fibre rings around cities so traffic reroutes the other way if a cable is cut. Full mesh topologyGeneral networking concept · Concept · Current Every device links directly to every other device: maximum redundancy, but cabling grows very quickly and costs a lot. Four core routers in a bank each connect to the other three, giving six links in total. Partial mesh topologyGeneral networking concept · Concept · Current Only the most important devices get multiple links, balancing redundancy against cost. A company's head office and data centre have two links each, while small branches have just one. Tree (hierarchical) topologyCisco three-tier model (access, distribution, core) · Concept · Current Stars connected to higher-level stars, like branches on a tree; easy to expand floor by floor or building by building. Floor switches connect to a building distribution switch, which connects to the campus core. Hybrid topologyGeneral networking concept · Concept · Current A mix of two or more topologies in one network, which describes almost every real organisation. A hospital uses stars on each ward, a tree across buildings and a partial mesh in its core. Point-to-pointIETF RFC 1661 (PPP); leased lines · Concept · Current A direct dedicated link between exactly two endpoints, with nothing shared in between. Two office buildings across a street joined by a point-to-point wireless bridge or one fibre pair. Point-to-multipointGeneral networking concept · Concept · Current One central site communicates with many remote sites over a shared medium, like spokes from a hub. A rural wireless ISP tower serves dozens of farmhouse antennas from one base station. Spine-leaf (Clos) topologyClos network design (Charles Clos, 1953) · Concept · Current Every leaf (rack) switch connects to every spine switch, so any server reaches any other in the same number of hops. A cloud data centre has 4 spine switches and 40 leaf switches; each leaf has one uplink to every spine. Daisy chainGeneral networking concept · Concept · Current Devices connected one after another in a line; simple, but a failure in the middle cuts off everything beyond it. A small shop chains three switches together; when the middle one fails, the last switch's users go offline. Hub-and-spoke topologyGeneral WAN design concept · Concept · Current Branch sites (spokes) connect only to a central hub site; spoke-to-spoke traffic passes through the hub. A bank's 50 branches each link to head office: 50 links instead of the 1,225 a full mesh would need.

docs.title: 1.3 Network Architectures & Communication Models
docs.text:
An architecture describes who does what on a network: dedicated servers serving many clients, equal peers sharing with each other, or services rented from the cloud. Communication models describe how many receivers a message has (one, all, a group or the nearest) and whether data can flow one way or both ways at once. Switching describes whether a fixed path is reserved for a conversation or data is chopped into packets that share the links.

Four ways to address receivers

Who receives IPv4 example IPv6 Unicast Exactly one host 192.168.1.20 Yes, e.g. 2001:db8::20 Broadcast Everyone on the local segment 255.255.255.255 None: uses ff02::1 multicast Multicast Hosts that joined a group 239.1.1.1 (224.0.0.0/4) ff00::/8 groups Anycast Nearest of many servers 1.1.1.1 announced worldwide Yes, same format as unicast

IPv6 dropped broadcast entirely and uses multicast to reach groups instead.

Think of it like…

Unicast is a private phone call, broadcast is a shout across a room, multicast is a group chat, and anycast is calling a taxi company that sends whichever car is closest.

Real-world example

Leo streams a football match: the streaming servers (client-server) send unicast video to his laptop. His TV box gets the same channel via multicast from the ISP, so the ISP sends one stream to many homes. When his laptop first joins the network it broadcasts a request for an address, and his DNS queries to 1.1.1.1 go by anycast to the nearest of hundreds of identical servers. All of it rides over packet switching, sharing links with thousands of other users.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Pick an architecture: client-server for central control, peer-to-peer for simple sharing, cloud for rented, scalable services.
  2. Choose how to address receivers: unicast (one), broadcast (everyone on the local network), multicast (subscribers), anycast (nearest).
  3. Links run in simplex (one way), half-duplex (both ways, taking turns) or full-duplex (both ways at once).
  4. Old telephone networks reserved a circuit for each call; the Internet breaks data into packets that share every link.
  5. Each packet carries its own destination address and can be routed independently.

Who uses it

System and cloud architects choose architectures; network engineers configure multicast, anycast and duplex settings; IPTV, DNS and CDN providers rely on them daily.

Key takeaway

IPv6 has no broadcast at all; it uses multicast instead, a favourite exam fact.

Going deeper

  • Hosts join multicast groups with IGMP (IPv4) or MLD (IPv6); switches use IGMP snooping to send group traffic only to interested ports, and routers build delivery trees with PIM.
  • IPv4 multicast maps to Ethernet MACs starting 01:00:5E plus the low 23 bits of the group address; IPv6 multicast maps to 33:33 plus the low 32 bits.
  • Anycast works purely through routing: the same prefix is announced by BGP from many sites and each network picks its best path, which suits short UDP exchanges such as DNS.
  • A limited broadcast (255.255.255.255) never leaves the segment; a directed broadcast (e.g. 192.168.1.255) could once be routed, but RFC 2644 made routers drop it by default after Smurf attacks.
  • NIST SP 800-145 defines cloud service models (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS) and deployment models (public, private, community, hybrid); networking skills now include cloud VPCs and security groups.
  • Packet switching relies on statistical multiplexing: bursty users rarely peak together, so links are shared efficiently, at the price of queuing delay and loss when they do.
  • Many 'peer-to-peer' apps are hybrids: video calls use servers for signalling and STUN/TURN for NAT traversal, then send media directly between peers whenever possible.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Saying IPv6 uses broadcast: it has none; neighbour discovery and similar tasks use multicast such as ff02::1 (all nodes).
  • Expecting multicast to save bandwidth on any switch: without IGMP snooping, switches flood multicast to every port like broadcast.
  • Thinking anycast load-balances evenly: routing sends each user to the topologically nearest site, which may be busy while others idle.
  • Assuming full-duplex just works everywhere: a duplex mismatch (one side half, one full) causes late collisions, CRC errors and painfully slow transfers.

docs.title: Try it: Check your link speed and duplex mode
docs.text:
Get-NetAdapter | Select-Object Name, LinkSpeed, FullDuplex   # Windows PowerShell
ethtool eth0 | grep -Ei 'speed|duplex'                       # Linux

docs.title: Key protocols, devices, standards & tools
docs.text: Name What it does Example Client-server modelGeneral networking concept · Concept · Current Clients request services and dedicated servers provide them, giving central control, security and backups. Your browser (client) asks a web server for a page; an email app fetches mail from a mail server. Peer-to-peer (P2P) modelGeneral concept; BitTorrent (BEP 3, BitTorrent.org) · Concept · Current Every device is equal and can both offer and use resources, with no central server required. Linux distribution ISOs downloaded via BitTorrent arrive in pieces from many other users at once. Cloud computing modelNIST SP 800-145 (definition of cloud computing) · Concept · Current On-demand computing, storage and networking rented over the Internet from a provider and paid for by use. A start-up runs its website on AWS, Microsoft Azure or Google Cloud instead of buying its own servers. UnicastIETF RFC 791 / RFC 8200 (IP addressing) · Concept · Layer 3 · Current One sender delivers to exactly one receiver, the most common type of network traffic. Downloading a file from a website is unicast between the server and your computer. BroadcastIETF RFC 919 / RFC 922; Ethernet ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff · Concept · Layer 2 · Current One sender delivers to every device on the local network segment; routers do not forward it to other networks. A new laptop sends a DHCP Discover to 255.255.255.255 because it does not yet know the server's address. MulticastIETF RFC 1112, RFC 5771 (IPv4 224.0.0.0/4); IPv6 ff00::/8 · Concept · Layer 3 · Current One sender delivers to a group of receivers that chose to join, sending each packet only once per link. An ISP delivers live IPTV channels by multicast so one stream feeds thousands of subscribers' set-top boxes. AnycastIETF RFC 4786 (anycast operations) · Concept · Layer 3 · Current The same IP address is announced from many locations, and routing delivers each user to the nearest one. Queries to Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 or Google's 8.8.8.8 reach a nearby data centre wherever you are. SimplexGeneral communications concept · Concept · Current Data flows in one direction only; the receiver can never reply on the same channel. A TV broadcast tower or GPS satellite transmits; your television or GPS receiver only listens. Half-duplexIEEE 802.3 (CSMA/CD), IEEE 802.11 · Concept · Layer 1 · Current Data can flow both ways, but only one side can transmit at a time, so devices take turns. Walkie-talkies ('over'); old Ethernet hubs; a Wi-Fi channel where one station transmits at a time. Full-duplexIEEE 802.3x (full-duplex Ethernet) · Concept · Layer 1 · Current Both sides send and receive at the same time on separate paths, doubling usable capacity and removing collisions. A PC on a 1 Gbps switch port can upload and download 1 Gbps simultaneously, like a phone call. Circuit switchingITU-T (traditional PSTN telephony) · Concept · Legacy A dedicated path is reserved end to end for the whole conversation, even during silence. Classic landline calls reserved a 64 kbps channel for the entire call, whether anyone spoke or not. Packet switchingPaul Baran & Donald Davies (1960s); ARPANET (1969); IP · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Data is split into small packets, each labelled with a destination, that share links and may take different routes. An email is split into packets that cross several routers, then are reassembled in order at the receiver. Cloud service models (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS)NIST SP 800-145 · Concept · Current IaaS rents virtual servers and networks, PaaS rents a managed platform for your code, and SaaS rents a finished application. AWS EC2 is IaaS, Google App Engine is PaaS, and Microsoft 365 is SaaS. Statistical multiplexingGeneral networking concept · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Many bursty users share one link because they rarely all transmit at once; queues absorb short peaks. A 1 Gb/s office uplink comfortably serves 200 staff with 1 Gb/s ports, since few download simultaneously.

docs.title: 1.4 Measuring Networks: Bandwidth, Throughput, Latency & More
docs.text:
To judge a network you need a few measurements. Bandwidth is the maximum capacity of a link, throughput is how much data actually gets through, and latency is how long data takes to arrive. Jitter (variation in delay) and packet loss (data that never arrives) decide whether calls and games feel smooth.

Typical round-trip times. Distance and medium dominate latency; more bandwidth cannot shorten these.

Think of it like…

Think of a motorway: bandwidth is the number of lanes, throughput is how many cars actually pass per minute, and latency is how long one car takes to drive from one end to the other.

Real-world example

Aisha pays for a 500 Mbps broadband line and wants to download a 2 GB game. Network speeds use bits but file sizes use bytes, so she divides by 8: 500 Mbps / 8 = 62.5 MB/s. Then 2,000 MB / 62.5 MB/s = 32 seconds in a perfect world. In reality protocol overhead, Wi-Fi conditions and a busy server give her about 45 MB/s of goodput, so it takes around 45 seconds.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Bandwidth sets the ceiling; throughput is what you measure in practice; goodput is the useful data minus all overhead.
  2. Latency adds up from propagation (distance), transmission, processing and queuing delays.
  3. Round-trip time (RTT) is there-and-back delay, which is what ping reports.
  4. Jitter and packet loss matter most for real-time apps such as voice, video calls and gaming.
  5. Always check units: lower-case b = bits, upper-case B = bytes; divide Mbps by 8 to get MB/s.

Who uses it

Network administrators, help-desk staff, ISPs, gamers, VoIP and video-conferencing engineers measure these every day to troubleshoot 'the network is slow'.

Key takeaway

For good voice quality aim for one-way latency under 150 ms, jitter under 30 ms and packet loss under 1 percent.

Going deeper

  • Light in fibre travels at about two-thirds of its vacuum speed, roughly 5 microseconds per kilometre, so every 1,000 km of cable adds about 10 ms of round-trip time.
  • Serialisation delay is frame size divided by link rate: a 1,500-byte frame takes 12 microseconds at 1 Gb/s but 1.2 ms at 10 Mb/s, which matters on slow WAN links.
  • Ethernet adds 38 bytes per frame on the wire (preamble, header, FCS, interframe gap), so the best TCP goodput on gigabit is about 1460/1538, roughly 949 Mb/s.
  • TCP throughput is capped by window size divided by RTT: a 64 KB window over a 100 ms path gives at most about 5.2 Mb/s, however fast the link.
  • Bufferbloat happens when oversized router buffers fill under load, adding hundreds of milliseconds; smart queue management such as fq_codel or CAKE keeps latency low.
  • SLAs quote availability in 'nines': 99.9% allows about 8.8 hours of downtime a year, 99.99% about 53 minutes and 99.999% about 5 minutes.
  • Networking uses decimal prefixes (1 Mb/s = 1,000,000 bit/s) while operating systems often show binary units, so a '1 TB' drive appears as about 931 GiB.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Confusing Mbps with MB/s: a 100 Mbps plan downloads about 12.5 MB/s, not 100 MB/s.
  • Buying more bandwidth to fix lag: bandwidth raises capacity, but latency comes from distance, queuing and Wi-Fi conditions.
  • Blaming the ISP after a Wi-Fi speed test: test wired first, since weak Wi-Fi often caps throughput far below the plan.
  • Panicking at one slow hop in traceroute: routers deprioritise replies to probes, so only delay that persists to later hops is real.

docs.title: Try it: Measure RTT, jitter and loss to a public host, and throughput in your own lab
docs.text:
ping -n 20 example.com          # Windows: RTT min/avg/max and % loss
ping -c 20 example.com          # Linux/macOS (also shows mdev = jitter)
iperf3 -s                       # on your own lab server
iperf3 -c 192.168.1.50 -t 10    # on a client: measures throughput to it

docs.title: Key protocols, devices, standards & tools
docs.text: Name What it does Example BandwidthGeneral networking concept · Concept The maximum amount of data a link can carry per second, measured in bits per second (bps, Mbps, Gbps). A Gigabit Ethernet port has a bandwidth of 1 Gbps; a home fibre plan might be 900 Mbps down. ThroughputIETF RFC 6349 (TCP throughput testing) · Concept The actual rate of data successfully delivered over a link in real conditions, always at or below bandwidth. A speed test on a 1 Gbps link shows 940 Mbps because of headers and gaps between frames. GoodputGeneral networking concept · Concept The rate of useful application data delivered, excluding headers, retransmissions and protocol overhead. Throughput of 940 Mbps might give a file-copy goodput of about 110 MB/s, roughly 880 Mbps. Latency (delay)IETF RFC 7679 (one-way delay metric) · Concept The time a piece of data takes to travel from sender to receiver, usually in milliseconds (ms). Light in fibre covers about 200 km per millisecond, so London to New York is at least 28 ms one way. Propagation, transmission, processing & queuing delayGeneral networking concept · Concept The four parts of latency: travel distance, time to put bits on the wire, device processing time, and waiting in busy queues. A video call lags at 8 pm because a congested home router adds queuing delay, not because the distance changed. Round-trip time (RTT)IETF RFC 2681 (round-trip delay metric) · Concept The time for a message to reach the destination and a reply to come back; roughly twice the one-way latency. ping example.com reporting time=24ms means a 24 ms round trip. JitterIETF RFC 3550 (RTP interarrival jitter) · Concept Variation in latency between packets; high jitter makes calls choppy even when average latency is fine. Pings of 20, 85, 22 and 70 ms show high jitter, so a Teams call breaks up. Packet lossIETF RFC 7680 (one-way loss metric) · Concept The percentage of packets that never arrive, caused by congestion, faulty cables or weak wireless signals. ping shows 5 of 100 replies missing: 5 percent loss, enough to make online games stutter. MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit)IEEE 802.3 (1500 bytes); IETF RFC 8200 (IPv6 minimum 1280); RFC 1191 / RFC 8201 (Path MTU Discovery) · Concept · Layer 2 The largest packet size, in bytes, a link can carry in one frame without splitting it up. Standard Ethernet MTU is 1500 bytes; data centres often enable 9000-byte jumbo frames for storage traffic. MSS (Maximum Segment Size)IETF RFC 9293 (TCP) · Concept · Layer 4 The largest chunk of application data TCP puts in one segment, equal to MTU minus IP and TCP headers. 1500 MTU minus 20-byte IPv4 header minus 20-byte TCP header gives the common 1460-byte MSS. Bits vs bytesIEC 80000-13 (units of information) · Concept A bit (b) is a single 0 or 1; a byte (B) is 8 bits. Network speeds use bits, file sizes use bytes. A 100 Mbps link moves at most 12.5 megabytes per second (100 / 8). Mbps vs MB/s (worked conversion)General networking concept · Concept Mbps is megabits per second; MB/s is megabytes per second. Divide Mbps by 8 to get MB/s. A 4 GB film over 80 Mbps: 80 / 8 = 10 MB/s, then 4,000 MB / 10 = 400 seconds, under 7 minutes. Bandwidth-delay product (BDP)IETF RFC 7323 (TCP window scaling) · Concept Bandwidth multiplied by RTT: the amount of data 'in flight' needed to keep a long, fast link fully busy. 1 Gbps x 0.1 s RTT = 100 Mb, about 12.5 MB in flight, so TCP needs a large window. Availability (the nines)Industry SLA practice · Concept · Current Percentage of time a service works; each extra 'nine' cuts allowed downtime tenfold. A 99.99% SLA allows about 53 minutes of outage per year; 99.9% allows almost 9 hours.

docs.title: 1.5 The OSI Model — 7 Layers
docs.text:
The OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) model splits network communication into seven layers, each with one job, from electrical signals at the bottom to applications at the top. It is mainly a teaching and troubleshooting map: real protocols are built on the simpler TCP/IP model, but engineers still say things like 'that is a Layer 2 problem'. Each layer has a name for its chunk of data, called a PDU (protocol data unit).

The seven OSI layers. Data moves down the stack on the sender and up on the receiver.

Think of it like…

Sending data is like sending a parcel through a company: the manager writes the letter (application), a translator formats it, a secretary tracks the conversation, the shipping desk splits and numbers boxes, the logistics team picks the route, the local courier drives between depots, and the road itself carries the truck.

Real-world example

Noah cannot load a website, so he works up the layers. Layer 1: the cable is plugged in and the link light is green. Layer 2: the switch shows his laptop's MAC address. Layer 3: he can ping his router at 192.168.1.1 and 8.8.8.8. Layer 7: DNS does not resolve names, so he fixes his DNS server setting. Working layer by layer turned a vague problem into a quick fix.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Layer 7 Application: the network services apps use (HTTP, DNS, SMTP). PDU: data.
  2. Layers 6 and 5: Presentation formats, compresses and encrypts data; Session opens, manages and closes conversations. PDU: data.
  3. Layer 4 Transport: end-to-end delivery between apps using ports, reliability and flow control (TCP, UDP). PDU: segment or datagram.
  4. Layer 3 Network: logical addressing and routing between networks (IP, routers). PDU: packet.
  5. Layer 2 Data Link: delivery on the local network using MAC addresses (Ethernet, switches). PDU: frame. Layer 1 Physical: bits as signals on cables or radio. PDU: bits.
  6. Mnemonic from Layer 1 up: Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away (Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application).

Who uses it

Every network and security professional uses OSI layer numbers to troubleshoot and describe devices; it is core content for CompTIA Network+, Security+ and Cisco CCNA.

Key takeaway

Learn the PDUs with 'Do Some People Fear Birthdays': Data, Segments, Packets, Frames, Bits, from Layer 7 down to Layer 1.

Going deeper

  • Each layer offers a service to the layer above and talks logically to the same layer on the far device through its header, called peer-layer communication.
  • Layers have sublayers: IEEE splits Layer 2 into LLC (802.2) and MAC, and Ethernet's Layer 1 into PCS, PMA and PMD sublayers that handle coding and the medium.
  • Real protocols blur the lines: ARP links Layers 2 and 3, MPLS is called 'Layer 2.5', and TLS sits between transport and application; exams use the conventional mapping.
  • OSI was also a complete protocol suite (CLNP, X.400 mail, X.500 directory) that lost to TCP/IP in the 1990s; IS-IS routing, X.509 certificates and LDAP are its survivors.
  • Layer-based troubleshooting has three styles: bottom-up (cable first), top-down (application first) and divide-and-conquer, which starts with ping at Layer 3 and moves up or down.
  • Security maps onto layers too: wiretapping and jamming at L1, ARP spoofing and MAC flooding at L2, IP spoofing at L3, SYN floods at L4, SQL injection at L7.
  • Load balancers are described by layer: a Layer 4 balancer chooses servers by IP and port, while a Layer 7 balancer reads HTTP hostnames, paths and cookies.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Believing the Internet runs on OSI protocols: it runs on TCP/IP; OSI is the reference map engineers use to talk about it.
  • Calling everything a 'packet': at Layer 2 it is a frame and at Layer 4 a segment or datagram, and exams test this.
  • Assuming a 'Layer 3 switch' is only Layer 2: it routes between VLANs in hardware, so it works at Layers 2 and 3.
  • Treating Layer 7 as the application program itself: it is the protocol the app uses, such as HTTP, not the browser.

docs.title: Try it: Troubleshoot bottom-up through the layers on your own PC
docs.text:
ipconfig                 # L1-L3: link up? got an IP address?
arp -a                   # L2: MAC addresses of local neighbours
ping 192.168.1.1         # L3: reach the default gateway
tracert example.com      # L3: path across routers (traceroute on Linux/macOS)
nslookup example.com     # L7: does DNS work?

docs.title: Key protocols, devices, standards & tools
docs.text: Name What it does Example Layer 1 — PhysicalISO/IEC 7498-1 · Concept · Layer 1 Turns bits into electrical, light or radio signals and defines cables, connectors, voltages and frequencies. PDU: bits. Ethernet cabling (Cat 6), fibre optics, RJ45 connectors, hubs, repeaters and Wi-Fi radio signals. Layer 2 — Data LinkISO/IEC 7498-1 · Concept · Layer 2 Delivers frames between devices on the same local network using MAC addresses and detects transmission errors. PDU: frame. Ethernet (IEEE 802.3), Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11) MAC, VLANs (802.1Q), switches, ARP, PPP. Layer 3 — NetworkISO/IEC 7498-1 · Concept · Layer 3 Gives devices logical addresses and chooses routes between different networks. PDU: packet. IPv4, IPv6, ICMP (ping), routing protocols like OSPF and BGP, routers and Layer 3 switches. Layer 4 — TransportISO/IEC 7498-1 · Concept · Layer 4 Carries data between applications using port numbers, adding reliability, ordering and flow control when needed. PDU: segment (TCP) or datagram (UDP). TCP for web pages and email; UDP for DNS, video calls and gaming; QUIC builds on UDP. Layer 5 — SessionISO/IEC 7498-1 · Concept Opens, maintains, synchronises and closes conversations between applications. PDU: data. NetBIOS sessions, RPC, SMB session setup, and resuming an interrupted file transfer from a checkpoint. Layer 6 — PresentationISO/IEC 7498-1 · Concept Translates, compresses and encrypts data so both sides understand the same format. PDU: data. Character encoding (ASCII, UTF-8), JPEG and PNG images, MPEG video, and encryption such as TLS. Layer 7 — ApplicationISO/IEC 7498-1 · Concept · Layer 7 The network services that user applications talk to directly; not the app itself, but its protocols. PDU: data. HTTP/HTTPS (web), DNS (names), SMTP/IMAP (email), FTP/SFTP (files), SSH (remote login), DHCP. ISO/IEC 7498-1 (OSI Basic Reference Model)ISO/IEC 7498-1:1994 (first edition 1984); ITU-T X.200 · Standard · Current The international standard that defines the seven-layer OSI reference model, published jointly by ISO and the ITU. Textbooks and certification exams base their seven-layer diagrams on this standard. PDU (Protocol Data Unit)ISO/IEC 7498-1 · Concept The name for the unit of data at each layer: data, segment/datagram, packet, frame, bits. A switch forwards frames (Layer 2) while a router forwards packets (Layer 3). Mnemonic: Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza AwayClassic study aid · Concept Bottom-up memory aid for Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application. Top-down alternative: 'All People Seem To Need Data Processing' (Application down to Physical). Device-to-layer mappingGeneral networking concept · Concept · Multi-layer Devices are classed by the highest layer they inspect: hubs Layer 1, switches Layer 2, routers Layer 3, firewalls up to 7. A next-generation firewall inspects HTTP content (Layer 7), while a basic switch only reads MAC addresses. OSI protocol suite (CLNP, IS-IS, X.500)ISO / ITU-T (1980s) · Standard · Legacy The actual protocols designed to implement OSI; most lost to TCP/IP, but several ideas and standards survive. IS-IS routing in ISP cores and X.509 certificates in HTTPS both come from the OSI protocol family. Troubleshooting approaches (bottom-up, top-down, divide-and-conquer)General networking practice (Cisco CCNA) · Concept · Multi-layer Three ways to walk the OSI layers when diagnosing faults: from cables upward, from the application downward, or starting in the middle. A technician pings the server first (Layer 3); it succeeds, so she skips cabling checks and investigates DNS and the application.

docs.title: 1.6 The TCP/IP Model & Encapsulation
docs.text:
The TCP/IP model is the practical four-layer model the real Internet is built on: Application, Transport, Internet and Link. Many courses use a five-layer version that splits Link into Data Link and Physical. As data goes down the layers, each one wraps it with its own label (header), which is called encapsulation; the receiver unwraps each label on the way up, called decapsulation.

Encapsulating one HTTPS request. Each layer wraps the one above; the frame is rebuilt at every router hop.

Think of it like…

Encapsulation is like posting a letter: you write the letter, put it in an envelope with a room number, place that in a bigger envelope with the street address, and a courier loads it into a van; the recipient opens each layer in reverse order.

Real-world example

Zoe's browser requests https://www.example.com. The HTTP GET request (data) is handed to TCP, which adds a 20-byte header with source port 51544 and destination port 443 (now a segment). IP adds a 20-byte header with her address 192.168.1.20 and the server's 203.0.113.10 (now a packet). Ethernet adds a 14-byte header with her router's MAC address plus a 4-byte FCS trailer (now a frame), and the network card sends it as bits. At each router the frame is unwrapped and rewrapped for the next link, while the IP packet inside travels end to end.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Application layer creates the data (for example an HTTP request), often encrypted by TLS.
  2. Transport layer adds a TCP or UDP header with source and destination ports, making a segment or datagram.
  3. Internet layer adds an IP header with source and destination IP addresses, making a packet.
  4. Link layer adds a frame header (MAC addresses) and trailer (FCS error check), making a frame, then sends it as bits.
  5. The receiver decapsulates: each layer reads and removes its own header and passes the rest up.
  6. OSI mapping: TCP/IP Application = OSI 5-7, Transport = 4, Internet = 3, Link = 1-2.

Who uses it

Anyone who reads packet captures in Wireshark, configures firewalls or troubleshoots applications uses the TCP/IP model and encapsulation daily.

Key takeaway

Memorise the mapping (Application 5-7, Transport 4, Internet 3, Link 1-2) and that the IP packet stays the same end to end while the frame is rebuilt at every hop.

Going deeper

  • TCP/IP grew from Cerf and Kahn's 1974 paper; the ARPANET switched to it on 1 January 1983, the 'flag day' often called the Internet's birthday.
  • Header sizes worth memorising: Ethernet 14 bytes (+4 with an 802.1Q tag) plus 4-byte FCS, IPv4 20-60 bytes, IPv6 a fixed 40 bytes, TCP 20-60 bytes, UDP 8 bytes.
  • Demultiplexing uses a field in each header: EtherType (0x0800 IPv4, 0x86DD IPv6) picks the network protocol, IP's protocol number (6 TCP, 17 UDP, 1 ICMP) picks transport, and ports pick the application.
  • At every hop a router rewrites source and destination MACs, decrements TTL (or Hop Limit) and recalculates the IPv4 header checksum; the IP addresses stay put unless NAT changes them.
  • Tunnelling is encapsulation inside encapsulation: GRE, IPsec and VXLAN wrap whole packets or frames, VXLAN adding 50 bytes, which is why tunnels often cause MTU problems.
  • Overhead hurts small packets: a G.711 voice packet with 160 bytes of audio grows to 218 bytes with RTP, UDP, IP and Ethernet headers, about 87 kb/s per call.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking IP addresses change at each router: only the frame's MAC addresses change per hop; NAT is the exception that rewrites IPs.
  • Mapping the four TCP/IP layers one-to-one onto OSI: Application covers OSI 5-7 and Link covers OSI 1-2.
  • Forgetting that only the data link layer adds a trailer: IP and TCP add headers only, while Ethernet appends the FCS.

docs.title: Try it: Watch a real request and see each layer's headers
docs.text:
curl -v https://example.com            # shows TCP connect, TLS handshake, HTTP headers
tshark -i 1 -c 5 -V -f "tcp port 443"   # Wireshark CLI: prints Ethernet, IP, TCP layers of 5 packets

docs.title: Key protocols, devices, standards & tools
docs.text: Name What it does Example Application layer (TCP/IP)IETF RFC 1123 (application host requirements) · Concept · Layer 7 Top layer covering OSI layers 5-7: the protocols that applications use to exchange data. HTTP, DNS, SMTP, SSH and DHCP all live in the TCP/IP application layer. Transport layer (TCP/IP)IETF RFC 1122; TCP RFC 9293 (replaced RFC 793); UDP RFC 768 · Concept · Layer 4 Delivers data between applications using ports; TCP is reliable and ordered, UDP is fast and simple. Web traffic uses TCP port 443 (or QUIC over UDP 443); DNS mostly uses UDP port 53. Internet layer (TCP/IP)IETF RFC 791 (IPv4), RFC 8200 (IPv6), RFC 792 (ICMP) · Concept · Layer 3 Addresses and routes packets across many networks from source host to destination host. Routers read the destination IP in each packet to decide the next hop toward the server. Link layer / Network Access (TCP/IP)IETF RFC 1122; IEEE 802.3, IEEE 802.11 · Concept · Multi-layer Bottom layer covering OSI layers 1-2: moving frames across one physical link or local network. Ethernet on your office LAN or Wi-Fi in your home carries frames to the next device. Five-layer (hybrid) modelTextbook teaching model (e.g. Kurose & Ross, Tanenbaum) · Concept TCP/IP with the link layer split into Data Link and Physical: Application, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical. Many university courses and Cisco materials use five layers so Layer 1 and 2 numbers still match OSI. RFC 1122 / RFC 1123 (Host Requirements)IETF RFC 1122, RFC 1123 (1989) · RFC · Current The RFCs that define the four TCP/IP layers and what every Internet host must implement. RFC 1122 lists the link, IP and transport layers; RFC 1123 covers applications like Telnet, FTP and SMTP. EncapsulationGeneral networking concept · Concept · Multi-layer Each layer wraps the data from the layer above with its own header (and sometimes trailer) before passing it down. An HTTP request becomes a TCP segment inside an IP packet inside an Ethernet frame. DecapsulationGeneral networking concept · Concept · Multi-layer The reverse at the receiver: each layer reads its header, acts on it, removes it and passes the payload up. The server's NIC strips the Ethernet frame, IP checks the address, TCP reorders segments, the web server reads HTTP. HeaderGeneral networking concept · Concept Control information added in front of the data, such as addresses, ports, lengths and sequence numbers. A minimum IPv4 header is 20 bytes; a basic TCP header is 20 bytes; an Ethernet header is 14 bytes. Trailer & FCS (Frame Check Sequence)IEEE 802.3 (32-bit CRC) · Concept · Layer 2 Information added after the data; Ethernet's 4-byte FCS lets the receiver detect corrupted frames and drop them. A damaged cable causes FCS errors, visible as 'CRC errors' on a switch interface counter. Data (message)General networking concept · Concept · Layer 7 The PDU name at the application layers: the actual content the app wants to send. The text 'GET / HTTP/1.1 Host: www.example.com' is application data. SegmentIETF RFC 9293 (TCP) · Concept · Layer 4 The PDU at the transport layer when TCP is used: data plus a TCP header with ports and sequence numbers. A 4,000-byte web response may be split into three TCP segments of up to 1460 bytes each. DatagramIETF RFC 768 (UDP) · Concept · Layer 4 The PDU name for UDP data plus an 8-byte UDP header; sent without setting up a connection first. A DNS query is usually one small UDP datagram sent to port 53. PacketIETF RFC 791 / RFC 8200 (IP) · Concept · Layer 3 The PDU at the internet/network layer: a segment or datagram plus an IP header with source and destination IPs. Routers forward packets hop by hop using the destination IP address, for example 203.0.113.10. FrameIEEE 802.3 / IEEE 802.11 · Concept · Layer 2 The PDU at the data link layer: a packet plus a header with MAC addresses and an error-check trailer. Your PC sends a frame addressed to the router's MAC; the router builds a new frame for the next link. BitsIEEE 802.3 physical layers · Concept · Layer 1 The PDU at the physical layer: the frame turned into a stream of 1s and 0s sent as signals. On fibre, 1s and 0s become light patterns; on copper Ethernet, voltage changes; on Wi-Fi, radio waves.

docs.title: 1.7 Number Systems & Addressing Basics
docs.text:
Computers store everything as binary, a counting system with only two digits, 0 and 1. People find long binary strings hard to read, so networks also show numbers in decimal (our normal 0-9 system) and hexadecimal (16 digits, 0-9 then A-F). Learning to convert between them is essential for understanding IP addresses, subnet masks, MAC addresses and ports.

One value, three notations

Binary Hex Where you meet it 10 00001010 0A 192.168.1.10 127 01111111 7F 127.0.0.1 loopback 128 10000000 80 Mask 255.255.255.128 (/25) 192 11000000 C0 192.168.0.0 private range 224 11100000 E0 Multicast start; mask /27 240 11110000 F0 Mask 255.255.255.240 (/28) 255 11111111 FF Broadcast, FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF

Learn these by heart: they appear in masks, ranges and MAC addresses.

Think of it like…

An octet is like a row of eight light switches worth 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1; to show a number you turn on the switches whose values add up to it.

Real-world example

Convert 192.168.1.10 to binary one octet at a time using the place values 128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1. 192 = 128 + 64, so 11000000. 168 = 128 + 32 + 8, so 10101000. 1 is 00000001 and 10 = 8 + 2, so 00001010. The full address is 11000000.10101000.00000001.00001010, and going backwards is just adding up the place values of the 1s.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Write the place values of one octet: 128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1 (powers of two, 2^7 down to 2^0).
  2. Decimal to binary: from the left, if the value fits, write 1 and subtract it; otherwise write 0.
  3. Binary to decimal: add up the place values wherever there is a 1.
  4. Binary to hex: split into groups of 4 bits (nibbles); each nibble is one hex digit (1010 = A, 1111 = F).
  5. Know the three address types: MAC (who you are on the local link), IP (where you are on the Internet), port (which app on the device).

Who uses it

Network technicians and engineers convert binary daily for subnetting and reading MAC or IPv6 addresses; it is heavily tested on CompTIA Network+ and Cisco CCNA.

Key takeaway

Powers of two to memorise: 2^1=2, 2^2=4, 2^3=8, 2^4=16, 2^5=32, 2^6=64, 2^7=128, 2^8=256, 2^10=1024, 2^16=65,536, 2^32 is about 4.3 billion.

Going deeper

  • Only nine values ever appear in a subnet mask octet: 0, 128, 192, 224, 240, 248, 252, 254 and 255, because mask bits are contiguous ones from the left.
  • Hex to decimal: multiply each digit by its place value of 16: 0x1F4 = 1 x 256 + 15 x 16 + 4 = 500. Programmers write 0x in front to mark hex.
  • Routers find a network address with a bitwise AND of IP and mask: 192.168.1.10 AND 255.255.255.0 gives 192.168.1.0. This single operation is the heart of subnetting.
  • RFC 5952 sets canonical IPv6 text: lower-case hex, no leading zeros, and :: replacing the longest run of two or more zero groups only once.
  • Address-space sizes: ports 2^16 (65,536), IPv4 2^32 (about 4.3 billion), MAC 2^48 (about 281 trillion) and IPv6 2^128 (about 3.4 x 10^38).
  • Networks send multi-byte numbers big-endian ('network byte order', most significant byte first), so programmers convert with htons() and ntohl() when using sockets.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Dropping leading zeros when converting octets: always write eight bits, so 10 is 00001010, otherwise masks and ANDs line up wrongly.
  • Using :: twice in one IPv6 address: it is ambiguous and invalid; compress only one run of zero groups.
  • Reading hex as decimal: hex 10 is sixteen, and hex digits A-F stand for 10-15.
  • Thinking MAC addresses route across the Internet: they only matter on the local link and are replaced at every router hop.

docs.title: Try it: Convert between binary, decimal and hex (Python, or Windows Calculator in Programmer mode)
docs.text:
python -c "print(format(192,'08b'), int('10101000',2), hex(255), int('ff',16))"
# output: 11000000 168 0xff 255
python -c "print([2**n for n in range(9)])"
# output: [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256]

docs.title: Key protocols, devices, standards & tools
docs.text: Name What it does Example BitGeneral computing concept · Concept The smallest unit of data: a single binary digit, 0 or 1 (off or on). An IPv4 address is 32 bits long; an IPv6 address is 128 bits long. NibbleGeneral computing concept · Concept Four bits, which can hold 16 values (0-15) and maps exactly to one hexadecimal digit. The byte 10101111 splits into nibbles 1010 (A) and 1111 (F), giving hex AF. Byte / OctetGeneral computing concept; IETF uses 'octet' · Concept Eight bits, holding values 0-255. Networking standards say 'octet' to mean exactly 8 bits. Each of the four numbers in 192.168.1.10 is one octet, so none can exceed 255. Binary (base 2)General mathematics concept · Concept A number system using only 0 and 1, where each position is worth double the one to its right. Binary 11111111 = 128+64+32+16+8+4+2+1 = 255. Decimal (base 10)General mathematics concept · Concept Our everyday system with digits 0-9; used to write IPv4 addresses, port numbers and prefix lengths. The subnet mask 255.255.255.0 is written in decimal, though routers use its 32-bit binary form. Hexadecimal (base 16)General mathematics concept · Concept Uses digits 0-9 and letters A-F (10-15); each hex digit equals 4 bits, giving compact notation. Decimal 255 = binary 11111111 = hex FF; MAC and IPv6 addresses are written in hex. Powers of two (place values)General mathematics concept · Concept Bit positions are worth 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256... Each extra bit doubles the number of combinations. 8 host bits give 2^8 = 256 combinations, which is why a /24 network has 256 addresses. Dotted-decimal notationIETF RFC 791 (IPv4) · Concept · Layer 3 Writing a 32-bit IPv4 address as four octets in decimal separated by dots. 11000000.10101000.00000001.00001010 is written 192.168.1.10. MAC address notation (EUI-48)IEEE (EUI-48; OUI assigned by IEEE Registration Authority) · Concept · Layer 2 A 48-bit hardware address written as 12 hex digits in six octets; the first 24 bits are the maker's OUI. 3C-22-FB-12-AB-9E (Windows), 3c:22:fb:12:ab:9e (Linux/macOS) and 3c22.fb12.ab9e (Cisco) are the same address. IPv4 addressIETF RFC 791 · Concept · Layer 3 · Current A 32-bit logical address (about 4.3 billion possible) identifying a device's location on a network. A home laptop might have 192.168.1.20 and reach a web server at 203.0.113.10. IPv6 addressIETF RFC 8200 (protocol), RFC 4291 (addressing), RFC 5952 (text format) · Concept · Layer 3 · Current A 128-bit address written as eight groups of four hex digits; leading zeros and one run of zero groups can be shortened. 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001 shortens to 2001:db8::1 (a documentation address). Port numberIETF RFC 6335; IANA port registry · Concept · Layer 4 A 16-bit number (0-65535) identifying which application on a device. Well-known 0-1023, registered 1024-49151, dynamic 49152-65535. HTTPS uses 443, SSH 22, DNS 53; your browser picks a random source port like 51544. SocketGeneral networking concept (BSD sockets API) · Concept · Layer 4 The combination of an IP address and a port; a connection is identified by both ends' sockets plus the protocol. 192.168.1.20:51544 talking to 203.0.113.10:443 over TCP uniquely identifies one web connection. Bitwise AND (masking)Boolean logic · Concept · Layer 3 Compares two binary numbers bit by bit, giving 1 only where both are 1; used to extract the network part of an address. 10101000 (168) AND 11110000 (240) = 10100000 (160), so 172.16.168.5/20 sits in network 172.16.160.0. Network byte order (big-endian)IETF RFC 791 Appendix B; BSD sockets API · Concept Protocols transmit multi-byte numbers most-significant byte first, whatever the computer's own internal order. Port 443 (0x01BB) is sent as bytes 01 then BB; a PC converts it with htons(443).

docs.title: 1.8 Who Makes the Rules: Standards Bodies & Internet Governance
docs.text:
Networking only works because thousands of companies build equipment that follows the same published rules, called standards. Different organisations write different standards: the IETF writes Internet protocols, the IEEE writes Ethernet and Wi-Fi, and others handle mobile networks, the web, and the global lists of names and numbers. No single company or government owns the Internet; it is coordinated by many cooperating bodies.

How IP addresses are handed out. Every public IP address traces back through an RIR to IANA's global pool.

Think of it like…

Standards bodies are like the people who agree the rules of football: once everyone uses the same rulebook, any team can play any other team anywhere in the world.

Real-world example

When Kofi's laptop joins a café Wi-Fi network, it uses IEEE 802.11 radio, gets Wi-Fi Alliance-certified WPA3 security, receives an IP address from a block his ISP obtained from its RIR (ultimately from IANA's pool), and looks up a domain name registered under ICANN's rules. The web page arrives using IETF protocols (TCP, TLS, HTTP) and is drawn using W3C and WHATWG web standards. Half a dozen organisations cooperated for one page to load.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Anyone can write an Internet-Draft and bring it to an IETF working group, by mailing list or at a meeting.
  2. The working group discusses and revises it until it reaches 'rough consensus', then holds a working group last call.
  3. The draft goes to IETF-wide last call so the whole community can comment.
  4. The IESG (Internet Engineering Steering Group) reviews and approves it.
  5. The RFC Editor edits and publishes it with a permanent number; published RFCs are never changed, only updated or obsoleted by newer RFCs.
  6. Standards-track RFCs start as Proposed Standard and can later become Internet Standard (RFC 2026, simplified by RFC 6410).

Who uses it

Network engineers read RFCs and IEEE standards to understand exact behaviour; ISPs and hosting companies deal with RIRs for IP addresses; vendors certify products with the Wi-Fi Alliance.

Key takeaway

Remember the address chain: IANA allocates big blocks to the five RIRs, RIRs allocate to ISPs and large organisations, and ISPs assign addresses to customers.

Going deeper

  • RFCs carry a status: Proposed Standard and Internet Standard (with an STD number), Best Current Practice (BCP), Informational, Experimental or Historic. Many famous RFCs are not standards at all.
  • IEEE 802 working groups include 802.1 (bridging, VLANs, security), 802.3 (Ethernet), 802.11 (Wi-Fi) and 802.15 (personal area); lettered amendments such as 802.3bt are later rolled into a full revision like 802.3-2022.
  • IANA gave its last IPv4 /8 blocks to the five RIRs in February 2011; most RIRs have since run out, relying on waiting lists, transfer markets and IPv6.
  • AS numbers identify networks in BGP: originally 16-bit, now 32-bit (RFC 6793), with private ranges 64512-65534 and 4200000000-4294967294 for internal use.
  • In October 2016 US government oversight of the IANA functions ended, handing stewardship to ICANN's multistakeholder community of governments, companies, engineers and users.
  • The DNS root is 13 named server identities (a to m) run by 12 organisations, served by well over a thousand anycast instances worldwide.
  • Other bodies matter too: TIA (cabling, TIA-568), ETSI (European telecoms and NFV), CableLabs (DOCSIS), MEF (Carrier Ethernet), Broadband Forum, Bluetooth SIG and the Ultra Ethernet Consortium.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking ICANN controls Internet content: it coordinates names and numbers only; content and laws are national matters.
  • Treating every RFC as a binding standard: many are Informational or Experimental, and April Fools' RFCs like RFC 1149 are jokes.
  • Confusing IEEE amendment names with marketing names: Wi-Fi 6 is the Wi-Fi Alliance label for IEEE 802.11ax.
  • Citing obsolete RFC numbers: TCP is now RFC 9293, not RFC 793; check the RFC Editor's 'obsoleted by' notes.

docs.title: Try it: See which registry and organisation hold an IP address (WHOIS / RDAP lookups)
docs.text:
whois 8.8.8.8                       # Linux/macOS: shows ARIN record for Google
curl -s https://rdap.org/ip/8.8.8.8 # RDAP (JSON) lookup, the modern WHOIS replacement

docs.title: Key protocols, devices, standards & tools
docs.text: Name What it does Example IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force)Founded 1986; organisational home: Internet Society · Organisation · Current Open volunteer community that develops core Internet protocols and publishes them as RFCs; anyone can join its mailing lists. TCP (RFC 9293), HTTP/3 (RFC 9114), QUIC (RFC 9000) and TLS 1.3 (RFC 9846, replacing RFC 8446) are IETF standards. IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers)IEEE Standards Association; IEEE 802 LAN/MAN Standards Committee · Organisation · Current Professional association whose 802 committee writes the standards for wired and wireless local networks. IEEE 802.3 (Ethernet), 802.11 (Wi-Fi), 802.1Q (VLANs) and 802.1X (port-based authentication). ITU (International Telecommunication Union)UN specialised agency, founded 1865; ITU-T, ITU-R, ITU-D sectors · Organisation · Current Coordinates global telecoms: radio spectrum (ITU-R) and telecom standards called Recommendations (ITU-T). ITU-T X.509 defines the certificate format behind HTTPS; ITU-T G.652 specifies common single-mode fibre. IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority)Operated by PTI, an affiliate of ICANN (since 2016) · Organisation · Current Keeps the Internet's master lists: DNS root zone, IP address and AS number pools, and protocol registries like port numbers. ARIN (American Registry for Internet Numbers)Regional Internet Registry, founded 1997 · Organisation · Current Regional Internet Registry managing IP addresses and AS numbers for Canada, the United States and parts of the Caribbean. A US hosting company applies to ARIN for an IPv6 /32 allocation for its network. RIPE NCCRegional Internet Registry, founded 1992, Amsterdam · Organisation · Current Regional Internet Registry for Europe, the Middle East and parts of Central Asia; also runs the RIPE Atlas measurement network. A German ISP becomes a RIPE NCC member to receive IPv6 space and an AS number. An Indian mobile operator obtains IP address blocks and AS numbers through APNIC. A Brazilian ISP requests IPv6 addresses from LACNIC (via Brazil's NIC.br) for its customers. A Kenyan university network obtains its own IPv6 block from AFRINIC. Web developers follow W3C's WCAG guidelines so sites work with screen readers. 3GPP (3rd Generation Partnership Project)Partnership of telecom standards bodies, founded 1998 · Organisation · Current Writes mobile network specifications, published as numbered Releases, from 3G UMTS through 4G LTE to 5G and 5G-Advanced. 5G NR began in Release 15; Release 18 is the first 5G-Advanced release; 6G work has started. ISOC funds IETF administration and runs community programmes to connect underserved regions. The IRTF's Crypto Forum Research Group (CFRG) advises the IETF on cryptographic algorithms.

docs.title: 1.9 A Journey: What Happens When You Type a URL
docs.text:
Typing a web address and pressing Enter starts a chain of a dozen protocols working together in under a second. Your device needs an address, must find the router, translate the name into an IP address, open a connection, set up encryption, ask for the page, and draw it on screen. Following this journey is the best way to see how every networking topic fits together.

Loading https://www.example.com. Several round trips happen before the first byte of HTML arrives.

Think of it like…

It is like visiting a friend for the first time: you get your own house key (DHCP), find the local post office (ARP), look up their address in a directory (DNS), drive across many roads (routing), knock and agree to talk (TCP), speak in a private code (TLS), then ask for what you came for (HTTP).

Real-world example

Priya opens her laptop in a café. DHCP gives her 192.168.1.23, gateway 192.168.1.1 and a DNS server. She types www.example.com; the browser upgrades to HTTPS, asks DNS for the IP (203.0.113.10), and uses ARP to find the gateway's MAC address. NAT on the café router swaps her private address for its public one, routers forward packets across several networks, a TCP or QUIC connection is opened, TLS 1.3 encrypts it, and an HTTP GET fetches the HTML. The browser then requests images and scripts and renders the page.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Get connected: Wi-Fi association, then DHCP gives the device an IP address, subnet mask, gateway and DNS server.
  2. Parse the URL and check the browser cache and HSTS list; resolve the name with DNS (cache, then resolver, root, TLD, authoritative).
  3. Find the gateway's MAC with ARP (or IPv6 Neighbor Discovery) and send frames to it; NAT translates the private address.
  4. Routers forward the packets hop by hop toward the server, guided by routing tables built with protocols like BGP.
  5. Open a TCP connection (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) and run a TLS 1.3 handshake, or use QUIC over UDP which combines both.
  6. Send an HTTP GET; the server replies with HTML; the browser fetches CSS, JavaScript and images, then renders the page.

Who uses it

This is the most famous networking job-interview question; help-desk staff, web developers, network and security engineers all use this mental model to troubleshoot.

Key takeaway

When a site will not load, test in journey order: IP address (ipconfig), gateway (ping), DNS (nslookup), connection (curl -v); the first step that fails is your culprit.

Going deeper

  • Name lookups pass through several caches: the browser, the operating system's stub resolver, then the recursive resolver; each obeys the record's TTL. Browsers increasingly use encrypted DNS (DoH, RFC 8484, or DoT, RFC 7858).
  • Happy Eyeballs (RFC 8305) asks for both AAAA and A records, tries IPv6 first and starts IPv4 if IPv6 has not connected within about 250 ms, hiding broken IPv6 from users.
  • Round trips decide speed: over TCP, the TCP handshake, the TLS 1.3 handshake and the HTTP request each cost one RTT, so first byte arrives after about three; QUIC needs about two.
  • Browsers discover HTTP/3 support through the Alt-Svc response header or the HTTPS DNS record (RFC 9460), then switch to QUIC on UDP port 443.
  • The TLS ClientHello normally reveals the hostname in the SNI field; Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) together with encrypted DNS hides which site you visit from on-path observers.
  • Big sites rarely serve you from one origin server: DNS steering or anycast sends you to a nearby CDN edge cache, which returns cached content or fetches it from the origin.
  • Connection reuse avoids repeating handshakes: HTTP/1.1 keep-alive, HTTP/2 multiplexing many requests on one TCP connection, and TLS session resumption for returning visitors.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking ARP looks up the web server's MAC: for remote destinations the laptop only ARPs for its default gateway's MAC.
  • Assuming DNS is always UDP: large answers and zone transfers use TCP port 53, and browsers may use DNS over HTTPS on port 443.
  • Reading the padlock as 'safe website': it proves encryption and the domain's identity, not that the site is honest.
  • Believing HTTPS hides which site you visit: DNS queries and the TLS SNI reveal the hostname unless encrypted DNS and ECH are used.

docs.title: Try it: Retrace the journey step by step from your own computer
docs.text:
ipconfig /all              # DHCP-assigned IP, gateway, DNS server (ip addr / ip route on Linux)
arp -a                     # ARP cache: gateway's MAC address
nslookup www.example.com   # DNS lookup
tracert www.example.com    # routers along the path (traceroute on Linux/macOS)
curl -v https://www.example.com   # TCP connect, TLS handshake, HTTP request and response

docs.title: Key protocols, devices, standards & tools
docs.text: Name What it does Example DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol)IETF RFC 2131 (IPv4); RFC 9915 (DHCPv6, replaced RFC 8415) · Protocol · Layer 7 · Current Automatically gives a joining device its IP address, subnet mask, default gateway and DNS servers using UDP ports 67/68. Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge (DORA): Priya's laptop receives 192.168.1.23 for a 24-hour lease. URL parsing & HSTSIETF RFC 3986 (URI syntax); WHATWG URL Standard; RFC 6797 (HSTS) · Standard · Layer 7 · Current The browser splits the URL into scheme, host, port and path, and HSTS forces HTTPS for sites that demand it. https://www.example.com/menu splits into scheme https, host www.example.com, default port 443, path /menu. DNS (Domain Name System)IETF RFC 1034, RFC 1035 · Protocol · Layer 7 · Current Journey step two: the browser asks a resolver to turn the hostname into the server's IP address (A or AAAA record). The resolver asks a root server, then the .com servers, then example.com's authoritative server for the A/AAAA record. ARP (Address Resolution Protocol)IETF RFC 826; IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery (RFC 4861) · Protocol · Layer 2 · Current Finds the MAC address that matches a known IPv4 address on the local network by broadcasting a question. 'Who has 192.168.1.1? Tell 192.168.1.23' — the router replies with its MAC so frames can be addressed. Ethernet / Wi-Fi framingIEEE 802.3, IEEE 802.11 · Standard · Layer 2 · Current Carries each packet across the local link inside a frame addressed to the next device's MAC address. Priya's packets travel by Wi-Fi to the café access point, then by Ethernet to the router. NAT (Network Address Translation)IETF RFC 3022; private addresses RFC 1918 · Technology · Layer 3 · Current Rewrites private source addresses to the router's public address so many devices share one public IPv4 address. 192.168.1.23:51544 leaves the café router as 198.51.100.7:40211, and replies are translated back. IP routingIETF RFC 791 (IPv4), RFC 8200 (IPv6) · Concept · Layer 3 · Current Each router looks at the destination IP, consults its routing table and forwards the packet one hop closer. tracert shows about 10-15 router hops between a café in Leeds and a server in Frankfurt. BGP (Border Gateway Protocol)IETF RFC 4271 (BGP-4) · Protocol · Layer 7 · Current The routing protocol networks use to tell each other which IP address ranges they can reach, stitching the Internet together. The café's ISP learns via BGP that 203.0.113.0/24 is reachable through a particular transit provider. TCP three-way handshakeIETF RFC 9293 (replaced RFC 793) · Protocol · Layer 4 · Current Opens a reliable connection with SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK before any data flows, agreeing starting sequence numbers. Laptop sends SYN to 203.0.113.10:443, server answers SYN-ACK, laptop sends ACK; one round trip. QUICIETF RFC 9000 · Protocol · Layer 4 · Current A modern encrypted transport over UDP that merges connection setup and TLS 1.3 into one round trip and underpins HTTP/3. Chrome visiting a large site often uses QUIC on UDP port 443 instead of TCP. TLS 1.3 (Transport Layer Security)IETF RFC 9846 (replaced RFC 8446) · Protocol · Multi-layer · Current Encrypts the connection and proves the server's identity with a certificate, completing its handshake in one round trip. The padlock in the address bar means TLS checked example.com's certificate and encrypted the traffic. HTTP (HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3)IETF RFC 9110 (semantics), RFC 9112, RFC 9113, RFC 9114 · Protocol · Layer 7 · Current The request-response protocol of the web: the browser sends methods like GET, the server returns status codes and content. GET / returns '200 OK' with HTML; a missing page returns '404 Not Found'. HTTP cachingIETF RFC 9111 · Standard · Layer 7 · Current Lets browsers and CDNs reuse previously downloaded content instead of fetching it again, saving time and bandwidth. On Priya's second visit the logo loads instantly from the browser cache because of a Cache-Control header. Rendering (HTML, CSS, JavaScript)WHATWG HTML Living Standard; W3C CSS; ECMAScript (Ecma TC39) · Standard · Current The browser builds the page structure from HTML, styles it with CSS, runs JavaScript and paints pixels on screen. One HTML page triggers 60 more requests for images, fonts, CSS and scripts before the page looks complete. Happy Eyeballs (RFC 8305)IETF RFC 8305 (replaced RFC 6555) · RFC · Layer 4 · Current Browser technique that races IPv6 and IPv4 connection attempts, preferring IPv6 but falling back quickly if it stalls. Priya's laptop tries 2001:db8::10 first; after 250 ms without reply it also tries 203.0.113.10, and the winner is used.

docs.title: Chapter 2: Physical & Data Link Layers — Cables, Signals, Ethernet & Switching
docs.text: Every network message eventually becomes electrical pulses, flashes of light or radio waves travelling over something physical. This chapter starts at the bottom of the stack: the cables, connectors and signals of Layer 1, then climbs to Layer 2, where Ethernet, MAC addresses and switches move frames between devices on the same local network. Master these foundations and everything above them becomes much easier to troubleshoot.

docs.title: 2.1 Copper Cabling
docs.text:
Most office and home networks use copper cables: thin copper wires that carry data as tiny electrical signals. Twisted-pair cable twists wires together in pairs so that outside electrical noise cancels out. Cables come in 'categories' (Cat5e, Cat6 and so on); a higher category can carry faster signals more cleanly.

Cat5e vs Cat6 vs Cat6a

Cat5e Cat6 Cat6a Rated frequency 100 MHz 250 MHz 500 MHz ISO/IEC class Class D Class E Class EA 1 Gb/s at 100 m Yes Yes Yes 2.5/5GBASE-T 2.5G yes; 5G often Yes Yes 10GBASE-T reach Not rated About 37-55 m Full 100 m Best for Existing homes Budget desk drops New builds, Wi-Fi 7 APs

Cat6a is the first category rated for 10GBASE-T over the full 100 m.

Think of it like…

Twisted pairs are like two people walking arm in arm through a noisy crowd: any shove hits both equally, so they stay together and the message between them survives.

Real-world example

Priya is cabling a new dental surgery. She runs Cat6a from the patch panel in the comms cupboard to each treatment room; the longest run is 82 m, safely under the 100 m channel limit. Both ends are terminated with the T568B pin order, making them straight-through cables. When she tests one run, the certifier shows it passes 10GBASE-T, so the surgery can upgrade its switch later without re-cabling.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Data is sent as voltage changes on pairs of copper wires (Ethernet cable has 4 pairs, 8 wires).
  2. Each pair carries a signal and its mirror image; the receiver subtracts them, cancelling noise that hit both wires.
  3. The tighter the twists and the better the shielding, the higher the frequency (MHz) the cable supports.
  4. Wires are punched into a patch panel or crimped into RJ45 plugs following the T568A or T568B colour order.
  5. A channel (patch cord + permanent link + patch cord) must be 100 m or less for twisted-pair Ethernet.
  6. Modern ports use Auto-MDIX to detect which pairs transmit and receive, so cable type rarely matters now.

Who uses it

Network and structured-cabling technicians, data-centre staff and anyone setting up a home or office LAN.

Key takeaway

Memorise the 100 m rule (90 m permanent link + 10 m of patch cords) and that Cat6a is the cheapest category that does 10GBASE-T at the full 100 m.

Going deeper

  • ISO/IEC 11801 shielding codes read 'overall/pair': U/UTP has no shield, F/UTP an overall foil, U/FTP foil per pair, and S/FTP a braid plus foil per pair. Shields only work when properly earthed.
  • 100BASE-TX uses just two pairs (pins 1-2 and 3-6), but 1000BASE-T and faster send on all four pairs in both directions at once, using echo cancellation to separate the signals.
  • Solid-conductor cable is for fixed horizontal runs punched into panels and sockets; stranded cable is flexible but loses more signal, which is why patch cords are limited to about 10 m.
  • Installation rules: keep the bend radius at least four times the cable diameter, pull with no more than about 110 N (25 lbf), and untwist no more than 13 mm at terminations.
  • TIA's structured-cabling family covers TIA-568 (components and testing), TIA-569 (pathways and spaces), TIA-606 (labelling) and TIA-607 (bonding and grounding); ISO/IEC 11801 is the international equivalent.
  • Wiremap tests catch opens, shorts, reversed pairs, crossed pairs and split pairs; a split pair passes simple continuity checks but fails NEXT, so only a certifier finds it.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Untwisting pairs too far at the jack: more than about 13 mm causes crosstalk failures, especially on Cat6 and Cat6a.
  • Buying 'Cat7' or 'Cat8' RJ45 patch leads for home speed: they add nothing over Cat6a and are often non-standard.
  • Running data cable tightly alongside mains power or fluorescent fittings: keep separation or use shielded cable to avoid interference.
  • Using cheap copper-clad aluminium cable: it fails standards, overheats with PoE and is not allowed in compliant installations.

docs.title: Try it: Check the negotiated speed and duplex of your wired link (Linux)

docs.title: 2.2 Fiber Optics
docs.text:
Fibre-optic cable sends data as pulses of light through a hair-thin strand of glass. Light does not suffer from electrical interference and fades very slowly, so fibre can carry huge amounts of data for many kilometres. There are two main types: multimode (short distances, cheaper optics) and single-mode (long distances).

Multimode vs single-mode fibre

Multimode (MMF) Single-mode (SMF) Core / cladding 50 or 62.5 µm / 125 µm About 9 µm / 125 µm Light source VCSEL laser or LED Laser Wavelengths 850 nm (to 953 nm on OM5) 1310 nm and 1550 nm 10G reach 300 m OM3, 400 m OM4 10 km LR, 40 km ER Jacket colour Orange, aqua, violet, lime Yellow Cost Cheaper optics Cheaper cable, pricier optics

Choose by distance: multimode inside buildings, single-mode between them.

Think of it like…

Fibre is like a mirrored tunnel: a torch shone in one end bounces along the walls and comes out the far end, even round gentle bends.

Real-world example

A hospital campus links two buildings 600 m apart. Multimode OM4 only reaches about 400 m at 10 Gb/s, so the contractor installs single-mode OS2 fibre with 10GBASE-LR optics, which reach 10 km. Each building gets a fibre patch panel, and the strands are fusion-spliced onto pigtails with a loss of under 0.1 dB per splice. The light meter shows a total link loss of 1.2 dB, well inside the budget.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A laser or LED in the transmitter turns bits into flashes of light (on/off or several brightness levels).
  2. The light travels in the glass core, kept inside by total internal reflection at the boundary with the cladding.
  3. Multimode fibre has a wide core (50 or 62.5 µm) so light takes many paths; single-mode has a 9 µm core and one path.
  4. Common wavelengths are 850 nm (multimode), 1310 nm and 1550 nm (single-mode), where glass absorbs least.
  5. A photodiode at the far end turns light back into electrical bits.
  6. WDM sends several wavelengths (colours) down one fibre at once to multiply capacity.

Who uses it

Data centres, ISPs, telecom carriers, campus networks and FTTH installers all rely on fibre.

Key takeaway

Remember: multimode = short reach, orange/aqua/lime jackets; single-mode = long reach, yellow jacket. Never look into a fibre or optic, as invisible laser light can damage your eyes.

Going deeper

  • Every fibre has a glass core and cladding (125 µm outer diameter), a 250 µm coating and often a 900 µm tight buffer; outdoor cables use gel-filled or dry loose tubes for protection.
  • Multimode reach is limited by modal dispersion (light paths arrive at different times); single-mode is limited by chromatic dispersion, which is near zero at 1310 nm, while loss is lowest near 1550 nm (about 0.2 dB/km).
  • TIA-568 loss allowances for budgets: 0.75 dB per mated connector pair, 0.3 dB per splice, 3.5 dB/km for multimode at 850 nm, 1.0 dB/km for indoor single-mode.
  • End-face polish matters: UPC (blue) has a flat polish with about 50 dB return loss, APC (green) an 8-degree angle reaching 60 dB or more; never mate APC with UPC.
  • Erbium-doped fibre amplifiers (EDFA) boost the whole C-band (about 1530-1565 nm) without converting to electricity, letting DWDM systems span 80-100 km between amplifier sites.
  • Bend-insensitive single-mode fibre (ITU-T G.657) tolerates tight corners inside homes, which is why FTTH drop cables can be stapled around skirting boards.
  • Fibre links need polarity: transmit must meet receive. Duplex cords use A-to-B polarity, and MPO trunks follow TIA-568.3 methods A, B or C.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Looking into a fibre or optic to 'see if it is lit': infrared light is invisible and can damage eyes; use a power meter.
  • Mixing multimode and single-mode patch cords or optics: the mismatch causes huge loss or no link at all.
  • Connecting fibres without inspecting and cleaning: dust on an end-face is one of the most common causes of errors and flapping links.
  • Forgetting polarity when a new link stays down: swap the transmit and receive strands at one end before replacing optics.

A 10GBASE-LR optic transmits at 1310 nm; a 10GBASE-ER optic uses 1550 nm to reach 40 km. A subsea cable carries over 100 wavelengths per fibre pair, each at hundreds of Gb/s, using DWDM. After a digger cuts a fibre, a technician uses a fusion splicer in a van to rejoin all 48 strands. The OTDR trace shows a break 3.2 km from the exchange, telling the repair crew exactly where to dig. Visual fault locator & light meterVarious vendors · Tool · Layer 1 A red laser pen that glows at fibre breaks, and a power meter that measures received light in dBm. A technician shines the red VFL down a patch cord and spots light leaking from a crushed bend in the tray. Fibre cleaning & inspectionIEC 61300-3-35 · Concept · Layer 1 Dirty connector end-faces are a top cause of fibre faults; inspect with a scope and clean before every connection. A 100G link keeps flapping; after cleaning a dusty LC connector with a click-cleaner, errors drop to zero. A new 10G link shows no light received; flipping the LC duplex clip at one end brings the link up immediately.
