A 600 km national backbone places EDFA huts roughly every 80 km so the signals reach the far city.

docs.title: 2.3 Connectors, Transceivers & Modules
docs.text:
Connectors are the plugs on the ends of cables, and transceivers are small swappable modules that convert electrical signals in a switch into light or copper signals on the cable. Using modules means one switch port can accept short-range, long-range or copper links just by changing the plug-in part.

Pluggable module families by speed. More lanes and faster lanes per module drive each new generation.

Think of it like…

A transceiver is like a travel adapter: the switch has one socket shape, and you choose the adapter that fits the country (cable type and distance) you are visiting.

Real-world example

Leo's core switch has 25G SFP28 ports. For a server in the next rack he uses a 3 m passive DAC cable, which is cheap and needs no optics. For an uplink to another floor 200 m away he inserts an SFP28 25GBASE-SR optic and connects an OM4 LC-LC duplex patch cord. For the 100G link to the data-centre spine he uses a QSFP28 port with an MPO-12 cable.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Pick the speed you need (1G, 10G, 25G, 100G, 400G...) which determines the module family (SFP, SFP+, SFP28, QSFP28...).
  2. Pick the reach and media: copper DAC for a few metres, multimode SR optics for hundreds of metres, single-mode LR/ER for kilometres.
  3. Match the connector on the optic (LC duplex, MPO) to your patch cords and fibre type.
  4. Insert the hot-swappable module; the switch reads its EEPROM to identify type, vendor and wavelength.
  5. Check light levels and that both ends use matching standards (e.g. both 10GBASE-LR).

Who uses it

Network engineers in enterprises and data centres choose and stock these daily; help-desk staff meet RJ45 and RJ11 constantly.

Key takeaway

Both ends of a fibre link must use the same optic standard and wavelength; an SR optic will never talk to an LR optic.

Going deeper

  • Optic names decode as speed, reach and lanes: 100GBASE-SR4 is short reach over four parallel multimode fibres; LR4 reaches 10 km using four wavelengths on one single-mode pair; DR is 500 m, FR 2 km, ER 40 km.
  • Digital diagnostics (SFF-8472 for SFP, SFF-8636 and CMIS for QSFP families) report temperature, voltage, laser bias and transmit/receive power, letting you spot a fading link early.
  • Breakout cabling splits one fast port into several slower ones: a 100G QSFP28 can feed four 25G SFP28 servers, and a 400G DR4 port four 100G DR links.
  • Coherent pluggables such as 400ZR and ZR+ put DWDM-capable optics in a QSFP-DD or OSFP slot, so routers connect directly over 80-120 km or more without separate transponders.
  • BiDi optics send and receive on two different wavelengths over a single strand, halving fibre use; both ends must use a matched pair, such as 1270 nm and 1330 nm.
  • Many switches check a module's EEPROM vendor code and may refuse unknown optics; third-party 'coded' optics programmed for each vendor are common and much cheaper.
  • Heat limits density: a 400G QSFP-DD optic can draw over 10 W, and RJ45 10GBASE-T SFP+ modules run hot with reduced reach, so check vendor support lists.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Pairing different optic types: SR and LR, or 850 nm and 1310 nm optics, will never link even though the connectors fit.
  • Plugging an LC duplex cord into a parallel optic: SR4 and DR4 modules need MPO cables, not LC.
  • Assuming every SFP+ port accepts a 1G SFP or every SFP28 port runs 10G: check the switch's supported speeds and optics list.
  • Ignoring rising receive-power alarms in DOM: they usually warn of dirty connectors or damaged fibre before the link fails.

docs.title: 2.4 〰️ Signals, Encoding & Modulation
docs.text:
To send bits, we must change something physical, such as voltage, light brightness or a radio wave, in a pattern the receiver understands. Encoding is the rulebook for turning 1s and 0s into those changes. Modulation lets one change carry several bits at once, which is how links keep getting faster.

Bits carried per symbol. Each extra bit per symbol needs a cleaner signal (higher SNR).

Think of it like…

Encoding is like signalling with a torch: one person blinks on/off (1 bit per blink), while a cleverer pair agrees on four brightness levels, sending 2 bits per blink.

Real-world example

A 400G Ethernet optic uses PAM4, which has four signal levels, so each symbol carries 2 bits. At about 53 billion symbols per second (53 GBd) per lane it carries about 106 Gb/s of raw bits per lane. Meanwhile Ana's Wi-Fi 7 router uses 4096-QAM, where each symbol carries 12 bits, but only works close to the router where the signal-to-noise ratio is high.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A digital signal has discrete levels (e.g. high/low); an analogue signal varies smoothly like a sound wave.
  2. Frequency (Hz) is how many cycles per second; bandwidth is the range of frequencies a channel can use.
  3. Baud is symbols per second; bit rate = baud × bits per symbol.
  4. Line codes (NRZ, Manchester, PAM4) turn bits into levels on a wire or fibre; QAM and OFDM modulate radio or cable carriers.
  5. Noise, attenuation and crosstalk blur the signal; a higher signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) allows more bits per symbol.
  6. Shannon's limit sets the maximum error-free rate for a given bandwidth and SNR; real systems add error correction (FEC).

Who uses it

Telecom and RF engineers, hardware designers and anyone studying for Network+ or CCNA who must explain why speeds and distances are limited.

Key takeaway

Bit rate = baud rate × bits per symbol: NRZ = 1 bit/symbol, PAM4 = 2, 256-QAM = 8, 1024-QAM = 10, 4096-QAM = 12.

Going deeper

  • Decibels are logarithmic: +3 dB doubles power and +10 dB multiplies it by ten. dBm is absolute power relative to 1 mW, so 0 dBm = 1 mW and -30 dBm = 1 µW.
  • QAM places symbols on an amplitude-phase grid called a constellation; each extra bit per symbol packs points closer together and needs roughly 3 dB more SNR to tell them apart.
  • PAM4 doubles bits per symbol versus NRZ but its three stacked eyes are each a third the height, costing about 9.5 dB of SNR, which is why PAM4 links rely on FEC.
  • Ethernet line codes by generation: 100BASE-TX uses 4B/5B with MLT-3, 1000BASE-T uses PAM-5 on four pairs, 10GBASE-T uses PAM-16 with LDPC coding, and 50G-plus lanes use PAM4.
  • Receivers recover the clock from signal transitions, so long runs of identical bits are dangerous; block codes and scramblers guarantee enough transitions to stay in sync.
  • Adaptive modulation picks the densest scheme the SNR allows: Wi-Fi steps down its MCS index and DOCSIS changes its profiles, which is why speed falls with distance.
  • Multiplexing shares one medium: TDM gives time slots, FDM separate frequencies, WDM separate wavelengths of light, and OFDM many overlapping orthogonal sub-carriers.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating baud and bit rate as the same: they match only when each symbol carries one bit, as with NRZ.
  • Expecting 4096-QAM speeds across the house: top modulation needs a very high SNR, typically only within a few metres of the access point.
  • Reading decibels as linear: -3 dB means half the power, and -10 dB means one tenth, not 'a little less'.
  • Ignoring rising FEC-corrected counts: they show a degrading link that will start dropping frames once FEC is overwhelmed.

docs.title: Key protocols, devices, standards & tools
docs.text: Name What it does Example Analogue vs digital signalSignal theory · Concept · Layer 1 Analogue signals vary continuously; digital signals use a fixed set of levels representing bits, making them easier to regenerate cleanly. A landline voice call was an analogue wave; the same call over VoIP is sampled into digital bits. Frequency, Hertz & bandwidthSI unit (Hz) · Concept · Layer 1 Hertz means cycles per second. Bandwidth is the width of frequency range available; more bandwidth allows more data. Cat6a is rated to 500 MHz; a Wi-Fi 6 channel can be 160 MHz wide, and Wi-Fi 7 can use 320 MHz. Baud vs bit rateSignal theory · Concept · Layer 1 Baud counts symbols per second; bit rate counts bits per second. They are equal only when each symbol carries one bit. A modem sending 2400 baud with 16 levels (4 bits each) transfers 9600 bit/s. NRZ (Non-Return-to-Zero)Line coding (used in many IEEE 802.3 PHYs) · Technology · Layer 1 · Current Simplest line code: one level for 1, another for 0, one bit per symbol. Used up to 25G per lane. A 10GBASE-SR optic sends NRZ: laser bright for 1, dim for 0, about 10.3 billion times a second. Manchester encodingIEEE 802.3 (10 Mb/s Ethernet) · Technology · Layer 1 · Legacy Each bit has a mid-bit transition (high-to-low or low-to-high), embedding the clock in the data at the cost of double the signal rate. Original 10BASE-T Ethernet uses Manchester, so its 10 Mb/s signal switches up to 20 million times a second. Block codes (4B/5B, 8b/10b, 64b/66b)IEEE 802.3 · Technology · Layer 1 · Current Map groups of data bits to slightly longer code groups to keep enough transitions for clock recovery and detect errors. 1000BASE-X uses 8b/10b (25% overhead); 10G Ethernet uses 64b/66b, which wastes only about 3%. PAM4IEEE 802.3bs/802.3cd/802.3df · Technology · Layer 1 · Current Pulse Amplitude Modulation with 4 levels, carrying 2 bits per symbol. Used for 50G, 100G and 200G per lane Ethernet. 400GBASE-DR4 sends 100 Gb/s per fibre using PAM4 at about 53 GBd. QAMUsed by IEEE 802.11, DOCSIS, DVB · Technology · Layer 1 · Current Quadrature Amplitude Modulation changes both amplitude and phase of a carrier, so each symbol can carry many bits. DOCSIS 3.1 cable uses up to 4096-QAM downstream; Wi-Fi 6 uses 1024-QAM and Wi-Fi 7 4096-QAM. OFDM / OFDMAUsed by IEEE 802.11a/g/n/ac/ax/be, 4G/5G, DSL (DMT), DOCSIS 3.1 · Technology · Layer 1 · Current Splits a channel into many narrow sub-carriers sent in parallel, resisting interference. OFDMA shares sub-carriers among users. A Wi-Fi 6 access point uses OFDMA to send small packets to several phones in the same transmission. Nyquist rateHarry Nyquist (1928) · Concept · Layer 1 A noiseless channel of bandwidth B can carry at most 2B symbols per second; max bit rate = 2B × log2(levels). A 3 kHz phone line with 2 levels could carry at most 6000 bit/s; with 16 levels, 24,000 bit/s. Shannon-Hartley theoremClaude Shannon (1948) · Concept · Layer 1 Maximum error-free capacity C = B × log2(1 + SNR). More bandwidth or a cleaner signal raises the ceiling. A 20 MHz channel with SNR of 1000 (30 dB) has a theoretical limit of about 20 × 10 = 200 Mb/s. Noise & SNRSignal theory (measured in dB) · Concept · Layer 1 Noise is unwanted random energy; SNR is signal power divided by noise power, usually in decibels. Higher is better. A laptop reports -55 dBm signal and -95 dBm noise: an SNR of 40 dB, excellent for fast Wi-Fi. AttenuationSignal theory · Concept · Layer 1 Loss of signal strength over distance, through connectors or obstacles, measured in dB (per km for fibre). Every 3 dB halves the power. A long Cat5e run attenuates high frequencies so much that a gigabit link falls back to 100 Mb/s. Crosstalk (NEXT / FEXT)ANSI/TIA-568 test parameters · Concept · Layer 1 Signal leaking from one wire pair into a neighbouring pair. Near-end (NEXT) and far-end (FEXT) are measured in cable tests. A technician untwisted 5 cm of pairs at a socket; the certifier flags a NEXT failure until it is re-terminated. Forward Error Correction (FEC)IEEE 802.3 (e.g. RS-FEC Clause 91/119), ITU-T · Technology · Layer 1 · Current Adds redundant bits so the receiver can fix errors itself without retransmission. Essential for PAM4 and long links. A 100G link shows 'corrected FEC codewords' rising but zero uncorrected ones: FEC is quietly doing its job. Decibels (dB and dBm)Logarithmic units (IEC 60027-3) · Concept · Layer 1 dB expresses a ratio such as gain, loss or SNR on a log scale; dBm is absolute power referenced to 1 milliwatt. An optic transmits at -2 dBm and the link loses 6 dB, so the receiver sees -8 dBm, about 0.16 mW.

docs.title: 2.5 Internet Access Technologies
docs.text:
The 'last mile' is the link between your home or business and your internet provider. It might use old phone wires (DSL), cable-TV coax (DOCSIS), fibre to the home, mobile radio (5G) or satellites. Each has different speeds, delays and costs.

Headline downstream line rates. PON and DOCSIS rates are shared by many homes; DSL rates fall fast with distance.

Think of it like…

Access technologies are like different roads to the motorway: a narrow country lane (dial-up), a B-road (DSL), a dual carriageway (cable) or a private express lane (fibre or a leased line).

Real-world example

Three friends compare connections. Raj in a city flat has XGS-PON fibre giving 2 Gb/s both ways and 8 ms ping. Ella in a rural village uses VDSL2 at 45 Mb/s down because she is 900 m from the street cabinet. Their friend on a remote farm uses LEO satellite at 150 Mb/s with about 35 ms latency, far better than older geostationary satellite at around 600 ms.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Your router or modem connects to the provider's access network over copper, coax, fibre or radio.
  2. Signals are modulated to fit the medium (e.g. DMT for DSL, OFDM/QAM for cable, light for PON).
  3. The provider's equipment (DSLAM, CMTS, OLT or base station) aggregates many customers.
  4. Traffic is handed into the provider's core network and on to the internet.
  5. Speed depends on technology, distance, sharing (contention) and plan; latency depends heavily on distance and medium.

Who uses it

Everyone who has broadband; ISP field engineers, help-desk staff and small-business IT choose and troubleshoot these daily.

Key takeaway

Asymmetric (ADSL, many cable plans) means download is faster than upload; GPON is 2.5/1.25 Gb/s shared, XGS-PON is 10/10 Gb/s shared.

Going deeper

  • A PON has an OLT at the exchange, passive splitters (often 1:32 or 1:64) and an ONT per home; downstream is broadcast and encrypted, while upstream uses timed slots so homes never collide.
  • PON generations share one fibre using different wavelengths: GPON 1490 nm down and 1310 nm up, XGS-PON 1577 nm down and 1270 nm up, and RF video overlay at 1550 nm.
  • DSL speed collapses with copper length: VDSL2 is best under about 1 km, vectoring cancels crosstalk between neighbours' lines, and G.fast suits drops of a few hundred metres.
  • DOCSIS 3.1 uses OFDM channels up to 192 MHz wide; DOCSIS 4.0 extends spectrum to 1.8 GHz and adds Full Duplex or Extended Spectrum modes for multi-gigabit upstream.
  • Behind the access node, a broadband network gateway (BNG) authenticates subscribers via PPPoE or IPoE with DHCP, applies speed plans and often performs carrier-grade NAT for IPv4.
  • Businesses choose between best-effort broadband and dedicated internet access with an SLA; SD-WAN often mixes both plus a 4G/5G backup link for resilience.
  • LEO dishes are electronically steered phased arrays that hand over between satellites constantly; Starlink reschedules connections about every 15 seconds and uses laser links between satellites.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming 'fibre broadband' means fibre to your home: many such products are FTTC, with copper VDSL2 for the last few hundred metres.
  • Comparing headline line rates with real throughput: PON and cable capacity is shared, and protocol overhead lowers usable speed.
  • Choosing GEO satellite for gaming or video calls: about 600 ms round trip is unavoidable physics.
  • Confusing modem and router: the modem or ONT terminates the access line, while the router does NAT, DHCP and Wi-Fi, even when combined in one box.

docs.title: 2.6 Ethernet & MAC Addresses
docs.text:
Ethernet is the rulebook almost every wired local network uses to package data into 'frames' and deliver them between devices. Each network card has a MAC address, a unique 48-bit hardware label, so frames can say exactly which device they are for. Ethernet has grown from 10 Mb/s in the 1980s to 800 Gb/s today.

An Ethernet II frame on the wire. 64-1518 bytes from destination MAC to FCS; 1522 with a VLAN tag.

Think of it like…

A frame is like an envelope inside a building's internal mail: the MAC addresses are the desk names on the front, and the FCS is a seal showing nobody damaged the contents.

Real-world example

Kai's laptop (MAC 3C:22:FB:1A:2B:3C) sends an IPv4 packet to the printer (MAC 00:1B:A9:44:55:66). The NIC adds a preamble, the printer's MAC as destination, its own MAC as source, EtherType 0x0800 to say 'IPv4 inside', the data and a 4-byte CRC. The printer recalculates the CRC; it matches, so the frame is accepted. The first 3 bytes 00:1B:A9 are the OUI showing the manufacturer.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The upper layer hands down a packet (e.g. IPv4) to the network interface card.
  2. The NIC builds a frame: destination MAC, source MAC, EtherType/length, payload (46-1500 bytes) and FCS.
  3. On the wire, a 7-byte preamble and 1-byte Start Frame Delimiter come first so the receiver can synchronise.
  4. Every receiving NIC checks the destination MAC: its own, broadcast or a multicast it has joined, otherwise it discards.
  5. The receiver recalculates the CRC-32; if it does not match the FCS, the frame is silently dropped.
  6. The payload is handed up to the protocol named in the EtherType field.

Who uses it

Every network engineer, sysadmin and security analyst; MAC addresses appear in switch tables, DHCP logs and Wireshark captures.

Key takeaway

Standard Ethernet frame: 64 bytes minimum, 1518 bytes maximum (1522 with an 802.1Q tag); MTU payload is 1500 bytes.

Going deeper

  • The 64-byte minimum comes from CSMA/CD: a frame had to last 512 bit times so a collision at the far end of the cable was detected while still sending; short payloads are padded.
  • A 12-byte interframe gap separates frames, so a 64-byte frame occupies 84 bytes of wire time and gigabit Ethernet peaks at 1,488,095 frames per second.
  • The same 2-byte field means two things: values of 1536 (0x0600) and above are an EtherType (Ethernet II), while 1500 or below are a length, as in 802.3 frames carrying LLC.
  • Phones and laptops randomise MAC addresses per Wi-Fi network (iOS 14+, Android 10+, Windows), protecting privacy but breaking MAC-based filters and DHCP reservations.
  • Well-known multicast MACs: 01:00:5E plus 23 bits for IPv4 multicast, 33:33 plus 32 bits for IPv6, and 01:80:C2:00:00:00 for spanning tree BPDUs.
  • Ethernet was invented by Bob Metcalfe at Xerox PARC in 1973, published as DIX Ethernet II in 1982, standardised as IEEE 802.3 in 1983, and ran over twisted pair from 1990.
  • MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE) can encrypt and authenticate every frame hop by hop between switches or between a host and its switch, protecting links in untrusted wiring closets.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Believing MAC addresses are permanent and unforgeable: they can be changed in software, randomised or spoofed, so never rely on them alone for security.
  • Blaming every CRC error on the cable: duplex mismatches, faulty optics, dirty fibre and electrical interference cause them too.
  • Enabling jumbo frames on only some devices: every switch, router and host on the path must agree, or large frames are silently dropped.
  • Treating frames over 1518 bytes as always faulty: VLAN tags, QinQ and MPLS legitimately make 'baby giant' frames a few bytes larger.

docs.title: Key protocols, devices, standards & tools
docs.text: Name What it does Example IEEE 802.3 (Ethernet)IEEE 802.3 · Standard · Multi-layer · Current The family of standards defining Ethernet's physical layers and MAC framing, first published in 1983 and amended constantly since. Each new speed, like 2.5GBASE-T (802.3bz) or 800G (802.3df), is an amendment to 802.3. Ethernet frame formatIEEE 802.3 · Concept · Layer 2 · Current Destination MAC (6 B), source MAC (6 B), EtherType/length (2 B), payload (46-1500 B), FCS (4 B). In Wireshark, expanding 'Ethernet II' shows Dst, Src and Type: IPv4 (0x0800) for a web request. Preamble & SFDIEEE 802.3 · Concept · Layer 1 · Current 7 bytes of alternating 1s and 0s plus a 1-byte Start Frame Delimiter that let the receiver lock onto timing before the frame. Wireshark normally does not show the preamble because the NIC strips it before passing the frame up. MAC addressIEEE (EUI-48) · Concept · Layer 2 · Current 48-bit hardware address written as 12 hex digits, e.g. 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E. Must be unique on its local network. A DHCP server reserves 192.168.1.50 for the MAC address of the office printer so its IP never changes. OUI (Organizationally Unique Identifier)IEEE Registration Authority · Concept · Layer 2 · Current The first 24 bits of a MAC address, assigned by IEEE to a manufacturer. The remaining 24 bits are set by the vendor. Looking up OUI 00:50:56 in the IEEE registry reveals a VMware virtual NIC. Unicast, multicast & U/L bitsIEEE 802 · Concept · Layer 2 · Current The lowest bit of the first byte marks multicast (1) or unicast (0); the next bit marks locally administered addresses. Phones using MAC randomisation show addresses like 'DA:...', where the locally administered bit is set. Broadcast address FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FFIEEE 802 · Concept · Layer 2 · Current All-ones destination MAC meaning 'every device on this LAN'. Switches flood broadcasts out of every port in the VLAN. An ARP request asking 'who has 192.168.1.1?' is sent to FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF. EtherTypeIEEE Registration Authority · Concept · Layer 2 · Current 2-byte field naming the payload protocol: 0x0800 IPv4, 0x86DD IPv6, 0x0806 ARP, 0x8100 802.1Q VLAN tag. A capture filter 'ether proto 0x0806' in tcpdump shows only ARP traffic. FCS / CRC-32IEEE 802.3 · Concept · Layer 2 · Current Frame Check Sequence: a 4-byte CRC-32 checksum used to detect corrupted frames, which are then discarded (not repaired). A switch port shows thousands of 'CRC errors', pointing to a damaged cable or bad connector. CSMA/CDIEEE 802.3 · Protocol · Layer 2 · Legacy Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection: listen first, transmit, and back off randomly if a collision is detected. Only needed for half-duplex. On a 1990s hub, two PCs sending at once collided; modern full-duplex switch ports never collide, so CSMA/CD is unused. Full vs half duplex & auto-negotiationIEEE 802.3 Clause 28/37 · Concept · Layer 1 · Current Full duplex sends and receives simultaneously; auto-negotiation lets both ends agree speed and duplex automatically. A server hard-set to 100/full facing a switch on auto ends in a duplex mismatch with late collisions and slow transfers. Copper speed standards (10BASE-T to 10GBASE-T)IEEE 802.3i, 802.3u, 802.3ab, 802.3bz, 802.3an · Standard · Layer 1 · Current 10BASE-T (10 Mb/s), 100BASE-TX, 1000BASE-T, 2.5G/5GBASE-T and 10GBASE-T over twisted pair. 'BASE' means baseband; T means twisted pair. A Wi-Fi 6 access point uses a 2.5GBASE-T port so it can run faster than 1 Gb/s over existing Cat5e. Fibre speed standards (1000BASE-SX to 10GBASE-LR)IEEE 802.3z, 802.3ae · Standard · Layer 1 · Current Suffixes tell the media: SX/SR short reach multimode, LX/LR long reach single-mode (10 km), ER extended (40 km). 10GBASE-SR runs 300 m on OM3; 10GBASE-LR runs 10 km on single-mode fibre. High-speed Ethernet (25G to 800G, 1.6T)IEEE 802.3ba, 802.3by, 802.3bs, 802.3df, 802.3dj · Standard · Layer 1 · Current 40/100G (2010), 25G (2016), 200/400G (2017), 800G (802.3df, 2024). 802.3dj adds 200G-per-lane PHYs and 1.6 Tb/s, nearing approval in late 2026. Hyperscale AI clusters moved from 400G to 800G links and are now deploying early 1.6T optics. Jumbo framesVendor practice (not part of IEEE 802.3) · Concept · Layer 2 · Current Frames with a payload larger than 1500 bytes, commonly 9000-byte MTU, reducing overhead for bulk transfers. Every device on the path must agree. A storage team sets MTU 9000 on iSCSI hosts and switches; one forgotten switch port causes mysterious timeouts. MAC address randomisationApple iOS 14+, Android 10+, Windows 10/11; IEEE 802c local addresses · Technology · Layer 2 · Current Devices use a random, locally administered MAC address per Wi-Fi network so they cannot be tracked between places. A school's MAC-based Wi-Fi allow-list breaks for new phones until staff switch to 802.1X logins instead.

docs.title: 2.7 Switching Fundamentals
docs.text:
A switch is a box with many Ethernet ports that connects devices on the same local network. It learns which MAC address lives on which port and then sends each frame only where it needs to go, instead of to everyone. This makes networks faster and more private than old hubs.

How a switch learns, floods and forwards. After one exchange the switch knows both ports and stops flooding.

Think of it like…

A switch is like a smart receptionist who notes which office each person sits in after they first walk past, then delivers their post straight there instead of shouting it down every corridor.

Real-world example

A new switch powers on with an empty MAC table. PC-A on port 1 sends a frame to PC-B. The switch records 'PC-A is on port 1', but does not yet know PC-B, so it floods the frame out of every other port. PC-B replies from port 5; the switch learns 'PC-B is on port 5' and forwards the reply only to port 1. From now on, A-to-B traffic travels only between ports 1 and 5.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Learn: read the source MAC of every incoming frame and record it with the port and VLAN in the MAC address table.
  2. Look up: check the destination MAC in the table.
  3. Forward: if found on another port, send it only there.
  4. Filter: if the destination is on the same port it arrived from, drop it.
  5. Flood: if the destination is unknown, broadcast or (by default) multicast, send it out every port in the VLAN except the source.
  6. Age out: entries not seen for a while (often 300 seconds) are removed so the table stays current.

Who uses it

Network administrators and technicians in every organisation; switches are the most common device in any wired network.

Key takeaway

Each switch port is its own collision domain; the whole VLAN is one broadcast domain. Only routers (or Layer 3 switches) separate broadcast domains.

Going deeper

  • Switches look up MAC addresses in CAM (exact-match memory) inside the forwarding ASIC; ACLs, QoS and routes use TCAM, which matches with masks. Table sizes range from a few thousand to hundreds of thousands of entries.
  • A non-blocking switch's fabric capacity equals the total of all port speeds counted in both directions: 48 x 1G plus 4 x 10G needs 176 Gb/s.
  • Access switches are usually oversubscribed at the uplink: 48 x 1G user ports sharing 2 x 10G uplinks is 2.4:1, which works because users rarely all transmit together.
  • Short traffic bursts (microbursts) can overflow port buffers and drop frames even when average utilisation looks low; deep-buffer switches suit storage and data-centre edges.
  • A third legacy method, fragment-free switching, checks the first 64 bytes before forwarding, catching most collision fragments with less delay than store-and-forward.
  • Unknown-unicast flooding often comes from asymmetric routing: MAC entries age out after 300 s while Cisco ARP entries last 4 hours, so the switch keeps flooding until timers align.
  • Managed switches are configured through a console port, SSH, a web GUI or APIs, and come as fixed, stackable or modular chassis designs.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Expecting a switch to stop broadcasts: it floods them across the whole VLAN; only routers or Layer 3 interfaces end a broadcast domain.
  • Letting users add unmanaged switches: a looped cable on one creates a broadcast storm, because cheap switches often lack spanning tree.
  • Setting port security to one MAC on desk ports with IP phones: the phone and PC behind it need at least two, or three on some designs.
  • Assuming all switches are equally fast: check fabric capacity, buffers and uplink oversubscription, not just port speeds.

In an exam scenario, replacing a hub with a switch stops collisions and stops PCs seeing each other's traffic. MAC address table (CAM table)IEEE 802.1Q bridging · Concept · Layer 2 · Current The switch's memory of which MAC addresses are reachable on which port and VLAN, built automatically by learning. To find which port a mystery device uses, an admin searches the MAC table for its MAC and traces the cable. MAC learningIEEE 802.1Q (transparent bridging) · Concept · Layer 2 · Current Recording the source MAC address of each received frame against the incoming port. When a laptop moves from desk 3 to desk 9, the switch relearns its MAC on the new port within one frame. FloodingIEEE 802.1Q bridging · Concept · Layer 2 · Current Sending a frame out of every port in the VLAN except the source, for broadcasts and unknown destinations. After a reboot, the first frames to a server are flooded until the switch learns where the server lives. Forwarding & filteringIEEE 802.1Q bridging · Concept · Layer 2 · Current Forwarding sends a frame to the single known port; filtering drops a frame whose destination is on the same port it came in on. Two PCs behind a small desk switch talk to each other; the main switch filters their frames rather than forwarding them. Collision domainIEEE 802.3 · Concept · Layer 1 · Current A segment where simultaneous transmissions collide. Every switch port, and every full-duplex link, is its own domain. A 24-port switch has 24 collision domains; a 24-port hub has just one. Broadcast domainIEEE 802 / IP networking · Concept · Layer 2 · Current All devices that receive each other's broadcasts. One per VLAN; routers mark its edge. Splitting 800 devices into four VLANs shrinks each broadcast domain and cuts noisy ARP traffic. Store-and-forward switchingVendor switching method · Concept · Layer 2 · Current The switch receives the entire frame and checks its CRC before forwarding, so corrupted frames are never passed on. Most enterprise switches use store-and-forward, adding only microseconds of delay while blocking bad frames. Cut-through switchingVendor switching method · Concept · Layer 2 · Current The switch begins forwarding as soon as it reads the destination MAC, lowering latency but possibly passing on errors. A stock-exchange trading network uses cut-through switches to shave nanoseconds off every order. Unmanaged switchVarious vendors · Device · Layer 2 · Current Plug-and-play switch with no configuration: no VLANs, monitoring or security features. A home user adds a cheap 8-port unmanaged switch behind the TV for a games console and streaming box. Managed switchVarious vendors · Device · Layer 2 · Current Configurable switch offering VLANs, STP, port security, SNMP monitoring, QoS and remote management via CLI or web. A school's managed switches put student, staff and CCTV devices in separate VLANs. Layer 3 switch (multilayer switch)Various vendors · Device · Multi-layer · Current A switch that can also route IP packets between VLANs in hardware at wire speed. A campus core Layer 3 switch routes between 30 VLANs much faster than an external router could. Port security & MAC floodingVendor features (e.g. Cisco port-security) · Concept · Layer 2 · Current Limits which or how many MACs a port accepts, defending against MAC-flooding attacks that overflow the CAM table. A port allows at most 2 MACs; when someone plugs in a rogue switch with 10 devices, the port shuts down. TCAM (Ternary CAM)Switch ASIC hardware (Broadcom, Cisco, Marvell and others) · Technology · Multi-layer · Current Special memory that matches 0, 1 or 'don't care' bits in one clock cycle, used for ACLs, QoS rules and route lookups. Adding a 2,000-line ACL fails with 'TCAM full', so the engineer summarises rules to fit the hardware. Oversubscription ratioNetwork design practice · Concept · Layer 2 · Current Total downstream port capacity divided by uplink capacity; shows how heavily a switch's uplinks could be overloaded. 48 x 1G access ports with 2 x 10G uplinks gives 48:20, or 2.4:1, acceptable for office users.

docs.title: 2.8 VLANs & Trunking
docs.text:
A VLAN (Virtual LAN) splits one physical switch into several separate logical networks. Devices in different VLANs cannot talk directly, even if plugged into the same switch, unless a router connects them. Trunk links carry many VLANs between switches by adding a small tag to each frame.

A student PC prints across VLANs. Tags exist only on trunks; the core routes between VLAN 20 and VLAN 10.

Think of it like…

VLANs are like colour-coded lanyards at a conference: everyone shares one building, but each colour has its own rooms, and a 'trunk' corridor lets all colours walk between buildings with their lanyards on.

Real-world example

Greenfield School puts staff PCs in VLAN 10, students in VLAN 20 and CCTV cameras in VLAN 30. Desk ports are access ports in one VLAN each. The link between the classroom switch and the core is an 802.1Q trunk allowing VLANs 10, 20 and 30. The core switch has SVIs (interface vlan 10 = 10.0.10.1, vlan 20 = 10.0.20.1) which route between them, while an ACL blocks students from reaching cameras.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Create VLANs on the switch and give each a number (1-4094) and name.
  2. Set end-device ports as access ports, each assigned to one VLAN; frames leave them untagged.
  3. Set switch-to-switch (or switch-to-router/hypervisor) links as trunks carrying multiple VLANs.
  4. On a trunk, each frame gets a 4-byte 802.1Q tag holding its 12-bit VLAN ID; native VLAN frames travel untagged.
  5. To let VLANs talk, route between them using a router-on-a-stick or SVIs on a Layer 3 switch.

Who uses it

Every enterprise, school, hospital and data centre uses VLANs to separate departments, guest Wi-Fi, voice and IoT devices.

Key takeaway

802.1Q tag = 4 bytes (TPID 0x8100 + 3-bit priority + 1-bit DEI + 12-bit VLAN ID); usable VLANs are 1-4094. Change the native VLAN from 1 to an unused VLAN for security.

Going deeper

  • VLAN IDs 0 and 4095 are reserved, VLAN 1 is the default, and Cisco reserves 1002-1005 for legacy Token Ring and FDDI; 1006-4094 form the 'extended' range.
  • The 4-byte tag raises the maximum frame from 1518 to 1522 bytes; IEEE 802.3ac allowed this, so switches must accept these slightly larger frames on trunks.
  • Good practice: one VLAN per IP subnet, no user traffic in VLAN 1, a dedicated management VLAN, and trunk allowed lists pruned to only the VLANs actually needed.
  • Double-tagging only works when the attacker's access VLAN equals the trunk's native VLAN, and it is one-way; tagging the native VLAN or using an unused one stops it.
  • With 802.1X, a RADIUS server can return the VLAN in its reply (Tunnel-Private-Group-ID), so staff land in the staff VLAN on any port in the building.
  • Hypervisors and Linux tag too: VMware port groups carry VLAN IDs, and 'ip link add link eth0 name eth0.20 type vlan id 20' creates a tagged interface.
  • The 12-bit VLAN ID allows only 4,094 segments, too few for multi-tenant clouds, so VXLAN's 24-bit VNI (about 16.7 million) with an EVPN control plane took over in data centres.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Typing 'switchport trunk allowed vlan 30' to add a VLAN: it replaces the whole list; use 'allowed vlan add 30'.
  • Leaving a native VLAN mismatch between switches: traffic leaks between VLANs and CDP or STP log errors; set the same unused native VLAN on both ends.
  • Assuming VLANs alone isolate traffic: once a Layer 3 switch routes between them, you need ACLs or a firewall to restrict access.
  • Forgetting the gateway: a new VLAN needs an SVI or router subinterface and DHCP scope, or its hosts cannot leave the subnet.

docs.text:
vlan 20

interface Gi1/0/5
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 20
interface Gi1/0/48

show vlan brief
show interfaces trunk

docs.title: Key protocols, devices, standards & tools
docs.text: Name What it does Example VLANIEEE 802.1Q · Concept · Layer 2 · Current A logical broadcast domain on shared switches, identified by a number 1-4094. Improves security and reduces broadcast traffic. Guest Wi-Fi is placed in VLAN 50 so visitors can reach the internet but never the finance servers. IEEE 802.1QIEEE 802.1Q · Standard · Layer 2 · Current The standard for VLAN tagging and bridging; inserts a 4-byte tag after the source MAC on trunk links. A Wireshark capture on a trunk shows '802.1Q Virtual LAN, PRI: 5, ID: 100' before the IPv4 header. Access portVendor term (IEEE 802.1Q untagged port) · Concept · Layer 2 · Current A switch port belonging to a single VLAN, sending and receiving untagged frames, used for end devices. Reception desk port Gi1/0/3 is an access port in VLAN 10 (Staff). Trunk portVendor term (IEEE 802.1Q tagged port) · Concept · Layer 2 · Current A port carrying frames for multiple VLANs, tagged with their VLAN ID, between switches, routers, APs or hypervisors. A Wi-Fi access point's uplink is a trunk so it can put staff and guest SSIDs into different VLANs. Native VLANIEEE 802.1Q (PVID) · Concept · Layer 2 · Current The VLAN whose frames cross a trunk untagged. Defaults to VLAN 1 on Cisco; both ends must match. A switch logs 'native VLAN mismatch' because one side uses VLAN 1 and the other VLAN 999. Voice VLANVendor feature (e.g. Cisco), uses 802.1Q/802.1p · Concept · Layer 2 · Current Lets one access port carry a tagged VLAN for an IP phone plus an untagged data VLAN for the PC plugged into the phone. Desk ports carry voice VLAN 110 for the IP phone and data VLAN 10 for the PC behind it. Router-on-a-stickCommon design using 802.1Q subinterfaces · Concept · Layer 3 · Current One router interface trunked to the switch, with a subinterface per VLAN acting as each VLAN's gateway. A small office router uses Gi0/0.10 (10.0.10.1) and Gi0/0.20 (10.0.20.1) to route between two VLANs. SVI (Switched Virtual Interface)Vendor term (e.g. Cisco 'interface vlan') · Concept · Layer 3 · Current A virtual routed interface for a VLAN on a Layer 3 switch, acting as the default gateway for that VLAN. 'interface vlan 20, ip address 10.0.20.1 255.255.255.0' gives the student VLAN its gateway on the core switch. VTP (VLAN Trunking Protocol)Cisco proprietary (v1, v2, v3) · Protocol · Layer 2 · Legacy Cisco protocol that copies VLAN definitions from a server switch to clients. Modes: server, client, transparent, off. A switch with a higher VTP revision number joins the network and wipes everyone's VLANs, so many admins use transparent mode. DTP (Dynamic Trunking Protocol)Cisco proprietary · Protocol · Layer 2 · Legacy Auto-negotiates whether a link becomes a trunk. Can be abused for VLAN hopping, so it is usually disabled. Security hardening adds 'switchport nonegotiate' on all user ports to stop DTP. VLAN hoppingSecurity attack class · Concept · Layer 2 Attacks (switch spoofing via DTP, or double tagging via the native VLAN) that reach a VLAN the attacker should not access. Disabling DTP and using an unused native VLAN blocks both classic VLAN-hopping tricks. Private VLANsCisco; described in RFC 5517 (Informational) · Technology · Layer 2 · Current Splits a VLAN into isolated and community ports that can reach the gateway (promiscuous port) but not each other. A hotel puts each guest room port in an isolated private VLAN so guests cannot see each other's devices. QinQ (IEEE 802.1ad)IEEE 802.1ad (now part of 802.1Q) · Standard · Layer 2 · Current Stacks a provider's outer VLAN tag (TPID 0x88A8) on top of the customer's tag, letting carriers carry customer VLANs transparently. A metro provider wraps all of a bank's 200 VLANs inside its single service VLAN 3001 across the city. VXLANIETF RFC 7348 · Protocol · Multi-layer · Current Tunnels Layer 2 frames inside UDP (port 4789) over an IP network, with a 24-bit ID allowing about 16 million segments. A data centre uses VXLAN with EVPN so virtual machines keep their subnet when moved between racks. Management VLANNetwork design best practice · Concept · Layer 2 · Current A dedicated VLAN holding the switches' own management addresses, kept separate from user traffic and reachable only by admins. All switches get addresses in VLAN 99 (10.0.99.0/24), and only the IT subnet may SSH into it. Dynamic VLAN assignmentIEEE 802.1X with RADIUS attributes (RFC 3580) · Technology · Layer 2 · Current The authentication server tells the switch which VLAN to put a user or device in after it logs in, instead of fixed port settings. When a contractor authenticates, RADIUS returns VLAN 60, so his laptop reaches only the internet, whichever port he uses.

docs.title: 2.9 Loop Prevention: Spanning Tree
docs.text:
Engineers connect switches with extra links so the network survives a cable failure, but Ethernet frames have no expiry timer, so a loop lets them circle forever. Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) finds loops and blocks just enough ports to leave a single loop-free path, unblocking a backup if the main path fails.

Spanning tree on a triangle. One port on the B-C link blocks, breaking the loop but keeping a backup path.

Think of it like…

STP is like a town council closing some side roads to stop traffic going round in circles, but keeping them ready to reopen if the main road is dug up.

Real-world example

Three switches A, B and C are wired in a triangle. All have default priority 32768, so A, with the lowest MAC, becomes root bridge. B and C each pick their direct link to A as their root port. On the B-C link, B's port is designated and C's port becomes alternate (blocked). When the A-C cable is cut, RSTP unblocks C's port to B in about a second, keeping the office online.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Switches exchange BPDUs (Bridge Protocol Data Units) carrying their Bridge ID (priority + MAC address).
  2. The switch with the lowest Bridge ID becomes the root bridge.
  3. Every other switch picks one root port: its lowest-cost path to the root.
  4. Each link segment gets one designated port (best path towards root); the remaining ports are blocked (alternate/backup).
  5. If a link fails, BPDUs stop arriving and the tree recalculates, unblocking a backup path.
  6. Edge ports to PCs use PortFast so they go straight to forwarding, protected by BPDU Guard.

Who uses it

Anyone running managed switches; STP problems are a classic cause of whole-site outages and a core CCNA topic.

Key takeaway

Lowest Bridge ID wins; priority must be a multiple of 4096 (default 32768). Set your core switch as root deliberately instead of letting the oldest switch win.

Going deeper

  • STP compares BPDUs in strict order: lowest root Bridge ID, then lowest path cost to root, then lowest sender Bridge ID, then lowest sender port ID. Learn this tie-break list for exams.
  • Classic 802.1D timers are hello 2 s, forward delay 15 s and max age 20 s, so reconverging after an indirect failure takes 30-50 seconds.
  • Path cost has two scales: the short method (100 Mb/s = 19, 1G = 4, 10G = 2) and the long method from 802.1t (1G = 20,000, 10G = 2,000), which handles faster links.
  • The extended system ID puts the VLAN number into the priority field, so priorities step in 4,096s and VLAN 10 at default priority shows 32778.
  • RSTP converges quickly through a proposal-agreement handshake on point-to-point links and treats edge ports as instantly forwarding; topology changes flush MAC tables.
  • Modern designs reduce reliance on STP: routed access layers, MLAG pairs and EVPN-VXLAN fabrics use every link actively, but STP stays on as a safety net.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Leaving root election to chance: the oldest, slowest switch may win; set priority 4096 or 'root primary' on the core.
  • Disabling STP to speed up PC boots: use PortFast with BPDU Guard on edge ports instead and keep loop protection.
  • Enabling PortFast on switch-to-switch links: a loop can form instantly before STP blocks anything.
  • Using BPDU Filter casually: it silently stops sending and receiving BPDUs and can hide a loop until the network melts down.

docs.title: Try it: Check and set the root bridge (Cisco IOS)
docs.text:
show spanning-tree
show spanning-tree root
conf t
 spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
 spanning-tree vlan 10,20 root primary
 interface Gi1/0/5
  spanning-tree portfast
  spanning-tree bpduguard enable

docs.title: Key protocols, devices, standards & tools
docs.text: Name What it does Example Switching loop & broadcast stormEthernet bridging behaviour · Concept · Layer 2 With redundant links and no STP, broadcasts multiply endlessly, maxing CPU and bandwidth and corrupting MAC tables within seconds. A visitor plugs both ends of a cable into wall ports; without STP, the whole floor's network freezes. STP (IEEE 802.1D)IEEE 802.1D (based on Radia Perlman's algorithm) · Protocol · Layer 2 · Legacy Original spanning tree. Ports pass through blocking, listening, learning and forwarding; convergence takes 30-50 seconds. On an old network, a PC plugged into a non-PortFast port waits about 30 seconds before getting a DHCP address. RSTP (IEEE 802.1w)IEEE 802.1w (folded into 802.1D-2004) · Protocol · Layer 2 · Current Rapid STP: uses handshakes instead of timers, converging in about a second or less. Port states: discarding, learning, forwarding. After a core uplink fails, RSTP moves traffic to the backup link before users notice. MSTP (IEEE 802.1s)IEEE 802.1s (now part of 802.1Q) · Protocol · Layer 2 · Current Multiple Spanning Tree: maps many VLANs to a few spanning-tree instances, each with its own root, saving CPU and enabling load sharing. A campus maps VLANs 1-100 to instance 1 (root = core A) and 101-200 to instance 2 (root = core B). PVST+ / Rapid PVST+Cisco proprietary · Protocol · Layer 2 · Current Cisco's per-VLAN spanning tree, running a separate tree for every VLAN. Rapid PVST+ uses RSTP per VLAN. Most Cisco campus switches run 'spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst' as their default design. Root bridge electionIEEE 802.1D/802.1Q · Concept · Layer 2 · Current The switch with the lowest Bridge ID (priority first, then MAC) becomes root; all paths are calculated towards it. Setting the core switch priority to 4096 ensures it beats access switches at the default 32768. Bridge ID & path costIEEE 802.1D/802.1Q · Concept · Layer 2 · Current Bridge ID = priority + extended system ID (VLAN) + MAC. Path cost reflects link speed: faster links have lower cost. Using classic costs, a 1 Gb/s link costs 4 and 100 Mb/s costs 19, so STP prefers the gigabit path. Port rolesIEEE 802.1w/802.1Q · Concept · Layer 2 · Current Root port (best path to root), designated port (forwards onto a segment), alternate (backup to root) and backup ports. 'show spanning-tree' lists Gi1/0/49 as Root FWD and Gi1/0/50 as Altn BLK. Port statesIEEE 802.1D / 802.1w · Concept · Layer 2 · Current Classic STP: disabled, blocking, listening, learning, forwarding. RSTP: discarding, learning, forwarding. A newly connected trunk spends 15 s listening and 15 s learning in legacy STP before forwarding. BPDUIEEE 802.1D/802.1Q · Concept · Layer 2 · Current Bridge Protocol Data Unit: STP messages sent every 2 seconds (hello time) to multicast MAC 01:80:C2:00:00:00. Wireshark on a switch port shows 'STP' frames every 2 s announcing the root bridge ID. PortFastCisco (equivalent to RSTP edge port) · Concept · Layer 2 · Current Puts a port connected to an end device straight into forwarding, skipping listening and learning delays. Enabling PortFast on desk ports lets PCs get DHCP leases instantly at boot. BPDU GuardCisco and other vendors · Concept · Layer 2 · Current Shuts down (err-disables) a PortFast port if it ever receives a BPDU, preventing rogue switches from joining. A student plugs a home switch into a classroom port; BPDU Guard disables the port and logs an alert. Root Guard & Loop GuardCisco and other vendors · Concept · Layer 2 · Current Root Guard stops a port from accepting a better root; Loop Guard stops a blocked port from forwarding if BPDUs vanish. Root Guard on distribution downlinks prevents a misconfigured access switch from becoming root. STP timers (hello, forward delay, max age)IEEE 802.1D · Concept · Layer 2 · Current Hello 2 s between BPDUs, forward delay 15 s per listening or learning stage, and max age 20 s before stored BPDU information expires. After an indirect link failure, legacy STP waits 20 s max age plus 2 x 15 s, about 50 seconds of outage. Topology Change Notification (TCN)IEEE 802.1D / 802.1w · Concept · Layer 2 · Current A message that tells the network a forwarding port changed state, making switches age out MAC entries quickly. Hundreds of TCNs a day trace back to PCs on non-PortFast ports; enabling PortFast stops the constant MAC flushing. BPDU FilterCisco and other vendors · Concept · Layer 2 · Current Stops a port sending or processing BPDUs; useful at some provider edges but dangerous because it can hide loops. An engineer finds BPDU Filter enabled on a server port that was later moved to a switch uplink, causing a storm.

docs.title: 2.10 Link Aggregation & Neighbour Discovery
docs.text:
Link aggregation bundles several physical cables between two devices into one logical link, giving more bandwidth and surviving the loss of a cable. Neighbour discovery protocols let devices announce who they are to directly connected neighbours, which makes mapping and troubleshooting a network much easier.

Ways to build a bundle

LACP Static (on) PAgP Standard IEEE 802.1AX None Cisco proprietary Modes active / passive on desirable / auto Bundle forms if At least one side active Both sides on At least one desirable Catches miscabling Yes, via LACPDUs No: loops or black holes Yes Active members Up to 8 (+ standby) Up to 8 Up to 8 Use today Default choice Devices without LACP Legacy Cisco only

LACP is the safe default because it detects mistakes before bundling.

Think of it like…

Link aggregation is like opening extra checkout lanes that all count as one shop entrance; neighbour discovery is like neighbours putting name plates on their doors.

Real-world example

A file server has four 10G ports bundled with LACP to the switch as one 40G logical link (Port-channel 1). Each conversation still uses one member link, chosen by a hash of addresses, so a single copy tops out at 10G, but 50 users together share the full 40G. When one cable is unplugged, traffic shifts to the other three within a second. Later, an engineer runs 'show lldp neighbors' to confirm exactly which switch port each server NIC is connected to.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Choose identical member ports (same speed, duplex and VLAN settings) on both devices.
  2. Configure them into a group using LACP (active/passive) or a static 'on' mode.
  3. LACP exchanges LACPDUs to confirm both ends agree, then bundles the links into one logical interface.
  4. Frames are distributed across members by hashing MAC/IP/port fields, keeping each flow on one link to avoid reordering.
  5. Separately, LLDP or CDP send periodic announcements (name, port, model, IP) to direct neighbours.
  6. UDLD checks fibre links still work in both directions and disables one-way links.

Who uses it

Data-centre and campus engineers use aggregation for server and uplink resilience; help-desk and NOC staff use LLDP/CDP daily to trace connections.

Key takeaway

Aggregation does not make one flow faster than a single member link; it adds total capacity and redundancy. LACP originated as 802.3ad and now lives in IEEE 802.1AX.

Going deeper

  • All members must match: speed, duplex, access VLAN or trunk mode, native VLAN and allowed VLANs; any mismatch leaves a port suspended outside the bundle.
  • LACP sends LACPDUs every 30 s (slow rate) or every 1 s (fast rate) and declares a member dead after three missed messages, so 90 s or 3 s.
  • Many hash algorithms use eight buckets, so bundles of 2, 4 or 8 members share load evenly, while 3 or 6 members end up uneven.
  • Servers aggregate too: Linux bonding offers modes such as active-backup (1) and 802.3ad (4), while Windows uses NIC Teaming or Switch Embedded Teaming in Hyper-V.
  • LLDP sends TLVs (chassis ID, port ID and TTL are mandatory) to multicast 01:80:C2:00:00:0E every 30 s by default, with a 120 s time-to-live.
  • UDLD exchanges echo messages (every 15 s by default); normal mode only flags a one-way link, while aggressive mode err-disables it.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Expecting one file copy to run at the bundle's total speed: each flow hashes onto a single member link.
  • Configuring passive on both ends: neither side starts negotiation, so the bundle never forms; at least one side must be active.
  • Mixing 'on' at one end with LACP at the other: the static side forwards while the LACP side does not, causing loops or lost traffic.
  • Leaving CDP or LLDP enabled on untrusted edge ports: it leaks device models, software versions and addresses to attackers.

docs.text:

show etherchannel summary
show lacp neighbor
show lldp neighbors detail
show cdp neighbors

Four stacked access switches appear as one device, with an uplink LAG spread across members 1 and 4. An admin runs 'lldpctl' on a Linux server and learns it is plugged into switch SW-R12 port Ethernet14. A new IP phone learns via LLDP-MED to use voice VLAN 110 and requests 7 W of PoE. 'show cdp neighbors' reveals that an unlabelled cable leads to router R2's Gi0/1. A damaged receive fibre leaves a link 'up' but one-way; UDLD aggressive mode shuts it before it causes an STP loop. Discovery protocol securityBest practice · Concept · Layer 2 LLDP and CDP reveal model, software version and IP addresses, so disable them on untrusted ports such as internet edges. A pentester sniffs CDP on a meeting-room port and learns the switch's exact IOS version; the team then disables it there. A Linux web server uses bond0 in 802.3ad mode across two 25G ports to a switch MLAG pair. LACP rate (fast / slow)IEEE 802.1AX · Concept · Layer 2 · Current How often LACPDUs are sent: every 1 s (fast) or every 30 s (slow); fast rate detects a failed member much sooner. A storage team sets 'lacp rate fast' so a silently failed link leaves the bundle in about 3 seconds, not 90.

docs.title: 2.11 Other Data Link Protocols
docs.text:
Ethernet dominates today, but many other Layer 2 protocols exist or once did. Some are still used for point-to-point links and broadband logins (PPP, PPPoE, HDLC), Wi-Fi has its own MAC rules, and older technologies like Token Ring, FDDI, Frame Relay and ATM appear in exams and history.

Data link technologies through time. Most legacy technologies were replaced by Ethernet, broadband and MPLS.

Think of it like…

Different data-link protocols are like different postal envelopes: a courier pouch, a recorded-delivery envelope or a parcel tube, each suited to a particular kind of journey.

Real-world example

Ella's VDSL router logs in to her ISP using PPPoE: it discovers the ISP's access concentrator, opens a PPP session and authenticates with CHAP. Because PPPoE adds 8 bytes of header, her router sets the MTU to 1492 instead of 1500. Meanwhile, her laptop on Wi-Fi uses CSMA/CA, waiting for a quiet moment before sending, because radios cannot detect collisions while transmitting.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Point-to-point links (serial, DSL) use simple framing like HDLC or PPP with no MAC addresses needed.
  2. PPP adds authentication (PAP/CHAP), link negotiation (LCP) and network setup (IPCP).
  3. PPPoE carries PPP sessions over Ethernet so ISPs can authenticate each broadband subscriber.
  4. PPPoE's 8-byte header cuts the MTU to 1492, so routers clamp the TCP MSS to 1452 to avoid fragmentation.
  5. Wi-Fi (802.11) uses CSMA/CA and acknowledgements because wireless stations cannot hear collisions.
  6. Legacy WAN/LAN technologies (Frame Relay, ATM, Token Ring, FDDI) were replaced by Ethernet, MPLS and broadband.

Who uses it

ISP engineers (PPPoE), WAN engineers, Wi-Fi specialists and students preparing for Network+ or CCNA history questions.

Key takeaway

PPPoE overhead reduces the MTU to 1492 bytes; Wi-Fi uses CSMA/CA (avoidance), old Ethernet used CSMA/CD (detection).

Going deeper

  • PPP moves through phases: link dead, establish (LCP negotiates MTU and authentication), authenticate (PAP, CHAP or EAP), network (IPCP or IPv6CP) and terminate.
  • PPPoE starts with four discovery messages, PADI, PADO, PADR and PADS, then carries session data; discovery uses EtherType 0x8863 and session traffic 0x8864, and PADT ends it.
  • Routers on PPPoE clamp the TCP MSS to 1452 bytes (1492 minus 40 bytes of IP and TCP headers); RFC 4638 lets capable equipment carry a full 1500-byte MTU instead.
  • CHAP sends a random challenge and expects an MD5 hash of the ID, shared secret and challenge, and may re-challenge during the session; the secret itself never crosses the line.
  • An 802.11 frame can carry four MAC addresses and each unicast frame is acknowledged; RTS/CTS reserves the air to avoid hidden-node collisions between stations that cannot hear each other.
  • Cisco's HDLC adds a proprietary protocol field, so connecting a Cisco serial port to another vendor requires PPP on both ends.
  • Frame Relay's DLCIs and ATM's VPI/VCI were early label-switched virtual circuits; MPLS carried the same idea into IP networks and replaced both.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Leaving MTU at 1500 on PPPoE: large packets get dropped and some sites hang half-loaded; set 1492 and clamp MSS.
  • Using PAP for authentication: it sends the password in clear text; prefer CHAP or EAP.
  • Mismatching serial encapsulation (HDLC on one end, PPP on the other): the interface shows 'up, line protocol down'.
  • Mixing up CSMA/CA and CSMA/CD: Wi-Fi avoids collisions; legacy half-duplex Ethernet detected them.

docs.title: Try it: Check a PPPoE link's MTU and probe the largest packet that fits (Linux and Windows)
docs.text:
ip link show ppp0                 # Linux: look for 'mtu 1492'
ping -M do -s 1464 example.com     # Linux: 1464 + 28 header bytes = 1492, must not fragment
ping -f -l 1464 example.com        # Windows equivalent

Setting 'ip tcp adjust-mss 1452' on a PPPoE dialer stops web pages stalling halfway through loading.

docs.title: 2.12 Power over Ethernet (PoE)
docs.text:
Power over Ethernet sends electrical power along the same network cable that carries data. A single cable can run a Wi-Fi access point, security camera or desk phone, so no power socket is needed where the device is mounted. The switch checks that a device actually wants power before sending any, so plugging in a normal laptop is safe.

PoE power at the switch port. The device receives less than the port supplies because the cable loses some as heat.

Think of it like…

PoE is like a garden hose that also carries a phone line: one connection delivers both what the device needs to live and what it needs to talk.

Real-world example

A school installs 20 Wi-Fi 6 access points (about 25 W each) and 10 cameras (about 13 W each) on one 48-port PoE+ switch with a 740 W PoE budget. The total load is 20 × 25 + 10 × 13 = 630 W, inside the budget with headroom. A later plan to add six 60 W pan-tilt-zoom cameras would exceed it, so the team adds a second switch rather than overloading the first.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The switch or injector (PSE, Power Sourcing Equipment) tests the port for a special signature resistance.
  2. Only if a valid Powered Device (PD) is detected does classification happen, telling the PSE how much power the PD needs.
  3. The PSE applies about 44-57 V DC over two pairs (802.3af/at) or all four pairs (802.3bt).
  4. The PSE deducts the allocated power from its total PoE budget.
  5. If the device is unplugged, the PSE notices and cuts power within milliseconds.

Who uses it

Installers of Wi-Fi access points, IP cameras, VoIP phones, door-entry systems, smart lighting and IoT sensors.

Key takeaway

Memorise power at the switch port: 802.3af 15.4 W, 802.3at (PoE+) 30 W, 802.3bt Type 3 60 W, Type 4 90 W. The device receives less because of cable loss.

Going deeper

  • Power-up runs in stages: the PSE applies a low voltage (about 2.7-10 V) to find a 25 kΩ signature, classifies at around 15-20 V, then switches on 44-57 V (50-57 V for PoE+ and 802.3bt).
  • Two-pair PoE uses Alternative A (power on data pairs 1-2 and 3-6) or Alternative B (spare pairs 4-5 and 7-8); devices must accept either, and 802.3bt uses all four pairs.
  • A powered device must keep drawing a minimum current (the Maintain Power Signature) or the PSE removes power; 802.3bt reduced this so devices can sleep at very low power.
  • Beyond the class, devices can fine-tune their allocation using LLDP (the Data Link Layer classification), letting a switch reserve, say, 18.3 W instead of a full 30 W.
  • Cable loss grows with power: at 90 W about 18.7 W is lost in 100 m of cable as heat, which is why TIA TSB-184-A limits bundle sizes and favours thicker conductors.
  • 'Endspan' PSEs are PoE switches; 'midspan' PSEs are injectors or patch panels inserted into the cable. Features such as perpetual and fast PoE keep power flowing during switch reboots.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming every port can supply full power at once: the switch's total PoE budget is usually far below ports x 30 W.
  • Quoting PSE power as device power: an 802.3at port gives 30 W but the device can rely on only 25.5 W.
  • Plugging standard devices into passive PoE injectors: always-on 24 V or 48 V can damage equipment that does not expect it.
  • Ignoring heat in large cable bundles: high-power PoE warms tightly packed cables, raising loss and shortening their life.

show power inline GigabitEthernet1/0/12 detail

docs.title: Ten Things Every Networking Student Should Master
docs.text: If you are comfortable with these ten skills, you understand networking better than most beginners — and you are ready for CCNA/Network+ level work.

docs.title: 1. Explain the OSI and TCP/IP models
docs.text: Know what each layer does and name a protocol and device for each.

docs.title: 2. Subnet in your head
docs.text: Convert masks and prefixes, and find network, broadcast and host range quickly.

docs.title: 3. Describe what happens when you type a URL
docs.text: DHCP, ARP, DNS, TCP/QUIC, TLS, HTTP and routing — in order.

docs.title: 4. Know TCP vs UDP
docs.text: Handshake, reliability, ports, and which apps use which.

docs.title: 5. Understand switching and VLANs
docs.text: MAC learning, 802.1Q trunks, and why spanning tree exists.

docs.title: 6. Understand routing
docs.text: Routing tables, longest-prefix match, static vs OSPF vs BGP.

docs.title: 7. Use the command line
docs.text: ping, traceroute, ipconfig/ip, nslookup/dig, netstat/ss — and read the output.

docs.title: 8. Capture and read packets
docs.text: Open Wireshark, filter traffic, and follow a TCP conversation.

docs.title: 9. Think about security
docs.text: Firewalls, ACLs, VPNs, 802.1X/NAC, WPA3, segmentation and zero trust are part of every design.

docs.title: 10. Build a lab
docs.text: Practise in Packet Tracer, GNS3 or Containerlab — hands-on beats memorising.

docs.title: Chapter 4: Transport & Application Layers — How Apps Talk
docs.text: Getting a packet to the right computer is only half the job; it also has to reach the right program, arrive in order, and be understood. This chapter covers the transport layer (TCP, UDP, QUIC) that moves data between programs, and the application protocols (DNS, HTTP, email, SSH and many more) that people and devices actually use every day. You will also learn the port numbers every network professional is expected to know by heart.

docs.title: 4.1 TCP — Reliable Delivery
docs.text:
TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) is the set of rules that makes sure data sent between two programs arrives complete, in the right order and without duplicates. It sets up a 'connection' first, numbers every byte it sends, and resends anything that goes missing. Web pages, email and file downloads all rely on it.

A TCP connection from open to close. ACK numbers name the next byte expected; each direction is closed separately with its own FIN.

Think of it like…

TCP is like sending a book chapter by chapter by registered post: you agree with the receiver before you start, every envelope is numbered, the receiver signs for each one, and you resend any envelope that is not signed for.

Real-world example

When Priya opens her bank's website, her laptop sends a SYN to the server on port 443, the server replies SYN-ACK, and her laptop answers ACK — the 3-way handshake, taking one round trip. Her laptop starts its byte count at a random sequence number such as 1,000,000; after sending 1,460 bytes the server acknowledges 1,001,460, meaning 'I have everything up to here, send the next byte'. If one segment is lost, the server keeps acknowledging the same number, and Priya's laptop resends the missing piece. When she closes the tab, each side sends a FIN and an ACK to close its half of the conversation.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Handshake: client sends SYN, server replies SYN-ACK, client sends ACK — the connection is open.
  2. Each byte gets a sequence number; the receiver returns an acknowledgement (ACK) number saying which byte it expects next.
  3. The receiver advertises a window (how much buffer space it has free) so a fast sender cannot overwhelm it — this is flow control.
  4. If an ACK does not arrive before the retransmission timer expires, or duplicate ACKs show a gap, the sender retransmits.
  5. Closing: each side sends FIN and gets an ACK (4 messages); the side that closed first waits in TIME_WAIT before forgetting the connection.
  6. RST (reset) aborts a connection instantly, for example when a port is closed or something has gone wrong.

Who uses it

Every web browser, email client, SSH session, database connection and file download depends on TCP; network engineers and security analysts read TCP flags in packet captures every day.

Key takeaway

Memorise the handshake as SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK, the six classic flags (SYN, ACK, FIN, RST, PSH, URG), and that TCP is connection-oriented and reliable while UDP is not.

Going deeper

  • Initial sequence numbers are randomised (RFC 6528) so attackers cannot guess them and inject data or resets into someone else's connection.
  • Throughput is capped at window ÷ round-trip time: a 64 KB window over a 100 ms path cannot exceed about 5 Mbit/s, which is why window scaling matters on fast long links.
  • Common options: MSS, window scale (shift up to 14, windows up to 1 GiB), SACK-permitted and timestamps, which give accurate RTT samples and protect against wrapped sequence numbers (PAWS).
  • Nagle's algorithm bundles small writes while delayed ACKs wait up to about 200-500 ms; together they can add lag to chatty apps, so games and SSH set TCP_NODELAY.
  • Many sockets stuck in CLOSE_WAIT point to an application bug (it never calls close), whereas lots of TIME_WAIT is normal on busy clients and proxies.
  • Firewalls, load balancers and NAT devices track TCP state; a stateful firewall drops mid-stream packets for which it never saw a SYN, which shows up as asymmetric-routing faults.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking sequence numbers count segments; they count bytes, so an ACK of 2461 after starting at 1001 means 1,460 bytes arrived.
  • Believing TCP guarantees delivery to the application; it only retransmits while the connection lives, so apps must still handle resets and timeouts.
  • Confusing a reset with a timeout: RST ('connection refused') means the host answered with no listener; silence usually means a firewall dropped the SYN.

docs.title: Try it: List open TCP connections and their states (ESTABLISHED, TIME_WAIT...) on your own machine
docs.text:
netstat -an | findstr TCP      # Windows
ss -tan                        # Linux
curl -v https://example.com    # watch a TCP + TLS connection open

docs.title: Key protocols, devices, standards & tools
docs.text: Name What it does Example TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)IETF RFC 9293 (replaced RFC 793, 2022) · RFC · Layer 4 · Current Connection-oriented, reliable, ordered byte-stream transport between two programs, identified by IP addresses and port numbers. A browser downloading a 2 MB image over HTTPS receives every byte in order, even if some packets were lost on Wi-Fi. TCP headerIETF RFC 9293 · Concept · Layer 4 · Current 20 bytes minimum, up to 60 with options: ports, sequence and ACK numbers, data offset, flags, window, checksum, urgent pointer. A Linux SYN shows 'Header Length: 40 bytes' in Wireshark because MSS, SACK-permitted, timestamp and window-scale options were added. Three-way handshakeIETF RFC 9293 · Concept · Layer 4 SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK exchange that opens a TCP connection and synchronises both sides' starting sequence numbers. Wireshark shows a laptop's SYN to 93.184.215.14:443, the reply SYN-ACK, then the laptop's ACK before any HTTPS data flows. Sequence and acknowledgement numbersIETF RFC 9293 · Concept · Layer 4 32-bit counters numbering every byte sent; the ACK number tells the sender the next byte the receiver expects. Sender transmits bytes 5001-6460; receiver replies ACK 6461, confirming all 1,460 bytes arrived. TCP flags (SYN, ACK, FIN, RST, PSH, URG)IETF RFC 9293 (ECE/CWR added by RFC 3168) · Concept · Layer 4 One-bit control fields in the TCP header that mark segments as connection setup, acknowledgement, close, reset or urgent/push data. A firewall log full of SYNs with no ACKs from one source suggests a port scan or SYN flood. Receive window and flow controlIETF RFC 9293; window scaling RFC 7323 · Concept · Layer 4 The receiver advertises how many bytes it can buffer; the sender never has more unacknowledged data in flight than that. A busy phone advertises a zero window, so the server pauses sending until the app reads its buffer. Window scalingIETF RFC 7323 · Standard · Layer 4 · Current Option negotiated in the handshake that multiplies the 16-bit window field, allowing windows far above 64 KB for fast links. A 1 Gbit/s transatlantic transfer needs several megabytes in flight, which only works with window scaling enabled. Retransmission timeout (RTO)IETF RFC 6298 · Standard · Layer 4 · Current Timer calculated from measured round-trip times; if no ACK arrives before it expires, the segment is resent. On a 40 ms path the RTO might be about 200 ms; a lost segment is resent after that delay. Selective Acknowledgement (SACK)IETF RFC 2018 · Standard · Layer 4 · Current Option letting the receiver report exactly which blocks arrived, so only the missing pieces are resent. Segments 3 and 7 are lost out of 10; SACK lets the sender resend just those two. Four-way close (FIN/ACK)IETF RFC 9293 · Concept · Layer 4 Each direction is closed separately: FIN, ACK from one side, then FIN, ACK from the other. A web server finishes sending a page, sends FIN; the browser ACKs, then sends its own FIN when done. TCP state machineIETF RFC 9293 · Concept · Layer 4 · Current Eleven connection states: LISTEN, SYN-SENT, SYN-RECEIVED, ESTABLISHED, FIN-WAIT-1/2, CLOSE-WAIT, CLOSING, LAST-ACK, TIME-WAIT and CLOSED. 'ss -tan state close-wait' listing hundreds of sockets reveals an application that never closes its connections. TIME_WAITIETF RFC 9293 · Concept · Layer 4 State held by the side that closes first for twice the maximum segment lifetime, so late packets cannot confuse a new connection. A busy proxy shows thousands of TIME_WAIT entries in 'ss -tan'; Linux keeps each for 60 seconds. RST (reset)IETF RFC 9293 · Concept · Layer 4 Segment that immediately aborts a connection, commonly sent when nothing is listening on the requested port. Connecting to port 8080 on a server with no service running returns RST, shown as 'connection refused'. MSS option & clampingIETF RFC 9293; RFC 879 history · Concept · Layer 4 TCP option each side places in its SYN announcing the largest segment it accepts; routers can rewrite ('clamp') it to fit tunnels. A PPPoE router configured with 'ip tcp adjust-mss 1452' rewrites passing SYNs so sessions avoid fragmentation on its 1492-byte link. KeepaliveIETF RFC 9293 (optional feature) · Concept · Layer 4 Optional empty probes sent on an idle connection to check that the other end is still there. An SSH session probes every few minutes so a home router's NAT table does not silently drop it. SYN flood and SYN cookiesIETF RFC 4987 (Informational) · Concept · Layer 4 · Current Attackers send masses of SYNs to fill the half-open connection queue; SYN cookies encode state in the server's ISN so no memory is used. Linux enables net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies by default, keeping a web server answering during a spoofed-SYN flood.

docs.title: 4.2 UDP & When Speed Beats Reliability
docs.text:
UDP (User Datagram Protocol) sends independent messages called datagrams with no handshake, no numbering and no resending. It just adds port numbers and an optional error check to the data and fires it off. That makes it fast and lightweight, perfect when late data is useless anyway.

TCP vs UDP

TCP UDP Connection setup 3-way handshake None Reliability ACKs and retransmission Best effort Ordering Byte stream, in order Datagrams, any order Header size 20-60 bytes 8 bytes Flow / congestion control Yes No (app's job) Broadcast / multicast No Yes Typical uses Web, email, SSH, files DNS, VoIP, games, QUIC

UDP trades every guarantee for speed and simplicity; applications add back only what they need.

Think of it like…

UDP is like shouting updates across a busy room or dropping postcards in a postbox: quick and cheap, but if one gets lost nobody automatically sends it again.

Real-world example

In a video call between Tom in London and Ana in Lisbon, each audio packet carries 20 ms of sound. If one packet is lost, waiting 100 ms for a resend would make the voice stutter, so the app simply skips or smooths over the gap. The same is true for DNS: a lookup is one small question and one small answer, so setting up a whole TCP connection would double the delay. UDP's header is only 8 bytes, compared with at least 20 for TCP.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The app hands UDP a message and the destination IP and port.
  2. UDP adds an 8-byte header: source port, destination port, length and checksum.
  3. The datagram is sent immediately — no handshake, no connection state.
  4. The receiver checks the checksum and passes the datagram to the program listening on that port, or drops it if corrupted.
  5. Any reliability, ordering or rate control needed is built by the application itself (as QUIC, DNS and RTP do).

Who uses it

Online gamers, VoIP and video-call users, live streamers, DNS and DHCP servers, and IoT sensors all depend on UDP.

Key takeaway

Exam favourite: UDP is connectionless, unreliable (best-effort), has no flow or congestion control, and uses an 8-byte header; TCP is connection-oriented and reliable.

Going deeper

  • The checksum covers a pseudo-header containing the IP addresses, protocol and length, so a datagram delivered to the wrong host is detected; it is optional in IPv4 but mandatory in IPv6.
  • A UDP datagram can carry up to 65,507 bytes over IPv4, but anything above the path MTU (about 1,472 bytes of data on Ethernet) fragments, so DNS now aims for answers under 1,232 bytes.
  • Applications rebuild only the features they need: RTP adds sequence numbers and timestamps, TFTP waits for an ACK per block, and QUIC rebuilds full reliability and congestion control.
  • Amplification factors reported by US-CERT range from about 28-54x for DNS to 556x for NTP 'monlist' and up to 51,000x for exposed memcached servers.
  • Firewalls and NAT treat UDP flows as pseudo-connections with idle timers of seconds to minutes, so long-lived UDP apps send keepalives to hold their mappings open.
  • Scanning UDP is slow and ambiguous: closed ports answer ICMP Port Unreachable (often rate-limited) while open ports frequently stay silent, so nmap reports 'open|filtered'.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Calling UDP 'bad because unreliable'; for live voice, games and DNS, avoiding retransmission delay is exactly the right design choice.
  • Assuming DNS uses only UDP; large answers, DNSSEC and zone transfers use TCP 53, so firewalls must allow both.
  • Building a UDP app with no rate control; without congestion control it can flood links and hurt everyone sharing the network.

docs.title: Try it: Send a DNS query over UDP and see the open UDP sockets on your machine
